guide.what_it_is_for: The public website is where a stranger first learns what AGI Workforce does, sees the apps and prices, and decides to sign up, download, or ask for a sales conversation. It also holds the public directories (integrations, plugins, skills, templates), the status page, help and legal pages, and shared-content previews. Signed-in visitors who open a product page are sent into the product instead of the sales page.
guide.who_uses_it: Every visitor, signed in or not. Signed-out visitors see marketing pages and directories. Signed-in visitors hitting a product route are rewritten into the product (apps/web/proxy.ts:124-134). Prospects use the Enterprise and partner forms. Operators read stored waitlist rows (apps/web/features/admin/services/operator-waitlist.ts:13). Paid-plan purchase is gated, so buyers depend on checkout being enabled.

how_it_works.detail: The request first passes the web proxy. For a marketing route that has a product behind it, a signed-in visitor (session cookie present) gets a rewrite to the product page. A signed-out visitor keeps the marketing page.

how_it_works.step: Identity provider mounted only where needed
how_it_works.detail: The client boundary checks the path. Only product, auth, and a fixed list of public prefixes (pricing, plugins, skills, gallery, connectors) load the browser identity provider.
Each page is a server component that builds its own metadata and content. Navigation items come from one shared nav file.

The pricing page reads the shared billing catalog. Checkout is a POST that first checks the checkout flag and the payment key, then rate limits, then checks the plan-change rule, then picks the price.

The dialog checks the required consent boxes, then calls the public waitlist client. The server records consent first, then inserts or updates one row keyed by email and source. A consent failure stores nothing.
The download page asks the release API which Mac builds exist and shows only those. The CLI install command points at the public install script, and the CLI update check reads the same install URL.
The status page runs checks on every request and shows the result. The plugin catalogue is read once per request from the published registry and cached.
The share page checks the token format, then reads the shared session. It returns not found for a bad token and hides expired shares.

guide.what_it_is_for: This area is how a person gets into their AGI Workforce account and is set up for first use. It covers signing in or creating an account on each app, proving an email address, recovering a lost password or second factor, accepting the Terms and passing an age check, and then the first-run setup (name, role, memory, apps, notifications, device pairing). It matters because nothing else works until a session exists, and the Terms, age and two-step checks decide whether an account may be used at all.
guide.who_uses_it: Every person before first use: new users creating an account, returning users signing in, users who lost a password or second factor, and users of organizations with enterprise single sign-on (organization sign-in). Workspace admins see the organization side only through the organization-domain check (apps/web/lib/services/organization-verified-domains.ts). Developer-class accounts are refused desktop sign-in grants (apps/web/app/api/auth/desktop/grant/route.ts:19-30 region). Guest use and plan selection are not built (see features 12).

features.name: Sign in to your account
features.use: Lets a person sign in on the web, desktop, mobile, CLI, VS Code extension or Chrome extension, and tells them when the account they typed does not exist or already exists.
how_people_use_it: Web: open the sign-in page, type the email, press continue, then type a password or enter an emailed code.
Desktop: choose sign-in; the system browser opens and the app receives the session when the browser finishes.
Mobile: tap sign in on the login screen (Clerk-based native flow).
CLI and VS Code: start the device or browser sign-in, then approve it in the browser and wait for the app to finish.
Chrome: the side panel opens the web sign-in page and returns the session.
how_it_should_work: Correct credentials create a session only after the account is allowed (access check at apps/web/app/login/complete/page.tsx:109 area) and Terms are current.
If the email has no account, the user is told and offered create-account instead. If an account exists during sign-up, the user is told to sign in.
A session that already exists in the browser sends the user to the completion page instead of failing.
Failure shows a classified message; rate-limit style notices show a retry wait.
features.on_each_app: Web: done (email code, password, passkey, social, enterprise SSO through the first-factor step). Desktop: done, via the system browser handoff, plus an embedded sign-in page. Mobile: done, native Clerk sign-in with a signed-out gate until Terms are accepted. CLI: done, device-style OAuth polling. VS Code: done, device authentication. Chrome: done, through the web sign-in page.

features.name: Create an account and confirm your email
features.use: New people create an account with an email and password, then prove the address with a code before the account is usable.
how_people_use_it: Open the sign-up page (apps/web/app/signup/page.tsx:43), type email and password.
Enter the six-digit style emailed code on the code step, or tap resend.
Browsers and password managers may autofill the one-time code.
how_it_should_work: The sign-up is not finished until the address is verified; an unverified address leads to the code step (IdentityAuthAdapter resolveSignUpState, apps/web/features/auth/IdentityAuthAdapter.tsx:436).
If the account is created but the address cannot be confirmed or the code cannot be sent, the user is told the account exists and to contact support; they are not signed in.
Resend is offered on the code step. Sign-up fields the page cannot collect produce a message to contact support.
Mobile verification is not confirmed by the brief.
features.on_each_app: Web: done (sign-up page and code step). Desktop: done (embedded through the same web flow). Mobile: create-account is handled in the native Clerk login screen; email verification is unverified. CLI, VS Code and Chrome: create-account happens on the web sign-up page and the app waits for the browser.

features.name: Email sign-in by magic link
features.use: Would let a person click an emailed link to sign in with no code. Not built.
how_people_use_it: Not available on any app. People sign in with a typed code or a password instead.
how_it_should_work: Per brief: clicking the emailed link signs the person in and shows a confirmation. Nothing in the reviewed code implements a link-based flow; the email factor is a typed code (IdentityAuthAdapter.tsx SECOND_FACTOR_KINDS and sendSignInEmailCode).
features.on_each_app: Missing on web, desktop, mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome.

features.name: Password reset
features.use: Lets a person who forgot a password request a reset code by email, then set a new password and be signed in.
how_people_use_it: On the password step, choose forgot password, enter the email, then enter the code sent to it.
On the new-password step, type a new password and submit; the session starts.
how_it_should_work: A reset code is sent to the email address. After the code is verified, the new-password step appears (AuthNewPasswordStep.tsx) and the account is signed in on success.
Errors from the identity provider are classified (apps/web/lib/auth/error-taxonomy.ts).
features.on_each_app: Web: done. Desktop: done (same web flow). Mobile: unverified in the brief; the native Clerk flow was not opened for reset.

features.name: Social and work sign-in
features.use: Sign in with Google, GitHub, Microsoft or Apple, start enterprise single sign-on, route a work email to its organization sign-in, and link or unlink extra sign-in methods on an existing account.
how_people_use_it: Click a provider button on the sign-in or sign-up page (AuthProviderButtons.tsx).
Type a work email; the page checks the domain and, if the organization uses single sign-on, the user is sent to its sign-in.
In Settings > Security, use Sign-in methods to link another provider or unlink one.
how_it_should_work: Provider sign-in completes and returns to the surface. Enterprise connections outrank personal sign-in on the same address (IdentityAuthAdapter.tsx comment near ENTERPRISE_SSO_STRATEGY).
On Electron the enterprise sign-in opens the system browser and waits for a handoff (browserSignIn.ts, startBrowserSignIn).
A provider return that fails shows its error; a transferable one is finished by the callback.
Unlinking should not remove the last way to sign in; that rule was not verified in code.
features.on_each_app: Web: done for social, enterprise and linking (linking lives in Settings). Desktop: done for social and enterprise through browser handoff; linking in Settings. Mobile: social and enterprise unverified; account linking missing. CLI, VS Code and Chrome: the sign-in provider runs on the web page, not in the app.

features.name: Passkey sign-in and passkey setup
features.use: Lets a person register a passkey (a device-bound login key) and sign in with it instead of a password or code.
how_people_use_it: Settings > Security > Passkeys: add a passkey, see it in the list, rename or remove it.
On the sign-in method picker, choose passkey (AuthMethodPicker.tsx:15).
how_it_should_work: A signed-in user can add, list, rename and remove passkeys. Removal is an action a user cannot undo, so it should ask first (repo rule AGENTS.md section 9); the code path for that confirmation was not verified.
Passkey sign-in is offered as a first factor when the account has one.
features.on_each_app: Web: done for both. Desktop: passkey enrolment unverified; passkey sign-in unverified. Mobile: passkey sign-in unverified.

features.name: Two-step sign-in and recovery codes
features.use: Lets a person turn on an authenticator app as a second factor, be challenged for it at sign-in, get one-time recovery codes, and recover an account that lost its password, email or second factor.
how_people_use_it: Settings > Security > Two-factor: scan the QR code or type the setup key, enter the six-digit code to confirm, then save the backup codes (copy, print or download).
At sign-in, after the password or code, enter the authenticator code or pick an alternative such as a backup code.
Lost access: open the recovery page (apps/web/app/recover/page.tsx) and follow the recovery steps; a support ticket may be opened.
how_it_should_work: Enrolment is rejected with a clear message if the identity provider refuses it; nothing changes in that case (verify/route.ts registerSignInFactor).

how_it_works.detail: The person opens the sign-in page on web. The Next.js route renders the auth entry screen. On desktop the system browser can be used instead of the in-app form.

how_it_works.step: Identity client chooses the next step
how_it_works.detail: A client hook wraps the Clerk sign-in and sign-up objects. It decides, from the vendor state, whether to ask for a password, a second factor, a code, a new password, or to start enterprise sign-in. Errors are classified into messages or notices.

Enterprise sign-in on the desktop opens the system browser with a random challenge. The app keeps the verifier in memory for 10 minutes. When the browser finishes, a desktop grant route issues a one-time code tied to the challenge.

When the account has an authenticator, the second factor is challenged before a session is issued. Enrolment writes the authenticator secret and backup codes to the identity provider. Enrolment is refused unless the authenticator path is enabled.

After sign-in the completion page checks account access and Terms standing. Accounts with no acceptance are shown the gate. Mobile reads the age-gate state from local storage and blocks routes until confirmed.
Once signed in, the user can link or unlink sign-in methods and manage passkeys from the security section of settings.
The wizard collects the preferred name, work description and use case. The name and work description are saved as a general preference namespace and the use case is dropped before saving.

how_it_works.step: Device pairing for the phone and extension
how_it_works.detail: Desktop shows a pairing code or QR. The phone or extension submits it. The desktop dispatcher checks the code and binds the pairing to the account.

key_files.role: Central client logic for every web sign-in and sign-up step: password, email code, second factor, enterprise SSO, provider return, and error mapping.
The step-by-step sign-in and sign-up screens that the adapter drives (email step, code step, password step, new password step).
Post-sign-in gate: account access check and the Terms acceptance screen before the session is used.
Terms version constants, standing rules (never accepted, current, notice, superseded) and the server read of an account's standing.
Server route that enrols an authenticator second factor and registers backup codes with the identity provider.
Desktop side of browser sign-in: builds the challenge, keeps the pending verifier for 10 minutes and opens the system browser.
Issues the one-time sign-in grant to the desktop after the browser sign-in completes; refuses developer-class accounts.
The web onboarding wizard for name, work description, use case and first-chat start.
Saves onboarding answers to the account preference store and drops the one-time use-case answer.
Decides where a mobile user goes on launch: auth, onboarding, age gate or the app, based on sign-in, onboarding and age state.
Mobile age-gate rule: the time-zone based age threshold and the stored confirmation record.
Mobile Terms state (checking, required, accepting, accepted) read from the Terms API.
Decides whether an account has a second factor enrolled, with a cache and a fail-closed rule when the identity lookup fails.

data_kept.what: Sign-in session and identity records (accounts, passwords, passkeys, second factors, social links)
data_kept.where: The sign-in vendor (Clerk), not the repo. Accessed through the identity provider calls in apps/web/app/api/settings/2fa/verify/route.ts.

data_kept.what: Authenticator secret and backup codes
data_kept.where: Sent to the identity provider with registerSecondFactor (apps/web/app/api/settings/2fa/verify/route.ts registerSignInFactor). Enrolment cache of second-factor state in the key-value store (apps/web/lib/mfa-policy-gate.ts).

data_kept.what: Terms acceptance record (version, time, surface)
data_kept.where: Recorded per account through recordTermsAcceptance in apps/web/lib/server/terms.ts; read by readTermsStanding. Storage table not opened.

data_kept.what: Desktop pending browser sign-in verifier and challenge
data_kept.where: Process memory in the desktop main process (apps/desktop/electron/browserSignIn.ts:14). Lost on app restart; expires after 10 minutes.

data_kept.what: Age-gate confirmation record (confirmed, minor flag, time, region, threshold)
data_kept.where: Device storage on mobile, MMKV key age-gate:v1 (apps/mobile/src/features/auth/services/ageGate.ts).

data_kept.what: Onboarding preferences (preferred name, work description)
data_kept.where: Account preference store, general namespace (apps/web/features/onboarding/lib/onboarding-preferences.ts). Store backend not opened.

data_kept.what: Mobile Terms state
data_kept.where: Client state store (apps/mobile/src/features/auth/store/termsAcceptanceStore.ts). Persistence not verified.

switches.name: MIN_REQUIRED_TERMS_VERSION
switches.effect: Null means no Terms revision is binding. Setting a version makes older accounts re-prompt after the effective date.

switches.name: MIN_REQUIRED_TERMS_EFFECTIVE_AT
switches.effect: Date a binding Terms revision starts to block accounts still on an older version.

switches.name: MATERIAL_TERMS_GRACE_DAYS
switches.effect: Days between a material Terms change and its binding date (30).

switches.name: mfaEmailFallback option
switches.effect: When true, the email code counts as a second factor. Default false, so email is not offered as a second factor.

switches.name: Enterprise SSO strategy
switches.effect: When the account has an enterprise connection for the address, that connection is used first and personal factors are skipped.

switches.name: Desktop browser sign-in availability
switches.effect: If the host bridge does not support browser sign-in, the user is told to update the app.

switches.name: Age rule by time zone
switches.effect: Region rule sets the age threshold (18 in Brazil and India, otherwise the account minimum).

switches.name: Developer-class accounts
switches.effect: Desktop sign-in grant is refused for developer-class accounts.

switches.name: Rate limits on second-factor verify and desktop grant
switches.effect: Requests over the limit are refused.

guide.shared_code: Shared: the web auth screens (apps/web/features/auth) are used by the web app and, embedded, by the desktop window (AuthLayout embedded flag in apps/web/app/login/complete/page.tsx). Shared client helpers for sign-in provider names are in packages/client/client-runtime/src/authProviders.ts. Error classification is in apps/web/lib/auth/error-taxonomy.ts. Terms and standing logic are server-side in apps/web/lib/server/terms.ts. Separate per app: mobile uses its own native Clerk integration (apps/mobile/src/integrations/clerk.ts) and its own age gate, Terms store and routing; the CLI has its own Rust OAuth and onboarding (apps/cli/src/oauth.rs, apps/cli/src/onboarding.rs); the VS Code extension has its own device authentication (apps/extension-vscode/src/features/account-auth/deviceAuth.ts); the Chrome extension has its own pairing and side panel (apps/extension/src/side_panel.ts, apps/extension/src/features/native-bridge/pairing.ts).

things_that_look_wrong.what: The brief's Chrome and API Terms item refers to TERMS_GATE_EXEMPT_SURFACES in auth-gate.ts and a patch file. Neither the constant nor auth-gate.ts appears in the repository source (search found it only in the audit notes). The 'mobile' exemption that item asks to remove cannot be located.
The brief says the use-case answer should tailor replies. The code deliberately drops it before saving and uses it only for the first-chat starter prompts. This contradicts the S3.23 'Should'.
The age-gate region rule uses the device time zone, not a verified country or birth date. A traveller or a device with a different time zone gets the wrong threshold.

Mobile Terms state is set through the mobile terms store, but the brief's own unfinished note says mobile sign-in hard-blocks every revision unless the standing check is used. The check in the store reads strict 'current' rather than the standing function.
Magic-link confirmation (S3.05) has no code in any app; the email factor is a typed code only.

not_sure: Nothing was run. This was a read-only code reading. No tests, builds or servers were started, as the task required.
The full Terms-acceptance write path (/api/terms/accept), the database table behind recordTermsAcceptance, and whether its GET reports the standing or the strict current version were not opened.

The mobile sign-in screen (apps/mobile/app/(auth)/login.tsx) and its Clerk integration (apps/mobile/src/integrations/clerk.ts) were listed in the brief but not opened, so mobile social, passkey and reset claims come from the brief only.

guide.area: Application shell and navigation components (brief area 5, items S5.01 to S5.39)
guide.what_it_is_for: The shell is the frame around every screen: the header, the left navigation with recent chats, projects and tasks, the search and new-chat controls, and the menus for account, help and upgrade. It lets a person find an old conversation, start a new one, or jump to any part of the product in a few taps or keystrokes. It also tells the person when something is running, when a reply is waiting for them, and when the connection is lost.

The web shell builds navigation for signed-in users only (apps/web/shared/components/layout/app-nav-items.ts:85-88 says every signed-in surface shows the rail except entries marked adminOnly). The notification bell returns nothing when the person is not signed in (apps/web/features/notifications/components/NotificationBell.tsx:85-89). how_it_works.step: Pick the layout for the screen size
how_it_works.detail: The web shell reads the window width and height and chooses compact, tablet or regular, and the sidebar mode drawer, rail or persistent. The first paint assumes a desktop window so a wide page does not flash a mobile header. Resize and orientation events update the choice.

The shell loads conversations and projects through hooks. Each conversation is turned into a sidebar row. The row gets extra marks: running (the chat store says it is loading or streaming), needs-you, and task (work mode).
code: apps/web/shared/components/layout/WebAppShell.tsx:262-300 region (useConversations, useManagedCloudProjects, useChatStore reads; sidebarSessions useMemo)

how_it_works.detail: One shared list defines the rail items in order. Chat cannot be hidden. Each item has a label, an icon, an href and an isActive test. A destination can carry a feature key or a health-space requirement.

how_it_works.step: Render the sidebar in the right place
how_it_works.detail: On regular screens the sidebar is always on the left. On a tablet in portrait it is a rail. On a phone the sidebar is put inside a sheet that slides from the left and is made inert behind it. The shell passes the same set of handler props to each copy.

The shared sidebar component draws the header (collapse, new chat, search), the rail buttons, the projects section, the Recents heading with its organize menu, and the list of rows. Rows are grouped by date using the temporal helper.

how_it_works.step: Draw each row and its menu
how_it_works.detail: Each row shows status dots, the title and the unread dot. The overflow menu holds the row actions. Rename is done in place. A click opens the chat unless a modifier key is held.
The collapsed flag is kept in a shared store. Only that one flag is written to browser storage. The store is named agi-ui-store.

The notification bell reads the feed for the signed-in person. The offline indicator subscribes to the sync manager and shows when offline, syncing, queued, or in error. It is mounted once for the whole app.

A link to a chat, project or task goes to the open route. It checks the target and id, then needs a signed-in user. It asks the resolver where to send the person. If the item is ready, it redirects there. If not, it shows the unavailable screen inside the shell.
The menu shows Upgrade only for eligible users. Paid checkout stays behind the waitlist until the environment value or the run-time flag opens it, or the person redeems an access code.

key_files.role: The shared navigation sidebar used by web and desktop: header, rail, projects, Recents, date groups, organize menu and the list of rows.

The one ordered list of primary navigation destinations for the web app.
Shared UI store; keeps the sidebar collapsed flag in browser storage.
Status bar for offline, syncing, queued and error states, with Retry on error.
Notification bell, unread badge and popover list.
Shared-link route for chats, projects and tasks; redirects, shows not-found or unavailable.
Mobile drawer and route list; hides screens from the drawer and sets gesture rules.
Mobile tab group with the bottom tab bar turned off (tabBar returns null).
Account menu items: Upgrade entry, keyboard help and profile actions.

guide.area: Visual foundations and spacing conventions (brief area 6, S6.01 to S6.35)
guide.what_it_is_for: This area is the shared visual language: colours by role, one type scale, one spacing and radius set, one z-index (stacking) ladder, one motion set, and the light, dark, system, high-contrast and reduced-motion switches. A person gets a product that looks the same across apps, stays readable in every theme, and can be calmer or easier to read on their own terms. It matters because each value is named once, so a change lands everywhere and contrast can be checked against the named values.
guide.who_uses_it: Every user, on every app, as far as the code shows. The appearance controls I opened (web Appearance settings, mobile Appearance screen, CLI /theme and config keys, Chrome Options Appearance) have no plan gate and no admin gate in the files I read. Developers use the token files and the shared primitives. No paid-plan or workspace-admin rule was found.

how_it_should_work: Every surface paints from named tokens per theme. Components do not hold their own colour literals.

Text tokens must meet 4.5:1 on every surface they land on, and text is never dimmed with opacity. Stated in foundation.css comments and checked by apps/web/shared/components/__tests__/theme-contrast.test.ts (I did not run it).
Raised surfaces (cards, menus, dialogs) use an elevated token that differs from the page ground.
Accent has separate fill, text and on-fill roles.

guide.area: Basic interactive elements (brief area 8, items S8.01 to S8.50)
guide.what_it_is_for: These are the basic controls a person uses in every app: buttons, text fields, switches, checkboxes, menus, tabs, pickers, file upload areas, and the messages that tell a person something is loading, empty, failed or done. They make the apps usable with a mouse, touch, keyboard and screen reader in the same way. Most of them are shared building blocks, so one fix to a control can fix every screen that uses it.
guide.who_uses_it: Every user of every app, on every plan. These are generic UI parts, not a paid feature. The code read here shows no plan gate on the shared primitives. Which screens show a given control can depend on plan or role, but that was not checked.

Irreversible actions use the destructive (red) style. Its label must meet contrast on the red fill.
Icon-only buttons must have an accessible name.
While loading, the button is inert, reports busy to assistive tech, and says Loading, please wait to a screen reader.
Disabled buttons cannot be clicked and are dimmed.
Split buttons: should exist. Not built in any app (no component found).
Button groups should have a group label. Mobile tool approval rows do not (brief item S8.07 says partial).

how_it_works.detail: Screens import the shared Button from the UI package. The look comes from a class-variance table: default (primary fill), destructive (red), outline, secondary, ghost and link. Sizes are default, xs, sm, lg and icon.

how_it_works.step: Button renders with loading and disabled state
how_it_works.detail: The button is inert when disabled or loading. It sets aria-busy while loading and adds a screen-reader text Loading, please wait.

how_it_works.step: Mobile button uses a 44 point touch target
how_it_works.detail: On phones the button has a minimum touch area of 44 points. Small sizes get extra invisible padding (touch slop) to reach it. It is a native Pressable with the button role and a disabled state.

how_it_works.step: Segmented control handles keys and selection
how_it_works.detail: Each segment shows its selected state with aria-pressed. Left and Right arrows move the selection by one, and Home and End jump to the first and last segment.

how_it_works.step: Switch and checkbox wrap a headless library
how_it_works.detail: The web switch and checkbox are thin wrappers around a headless (unstyled, accessible) switch library. On mobile the switch is the native platform switch with an accessibility label.

guide.area: Modal and dialog inventory (brief area 10, items S10.01 to S10.48)
guide.what_it_is_for: Dialogs are the places where a person makes a choice that matters: naming or moving a chat, sharing a link, inviting a teammate, allowing the assistant to touch the computer, buying more usage, or deleting something. A good dialog says what will happen, names the item, asks before anything irreversible, and explains what to do next when a limit or error stops the action. This area is the shared set of those dialogs across the six apps, so the same action feels the same wherever the person is.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user meets the everyday dialogs (rename, archive, delete, share, upload, feedback, export, privacy). Workspace owners and admins use the team dialogs (invite, role change, transfer ownership). Paid or upgrading users reach the usage, credit and billing dialogs, and paid upgrades are currently gated behind a waitlist or access code (apps/web/lib/server/billing-waitlist-access.ts:22-60). Developers and terminal users reach the CLI and VS Code variants. Sensitive actions require a fresh identity check for any signed-in user (apps/web/features/auth/StepUpDialog.tsx:103).

how_it_works.step: Menu or button opens a dialog
how_it_works.detail: The person picks archive, delete, or another action in a row or chat menu. The web shell asks for a delete confirmation through the shared hook, after the menu closes.

useConfirmAction records which element had focus at the moment of the request, so focus returns there on cancel. It shows an alert dialog with the title, description and confirm label, and runs the action only on confirm.

how_it_works.step: Copy names the item and the consequence
how_it_works.detail: The delete copy names the chat or project and says what survives (generated media stays in the library; schedules are not named because they cannot be linked to a chat). Archive shows a toast with Undo and View archived.

The confirmed action calls the server. The brief places the delete request at the conversation route; the code comment says it stamps deleted_at on the conversation and does not erase it. Archive on mobile is a server write to the archived column and is limited to Cloud chats.

how_it_works.step: Sensitive actions need a fresh identity check
how_it_works.detail: For owner transfer and similar actions the page opens a step-up dialog (email code or passkey). The server route also calls requireStepUp before it changes anything, so the check cannot be skipped in the browser.

Paid upgrade and checkout paths first ask whether billing is open for this user. It is open if the forced environment switch is set or the run-time flag is on. Otherwise the user needs a redeemed beta record.
The desktop app asks once per capability and scope, records the answer, and joins any identical open question so the person does not see stacked dialogs.

The extension stores the sites the person allowed for browser control in extension storage, and checks both that stored consent and the browser's host permission before acting on a site. Account pages are always refused.
Editors register as dirty. Clicking an in-app link or closing the page is intercepted while any editor has unsaved edits, and the shared prompt offers keep editing or discard.

how_it_works.detail: The web app reads its appearance settings (text size, code wrap, accent, high contrast, motion, font) and writes them as attributes on the html element. CSS reads those attributes. Reduced motion is set as data-motion='reduced'. There is no option to force full motion.
The mobile hook reads the OS reduced-motion flag once, listens for changes, and keeps the last value while the async re-read runs so a new screen does not play a full animation.

how_it_works.step: Keyboard behaviour for menus and dialogs
how_it_works.detail: Shared hooks listen in the capture phase so their Escape and arrow handling runs before surrounding listeners. Menus move focus between items and return it to the trigger. Dialogs move focus in on open, keep Tab inside, and restore focus to the opener on close.

While a reply streams, a timer every 2 seconds takes the text that arrived since the last tick, cut at the last space, strips Markdown symbols, and writes it into a visually hidden polite live region. When streaming ends, the leftover tail is announced once. The message bubble wraps its body in this announcer.

The chart builds a plain-text summary from its data (lowest and highest points, pie shares). The summary is linked to the chart with aria-describedby in a visually hidden paragraph. A details disclosure holds the data as a table. The PNG download button has a name that includes the chart title.
The captions panel shows lines labelled You or Assistant with a waiting message when empty. It sets aria-live to off, so the transcript carries the spoken words and the panel does not repeat them.

how_it_works.step: Language start-up and direction on web
how_it_works.detail: The web app reads the language from a cookie or local storage before setup, then sets the language. When the language changes it sets the html lang and dir attributes from the language table, so right-to-left languages flip the page.

The mobile app picks a language from the device, or the stored preference (device or a language code). Right-to-left is applied to the native layout with a forced layout direction, which only takes effect when the value changes.

Amounts are stored as minor units (for example cents). The shared helper finds the currency's digits, divides, and formats with the device locale. A fallback prints two digits and the code if the currency is not recognised.
At start-up the CLI sets a global plain flag from the --plain option, the AGI_PLAIN environment variable, or screen reader mode. Colour helpers return no colour when plain mode or NO_COLOR is set.

guide.what_it_is_for: The new-chat screen is the first thing a person sees when they open the product. It shows an empty conversation with a ready message box, a greeting, and shortcuts to the common next steps: attach a file, pick a project, switch to search, research, image or video, start voice, or start a temporary chat. It matters because it decides how fast a person can start useful work and which mode and model their first message will use.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in person on the web, desktop, mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome surfaces, as the brief lists per app. Signed-out visitors reach a limited version on the web (guest chat) and on mobile onboarding. Some shortcuts depend on the plan or a capability, for example voice (canUseVoice), connectors (canUseConnectors) and organization workspaces. Workspace admins see organization names in the workspace line. Developers reach the same screen through deep links (web new-chat entry parameters).

features.use: Keeps a typed but unsent message so it comes back after navigating away or reloading.
how_people_use_it: Type a message, leave the page, come back: the text is still there.
Mobile: the draft is restored in the chat input when the screen returns.
how_it_should_work: Drafts are saved on the device per owner (web: browser local storage; mobile: chat input storage).
On reload, old draft owners are retired so stale drafts do not come back in other documents.
Sending or clearing the draft removes it.
CLI: not restored (missing).
features.on_each_app: Web: done. Desktop: done. Mobile: done. CLI: missing. VS Code: done (webview restore). Chrome: missing.

features.name: Guest use and sign-in prompt
features.use: Lets a signed-out visitor try the product within limits, then prompts them to sign in to lift the limits.
how_people_use_it: Web: open the chat as a visitor; guest chat is shown when the guest switch is on.
Mobile: onboarding and the chat screen prompt sign-in.
CLI: onboarding prompts sign-in.
how_it_should_work: Guest chat is off unless bot protection is ready (enforced or not on a hosted platform) and the guest.chat feature flag is on for the visitor's surface.
If the switch cannot be read, guest chat stays off and a warning is logged.
Guest spend is tracked per visitor (guest-chat:spend key prefix) and refused when over the limit.
Desktop: guest chat is declined; desktop requires sign-in.
features.on_each_app: Web: partial (switch is off by owner decision, per brief). Desktop: partial, declined by ruling (guest chat web-only). Mobile: done per brief (guest access in mobile chat and onboarding; the guest service itself was not opened). CLI: done per brief.

how_it_works.detail: The web route reads an x-agi-pathname header; the AGI work path switches the initial work mode to agiwork. It renders WebChatRoot with that mode. WebChatRoot loads the chat page client-only (no server rendering), finishes any sign-in handoff and applies the new-chat entry.

If the URL carries new-chat parameters (work mode, draft text), the hook writes them to the pending conversation in the chat store exactly once, then removes the parameters from the URL so a reload does not re-fill the draft.

The greeting picks a time-of-day headline. It uses the preferred name, then the account name, unless the person opted out. The opt-out is read from the general preference namespace and updates live when the preference is saved.

The workspace line reads the account's workspaces. It shows the organization name when the active scope is an organization, and 'Personal' otherwise. If the account has no organization workspace, it renders nothing.

The composer holds the draft, the mode toggles (work, image, video, temporary, search, research), the project choice and the model. The plus menu rows and the slash command list set these. Temporary chat is allowed only when the project policy allows it. Voice needs the voice capability.
Typed text is saved in browser local storage under an owner key, with the owner list kept in session storage. A reload retires previous owners so an old draft does not leak into a new document.

A signed-out visitor is allowed to chat only when bot protection is ready and the guest.chat flag is on for the web surface. The flag is read through the feature-flag service; a read failure turns guest chat off.

The mobile empty state shows a greeting from the display name, a 'How can I help you?' line and, when allowed, the connector suggestion list. Dismissing the pairing banner or the connector card stores a flag on the device.
The start panel loads up to three recent projects, three enabled and consented skills and three connected apps. Each source is skipped when the person is signed out or the call fails.
The side panel builds a page-snapshot attachment chip (page or selected text) with a refresh control. This is the only chip code found under the cited lines; no prompt suggestions were found there.

Builds the time-of-day greeting and decides whether a name can be shown.
The composer: draft, mode toggles, temporary chat policy, voice, dictation, project choice and slash command handling.
The plus menu rows: image, video, temporary chat, local folder and connectors.
Shared built-in slash command list (search, think, image and others) used by the web composer.
Stores unsent drafts in browser storage per owner, with retirement after reload.
Decides whether guest chat is available for a signed-out visitor.
Mobile new-chat empty state: greeting, pairing banner and connector suggestions.
Loads VS Code start-panel suggestions (projects, skills, connectors).

guide.area: Attachment intake components (brief area 014: attaching files, images, screenshots, pages and library items to a chat message)
guide.what_it_is_for: A person adds a file, picture, screenshot or web page to the message they are writing, sees it as a small chip, and the assistant reads it when the message is sent. Without this, the assistant cannot work with the user's own documents or what is on their screen. Each app offers the subset of ways to add context that fits that app, and every app tells the person when a file is refused, cut short or cannot be read.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user of the web app, the desktop shell (which runs the same web composer) and the phone app. Phone camera use is gated by a capability flag. Large files (above the 25 MiB inline limit) are offered only when the server says the plan allows them and the server switch CHAT_LARGE_FILES_ENABLED is on. Developers and local users of the CLI, VS Code extension and Chrome side panel use the local variants (paths, pages, pasted images). No admin-only path was found in this area.

features.name: Pick files from the device
features.use: Lets the person choose one or more files from their computer or phone and attach them to the next message.
how_people_use_it: Web and desktop: open the plus menu in the composer and choose Add photos and files, or use the paperclip-style control. Select several files in the system chooser.
Phone: tap the attach control, then the File card (cloud mode only) and choose one or more documents.
CLI: type /attach followed by a file path (image, PDF or Office file), or /files followed by text file paths.
VS Code: use the plus button, Attach workspace files, and pick files in the system dialog.
Chrome side panel: open the attach menu and choose Upload from device.
how_it_should_work: The chosen files appear as chips in the composer before sending. Several files in one pick are all handled, and a summary says what was added and what was refused.
Empty state: no chips, and the send button only sends the typed text.
Waiting state: each chip shows its upload phase (see the progress feature).
Failure: a refused file keeps its name and a reason; the others still attach.
Limits by plan: the server sends per-message file counts and sizes. Web and desktop read them from the billing store; phone photo picks use a per-plan selection count.
features.on_each_app: Web: plus-menu row and hidden file input, multi-select. Desktop: same as web (the desktop window shows the web composer). Phone: Photos card in both modes; File card only in cloud mode. CLI: /attach for image, PDF and Office files (one at a time per command); /files for text only. VS Code: workspace-file picker (folders cannot be chosen). Chrome: Upload from device. Multi-select works on web, desktop, phone, CLI (/files), VS Code (up to 8 per batch) and Chrome (picker).

features.name: Drag, drop and paste into the composer
features.use: Lets the person drop files onto the chat or paste a copied image straight into the message.
how_people_use_it: Web and desktop: drag files over the chat; a drop overlay appears; release to attach. Paste an image with the usual paste shortcut.
VS Code: drag files onto the composer card or paste into the message box.
Chrome side panel: drag files onto the composer or paste into the input.
CLI: press Ctrl+V to stage the image on the clipboard; text pastes are separate.
Phone: no drop. A Paste image card appears in the attach sheet when the clipboard holds an image.
how_it_should_work: A dropped or pasted file takes the same path as a picked file: same checks, same chip, same notices.
Only files are taken from a drop; a plain text paste stays text.
Failure: a clipboard that is empty or unreadable shows a short notice; the chat is not changed.
Desktop: a screenshot taken by the shortcut is put on the clipboard and pasted into the composer; if the composer is not ready, the image stays on the clipboard and the person is told to paste it.
features.on_each_app: Web: drop overlay (ChatComposerNew mount) and paste handler. Desktop: same as web, plus screenshot paste. Phone: no drag-and-drop (missing); a Paste image card for images (present in code although the brief says missing). CLI: Ctrl+V image paste only (paste of files is not shown). VS Code: drop on the composer card and paste into the textarea. Chrome: drop on the composer shell and paste into the input.

features.name: Take a photo with the camera
features.use: Lets a phone user take a picture and attach it straight away.
how_people_use_it: Phone: open the attach sheet and tap the Camera card. The first time, allow camera access when asked.
how_it_should_work: The Camera card is shown only when the camera capability is on for the account (useCapability canUseCamera).
If permission is refused, an alert offers Not now or Open Settings.
The photo is cleaned of location and camera details before it is accepted; a photo that cannot be cleaned is refused with a recovery message.
Failure: the camera cannot open, a short alert tells the person to try again.
Plan limit: the usual image size limit applies (see the upload contract).
features.on_each_app: Phone only. Web, desktop and Chrome: missing (brief agrees). The CLI and VS Code have no camera.

features.name: Choose photos from the photo library
features.use: Lets the person pick one or several existing photos and attach them.
how_people_use_it: Phone: open the attach sheet and tap Photos. Pick one or several photos in the system picker.
Web and desktop: choose Add photos and files and pick image files.
Chrome: Upload from device, pick images.
how_it_should_work: Phone picks keep the order the person chose and stop at the per-plan photo count.
Each photo has its location details removed before it is accepted.
Failure: if Photos cannot open, an alert says so; if a photo cannot be cleaned, the picker says what to do.
Empty state: the picker opens with no selection; nothing is attached.
features.on_each_app: Phone: Photos card (multi-select, plan-limited count). Web, desktop and Chrome: through the OS file chooser (images are accepted). CLI and VS Code: not applicable.

features.name: Screenshot and window capture
features.use: Lets the person capture the whole screen or one window and attach it to the next message.
how_people_use_it: Desktop: press the screenshot shortcut (or use the app menu or tray item) to capture the screen; press the window-capture shortcut to capture the window in front of the app.
Chrome side panel: open the attach menu and choose Take a screenshot (captures the visible tab).
Web: the brief says done; in code the captures found run through the desktop shell bridge.
how_it_should_work: Desktop: the app window hides for the capture, the image goes to the clipboard, is pasted into the composer, and the earlier clipboard text is put back.
If no screen or window can be captured, a notice says to check the Screen recording permission and relaunch.
Failure: if the composer is not ready, the image stays on the clipboard and the person is told to paste it.
Plan gates: not seen in this code path.
features.on_each_app: Desktop: keyboard shortcut, app menu and tray item; whole screen and single window. Chrome: visible tab only (Take a screenshot). Web: the composer has desktop-only rows (Attach clipboard, Use this computer); no plain-browser screenshot found. CLI, VS Code: missing.

features.name: Attach a web page by its link
features.use: Lets the person give a web address; the page text is fetched and added as context.
how_people_use_it: CLI: /attach followed by an https link.
VS Code: plus menu, Web page, type or paste the link in the input box.
Chrome side panel: attach menu, Link item, paste the link.
how_it_should_work: The page is read once when attached; its text goes into the conversation. HTML is turned into text.
The link must be http or https; other values are refused with a short message.
Failure: a bad status or a timeout shows Could not attach with the reason.
Limits: a body cap applies while reading the page.
features.on_each_app: CLI, VS Code and Chrome only (per the brief). The CLI runs a web fetch tool; VS Code fetches with a timeout; Chrome has a Link item.

features.name: Attach from the Library, a repository or a folder
features.use: Lets the person reuse a file already kept in the Library, or point the assistant at a repository or folder.
how_people_use_it: Web and desktop: plus menu, Add from library, pick an item (the list loads from the Library).
Phone: Attach sheet, Library section (cloud mode loads cloud Library items; local mode lists recent local files).
Code surface (web): the code composer attaches a repository.
CLI: @ followed by a folder name (for example @src/) inserts a listing of the folder's entry names.
VS Code: repository and folder attachment are reported as done in the brief.
how_it_should_work: A Library item becomes a normal attachment; it goes through the same checks as a new file.
Failure: if the Library list cannot load, the picker shows an error row.
Repository (code surface): the task uses the repository as context.
Folder: the CLI gives the model a listing of names, not the file contents (see things that look wrong).
features.on_each_app: Library: web, desktop, phone (not CLI, VS Code, Chrome). Repository: web code surface, desktop, CLI, VS Code per brief (not confirmed in code), phone and Chrome missing. Folder: CLI (listing only), VS Code per brief (not confirmed; the picker cannot choose folders).

features.name: Cloud drives, audio and video
features.use: Would let a person attach files from a cloud drive or attach audio and video. None of this exists yet.
how_people_use_it: Not available in any app. No cloud-drive picker exists. The accepted file types list has no audio or video types.
how_it_should_work: Should: a cloud-drive browser in the composer; audio and video files are accepted and the model receives them.
Today: such files are refused by the type check with a notice that names the file.
features.on_each_app: Missing on web, desktop, phone, CLI, VS Code and Chrome (brief status agrees with the code).

features.name: See, preview, remove and replace attachments
features.use: Lets the person see each attachment before sending, tell files apart, check it is ready, and take one out.
how_people_use_it: Web and desktop: images show a thumbnail; documents show an icon, name and size. Tap the small X on a chip to remove it.
Phone: thumbnails for images, file-type icons, names and sizes; tap the X to remove; tap an image to view it full screen.
CLI: /attach list shows what is staged; /attach remove N or /attach remove all removes items.
VS Code and Chrome: chips with an icon, name and size, and an X to remove.
how_it_should_work: A chip shows the name, a file-type icon for documents (PDF, spreadsheet, code, presentation, text, other) and the size.
A ready chip shows no progress text; the send button is available only when all chips are ready.
Removing a chip removes the file from the draft; a removed file is not sent.
Replacement (S14.29) is not built on any app: the person must remove and add again.
Preview (S14.30): phone images open full screen; no other app has a preview of documents or the full content of a file before sending.
features.on_each_app: Web/desktop: thumbnails, icons, name and size, remove; no preview, no replace. Phone: thumbnails, icons, name and size, remove, full-screen image view (preview for images only); no replace. CLI: staged list with name and size, remove; no thumbnails, no icons (missing), no replace or preview. VS Code: chips with icon, name, size and remove; no preview or replace. Chrome: chips for documents and thumbnails; name and size missing per brief; no preview or replace.

features.name: Upload progress, retry and cancel
features.use: Lets the person follow an upload, try again after a failure, and stop an upload that is still running.
how_people_use_it: Web: the chip shows Preparing, Uploading or Verifying under the file name; a failed chip shows an error and a Retry link.
Phone: a progress bar with a percentage on the chip; a Retry control on a failed chip; tap X during an upload to cancel it (the label says Cancel upload).
Desktop: same as web.
how_it_should_work: Preparing: the file is being cleaned or checked. Uploading: bytes are sent. Verifying: the server checks the file. Complete: the chip is ready.
Retry runs the upload again for that file (phone retries up to two more times with backoff; web retries the whole attempt).
Cancel stops the upload and removes the chip. On web, a large file already sent may be kept after a cancel and shown as a kept attachment.
Parsing progress (S14.20) is missing: there is no phase after upload that says the content is being read.
Failure: the chip shows a per-file error, and the send is held until the file is fixed or removed.
features.on_each_app: Web, desktop and phone have all four. CLI, VS Code and Chrome: not applicable here (the brief gives them no upload status). Parsing progress is missing on web, desktop and phone.

features.name: Limits, duplicates and refusals
features.use: Tells the person when a file was refused, cut short, locked, a duplicate, or when a batch was partly refused.
how_people_use_it: Add a file that is too big, an unsupported type, a locked PDF, or one already attached; the notice says which file and why.
Add several files; the notice lists how many were attached and names the refused ones.
how_it_should_work: Refused file: named with the reason (empty, too large for the plan, image too large, unsupported type, too many files, total over the message budget, already attached).
Batch: 'Attached N of M files' with the refused names, or 'None of the M files were attached'.
Duplicate: a file with the same name, size, date and type is not added twice and the notice says it is already attached.
Partial extraction: when text was cut to a size limit, the sent message records the name, and the message shows a notice.
Locked PDF: the notice says the file is password protected and to remove the password and upload it again.
Limits: inline per file 25 MiB, images 20 MiB, per message 25 MiB, 20 files (policy file); a plan can lower these.
features.on_each_app: Web, desktop: all six, with a batch summary. Phone: refusals in the attach flow, duplicate Alert, partial notice on messages, locked-PDF message (no batch summary found in the Alert path). CLI: /files reports added, already attached, truncated to budget and failed lines; /attach reports duplicate and unsupported type. VS Code: unsupported, too large (10 MB), truncated (40,000 characters) notices; no duplicate check and no batch summary. Chrome: unsupported and too-large notices; no duplicate check and no batch summary.

features.name: Retention and model fit
features.use: Explains how long attached files are kept, warns when the chosen model cannot read a file, and offers a fix; also covers indexing of knowledge files in a project.
how_people_use_it: Web and desktop: the plus menu shows a note under Add photos and files; a warning box appears above the composer when the model cannot read the file, with a button to switch to a model that can.
Phone: the attach sheet shows a retention note (cloud or temporary chat variant).
Project knowledge (web and desktop): the project files list shows indexing progress and a retry.
how_it_should_work: Retention note: saved to the Library until deleted; deleted files can be restored for 30 days (web). A temporary chat's files are kept out of the Library and deleted with the chat.
Model warning: appears before send when the selected model cannot read the attached type; the button switches to the automatic model or a capable one.
Alternative path: the warning names the fix (switch model, remove the file, or convert). CLI: attaching an image with a text-only model is refused with a switch-model instruction.
Indexing: the list polls while files are indexing; a failed index can be retried; a removed file is deleted.
features.on_each_app: Retention note: web, desktop, phone; Chrome has no per-file note (only a general privacy page); CLI and VS Code missing. Model warning: web and desktop; phone, CLI, VS Code, Chrome missing. Alternative path: web, desktop, phone, CLI; VS Code and Chrome missing. Indexing: web and desktop (project knowledge); phone missing.

how_it_works.step: 1. The person adds a file (pick, drop, paste, camera, capture or Library)
how_it_works.detail: On web and desktop the plus menu, the hidden file input and the drop overlay all call the same handler that adds files to the draft. A paste is first sorted into text or files before it reaches the handler.

how_it_works.step: 2. The draft checks each file in one place
how_it_works.detail: useAttachments.admitFiles checks, in order: duplicate, slot count, empty, size for the plan, supported type, image size, large-file offer, message budget. Each refused file gets one reason; the notice is built from all of them.

how_it_works.step: 3. Pictures get their location and camera details removed
how_it_works.detail: Files that carry picture metadata are cleaned before they are accepted. While this runs the draft shows a preparing state. A file that cannot be cleaned is refused with its own notice.

how_it_works.step: 4. The chip is drawn and can be removed
how_it_works.detail: Each accepted file gets an object URL for its thumbnail, then a chip with icon, name, size and upload status. Removing a chip revokes its URL and drops it from the draft.

how_it_works.step: 5. On send the files upload to private storage
how_it_works.detail: WebChatPage starts the upload for the message's files. The upload service prepares files and calls the managed-cloud client, which asks the server for an upload address, sends the bytes, then asks the server to complete. Phases are preparing, uploading, verifying, complete or failed.

how_it_works.step: 6. The server checks and stores the file
how_it_works.detail: The presign route issues the address. The complete route checks the owner, the type and the size, then the storage quota (not for temporary chats), malware scan, and the workspace data-loss check, then writes the file and creates the attachment record. Failed checks delete the uploaded copy.

how_it_works.step: 7. The server tells the client its limits
how_it_works.detail: For each plan the server computes the per-file, per-image and per-message limits. For a large-file offer it also computes the storage left and the inline budget. If the large-file check is not ready, the inline limits are sent instead.

how_it_works.step: 8. The chat request reads the attachments and drops what does not fit
how_it_works.detail: The chat request carries file parts that name an asset. The server looks up each asset, reads its text or pages within the turn budget, and records which files were cut short or left out.

how_it_works.step: 9. The client shows the partial-read notice
how_it_works.detail: The server sends the cut-short file names in a response header. The stream code stores them on the user message, and the message bubble shows a notice naming the files.

key_files.role: Web intake rules: duplicate, size, type, budget and refusal notices for each draft.
Web composer: wires the file input, drop, paste, Library and clipboard into the draft, and shows the model-fit warning.
The plus menu: Add photos and files, Add from library, desktop-only rows and the retention note.
Web chips: thumbnails, icons, name and size, upload phase labels, Retry and cancel-or-remove.
Web upload service: prepares files, runs the managed upload, keeps large-file sessions in browser storage.
Server: checks an upload is complete, scans and checks content, stores it and creates the attachment record.
Server: reads each attachment into the model request inside the turn budget and reports cut-short files.
Shared numbers: per-file, per-image and per-message sizes, file count, accepted types and large-file settings.
Phone attach sheet: Camera, Photos, Paste image, File and Library cards, with the retention note.
Phone chips: thumbnails, icons, progress bar, Retry, cancel and full-screen image view.
Desktop capture: screen and window capture, clipboard handoff, paste into the composer, clipboard restore.
CLI /attach, staged list, Ctrl+V image paste, image and document staging with model checks.
CLI /files reader: text-only, per-file and total character budgets, duplicate and failure reporting.
VS Code webview: drop, paste, file reading, chips and the attachment acknowledgement.
VS Code host: decodes files, applies the 10 MB and text limits, returns the acknowledgement.
Chrome side panel: attach menu, screenshot, link, upload, drop and paste intake and chips.

guide.what_it_is_for: The model selector is the control where a person sees which AI model will answer the next message, and picks a different one. It also decides which models the person may use on their plan, and says when an answer came from a different model than the one picked. Without it, people cannot choose between quick, strong or reasoning models, or know what each one costs in usage, so the choice of model becomes guesswork.
guide.who_uses_it: Every person who opens a chat in the Web, Desktop, Mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome surfaces. What each person may pick depends on the plan (read from the billing store on Web, and from the plan lock helpers on each surface). On Web, a Free plan person has the catalogue closed by an effect (apps/web/features/chat/components/Composer/ComposerFooter.tsx:1052-1056), so the catalogue is shown only for paid plans in that code path. Developers use the public model list route (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/models/route.ts) and the CLI flags. Workspace admins affect fast mode through a workspace block prop (ComposerFooter.tsx:845, 861). No separate admin screen was opened.

how_it_works.step: 1. Open the selector and read the current model
how_it_works.detail: The composer footer reads the selected model id and routing profile from the model store, and the thinking and effort settings from the thinking store. The catalogue, favourites and local model hooks are set up here. The trigger text is built from the local model, Auto, or the model's provider and description.
The full list comes from the model store's AVAILABLE_MODELS, built from the shared catalogue. The store's selectable-model helpers repair stale ids.

how_it_works.step: 3. Decide which models are locked for this person
how_it_works.detail: For each model the plan tier, availability state and environment decide the lock. A lock is a coming-soon, environment or plan lock. Plan locks get a label from the shared routing package. Free plan people get the free slot and a promoted model.

how_it_works.step: 4. Build the short list and rows
how_it_works.detail: A shared function builds the recommended list, the favourites, the lock state, the guidance text, capability keys, price band and family slot for each row. Limits are 4 recommended and 3 favourites.

Selecting a row checks for a local-model fork and for incompatibilities with the chat (images, tools, context). A blocking finding opens a confirm dialog. Otherwise the choice is recorded as recent and saved to the chat (if a chat exists) or set as the global choice.

how_it_works.step: 6. Store the choice and apply defaults
how_it_works.detail: The global selection is persisted to local storage under 'agi-model-store'. The default model preference is loaded from the server preference store and applied only to new chats. Favourites are saved to the server preference store, with a local fallback key.

how_it_works.step: 7. Send the turn with the chosen model
how_it_works.detail: The chosen model id travels with the message. The public chat route turns the request into a provider call and can substitute a model. The send path that reads the composer selection was not traced end to end in this read.
The footer reads the fallback reason from the last finished assistant message, and repeats it with the model name. The shared helper describes the reason in words.

guide.area: Assistant-message components (area 17): the answer bubble and its actions, across Web, Desktop, Mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome
guide.what_it_is_for: Every answer the assistant gives shows up as a message with its own set of tools around it. A person can see which model answered and what it cost, watch the answer arrive, see the tools and sources it used, and act on it: copy, read aloud, share, regenerate, continue, branch, rate, or report it. Failed, stopped and refused answers are shown as their own states with a next step, so the person is never left with an empty bubble.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in person who chats, on every app that has the chat. Some parts are gated: follow-up suggestion generation is metered by plan tier on the server (generate-follow-ups.ts:153-165), Continue is blocked with an upgrade prompt when the trial is used up (WebChatPage.tsx:6433-6440), and some actions are shown only when the app supports them (read aloud needs isReadAloudSupported). I did not find any workspace-admin-only control in this area.

how_it_works.step: 1. The answer is shown with its actions
how_it_works.detail: The chat list renders each message and passes the turn's state (streaming, stopped, refused, continuable, follow-up target) into the bubble. The bubble draws the answer text, the activity and sources, the files, and the action row. The action row holds Copy, the good and bad rating buttons, Show sources, Regenerate, and a more-actions menu with the time sent, read aloud, branch and report.
code: apps/web/features/chat/components/messages/ChatMessageList.tsx:1353-1356 (continue is offered only when the turn is not stopped and can continue)

how_it_works.step: 2. The person sends a message and the answer streams in
how_it_works.detail: The stream hook chooses the completion route for the selected model. Paid Cloud models go to the Cloud completion route. Models from the free offering go to the free-quota completions route. The hook writes the streamed text into the bubble as it arrives. A regenerate request sets a parent message id, so the new attempt is added as a sibling instead of replacing the old one.

how_it_works.step: 3. The working indicator shows until text arrives
how_it_works.detail: A typing indicator and a status label ('Generating response') are shown while the turn is running and before text arrives. The status is announced through the chat's live region.

how_it_works.step: 4. Follow-up suggestions are gated, fetched and cached
how_it_works.detail: The list decides whether to show follow-ups: the setting must be on, the answer must be finished and long enough, the request must be sendable, and either the default flag or a searched last turn must allow it. If a cached list is stored on the message, it is shown. Otherwise the hook calls the follow-ups route. The route returns the cache, or generates new questions on the server with a quota reservation and saves them into the message's metadata.

how_it_works.step: 5. Copy and share use plain text
how_it_works.detail: Copy takes the answer text with rich blocks turned into plain text, writes it to the clipboard, shows a check mark for two seconds, and shows a toast. Share uses the system share sheet when it exists and falls back to copying.

how_it_works.step: 6. Read aloud calls the speech route
how_it_works.detail: The read-aloud hook asks the server for speech in chunks and plays it in the browser. Only one playback runs at a time, and a stop control ends it.

how_it_works.step: 7. Regenerate, continue and retry run through the page
how_it_works.detail: The chat page handles regenerate (same model or a chosen model), last-answer regenerate, and continue. Continue checks the trial and opens the upgrade dialog when it is used up. Each one calls the same stream hook as a new send.

how_it_works.step: 8. Ratings and reports are sent to the server
how_it_works.detail: A rating posts to the feedback route with a context tag of response rating, tied to the message. Removing a rating deletes that row. A report posts to the content-report route. The feedback route inserts a row into the feedback table.
code: apps/web/app/api/feedback/route.ts:37-44 (insert and delete SQL on public.feedback)

how_it_works.step: 9. Mobile runs the same ideas in its own store
how_it_works.detail: On mobile, the bubble draws its own action row (copy, read aloud, regenerate, more). Follow-up suggestions are shown in a footer that appears when there is a follow-up target and the composer is empty. Suggestions are saved into the message's metadata in the mobile chat store.

how_it_works.step: 10. CLI and extensions render the same states in their own code
how_it_works.detail: The CLI prints an answer, then a sources footer, and its terminal UI handles copy and states. The VS Code webview and the Chrome side panel build their own answer bubbles, sources list and error states from their own code. Nothing in these surfaces is shared with the web bubble.

Web stream hook: sends the turn to the chosen completion route and writes streamed text into the answer.
Server side of follow-up suggestions: builds the prompt, reserves the quota and calls the model.

guide.area: Streaming and response-presentation states (brief area 19, 29 items)
guide.what_it_is_for: This area is what a person sees between pressing send and getting a finished answer. It shows that the request was accepted, what the assistant is doing right now (searching, running code, calling a connected service, waiting for approval or for an answer), how the text arrives, and how the turn ends: completed, partly completed, stopped, or failed with a reason and a next step. It matters because a turn can take a long time or fail for many reasons, and a person who cannot tell waiting from hanging, or a stop from a crash, will retry, duplicate work or give up.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in chat user on every app (Web, Desktop, Mobile, CLI, VS Code extension, Chrome extension) sees these states. Managed Cloud runs (the paid, server-run turns) add the durable-run states (reconnecting, stopping the Cloud task, resuming, Cloud task waiting for approval or input). Local and own-key turns use the in-app streaming path. Plan limits decide which limit notices a user can hit (free allowance, plan restriction, usage limit). Workspace administrators affect the workspace-policy notice. Developers and QA use the CLI and the server endpoint directly; the brief marks the API status done, but the server endpoint was only partly read.

Cancel or edit a queued follow-up from its controls (VS Code queued controls, Chrome queued list).

A queued follow-up shows a Queued label and a count when more than one is waiting; it sends when the running turn ends.
Empty state: a waiting animation with the text Preparing (web) or Generating response (mobile). The text does not yet say which context is being read; only the CLI says Preparing context.
Failure: a queued follow-up that cannot be sent is kept with a failed marker on mobile (queueFailed); it is not dropped silently.

how_it_works.detail: On web, the user message and an empty assistant row are added synchronously before the first network await, so the turn appears in the same frame as the click. The turn's start time is set one millisecond after the user message to keep their order.

If a turn is already running, a new message is kept in a queue held in the composer's React state, and the send button shows a Queued chip with a count. Mobile keeps a similar list in its chat input and marks queued bubbles as queued offline.

how_it_works.step: Show preparing and waiting for the first token
how_it_works.detail: While loading with no streaming row yet, the list shows a Preparing indicator. A waiting ticker starts after the request is sent and writes a waiting summary with a model name and elapsed time into the activity record until the first real event arrives.

how_it_works.step: Receive events and update the activity record
how_it_works.detail: Each server event (text, reasoning, tool start and result, native search, pause, stop) updates the message's agent activity. Native web search gets a synthetic row that yields to a real row once one arrives. The activity timeline turns the record into a one-line summary and an announcement.

how_it_works.step: Pause for approval or an answer
how_it_works.detail: A pause sets the activity status to awaiting approval or paused with an input request. The approval card offers Approve and deny choices, and the screen announces the pause once.

The stop button (send mode stop) aborts the local stream and stamps the turn as stopped with the text kept. For a Cloud run, the app shows Stopping the Cloud task, sends a cancel, then polls the run once a second for up to 30 checks until it reaches a terminal state; if not confirmed, an error toast appears.

how_it_works.step: Reconnect and resume a Cloud run
how_it_works.detail: If the stream drops, the app marks the answer Reconnecting, then re-follows the durable run from the last sequence it saw, polling every 2.5 seconds, and clears the mark on the first event back.

how_it_works.step: Finish the turn and store its state
how_it_works.detail: When the stream settles, the app writes the final finish reason (stop, length, stopped or error), the stream error, and the activity summary onto the message, then saves the assistant message. A stopped run is saved through a separate path on the server.

A notice resolver decides which single notice owns the last message: continue, stop, provider failure, refusal, or the fallback for an unusable turn. The error code is mapped to a cause, which gives the sentence; a provider wait is added only when the provider stated one; a reference id is appended when the server logged one. A user message with no reply counts as incomplete only after 45 seconds.

The server route builds the tool list (connectors, operator tools, a gated search tool when approval is needed), runs durable streams with a first-event budget, and cancels the run when the client cancels. Only the first part of this route was read; the streaming and error code paths were not fully traced.

Also the stop action (around lines 5408-5455) and the Cloud stop confirmation call.
Sends a cancel for a Cloud run and polls until a terminal state (up to 30 checks, 1 second apart).

guide.area: Markdown and text rendering (Area 20): how assistant and user answers are drawn as formatted text across the six apps
guide.what_it_is_for: Answers from the assistant arrive as Markdown, a plain-text format with symbols for headings, lists, bold, links, tables and code. This area turns that text into the formatted page a person reads, so headings, lists, tables, code and maths look right instead of showing raw symbols. It also keeps the text safe: raw HTML and unsafe links must not run or open dangerously. It works while the answer is still streaming in, so the reader sees formatted text growing rather than raw symbols until the end.
guide.who_uses_it: Every user of every app who reads an answer, and every user who sends a message (user messages use the same renderer, but raw HTML in them is shown as plain text, MessageBubble.tsx:2900). The code shows no plan gate on rendering. Table copy and download are plain UI actions with no plan check seen. Developers change the renderer. Workspace admins and paid plans are not involved in this area as far as the code shows.

features.name: Text formatting

how_it_works.step: Pick the renderer for the message
how_it_works.detail: The web message bubble decides what to draw. It streams the answer through StreamingMarkdownContent while it arrives, and uses MarkdownContent once finished. User messages are told to show raw HTML as text.
While an answer streams, settled blocks are split off and drawn once. The unfinished tail is completed so an open bold, link or table still draws correctly.
Math delimiters are normalised, single-line display maths is lifted onto its own lines, citation markers and answer badges are linked, and task-list labels are restored.

The Markdown is parsed with GFM (tables, task lists, strikethrough), maths, line breaks, a lossless-table guard and an assistant-fence identity step. User messages use a version that turns raw HTML into text.
Raw HTML is passed through, then cleaned by an allow-list. Maths is typeset by KaTeX last.
Each Markdown element is mapped to a React component: headings, lists, tables, links, images and code blocks. Links and images pass through safety checks and the citation logic.
A table is wrapped with its copy, download and expand buttons. Copy reads the table cells and writes tab-separated text. Download builds a CSV and saves it as table.csv.
Find walks the message text nodes and sets browser highlights. Export converts the Markdown into a document model, then builds a PDF or DOCX file.

key_files.role: Main renderer shared by web and desktop: maps each Markdown element to a component and runs the sanitiser and maths.
Draws an answer while it streams: settled blocks once, the unfinished tail again each time.
Lists the parser plugins (GFM, maths, breaks, lossless tables) and the literal-HTML variant used for user messages.
The allow-list that decides which HTML tags, attributes and URL protocols survive.
Table wrapper with copy (tab-separated), download (CSV) and full-screen expand.
Closes open bold, links, code and fences in the streaming tail so partial text draws correctly.
Maths parser for the markdown-it renderers used by the VS Code and Chrome extensions.
Mobile renderer: headings, lists, tables with sort and copy, footnotes, right-to-left, fences and maths.
Terminal renderer for the CLI: pulldown-cmark events turned into coloured terminal lines.
VS Code sidebar renderer using markdown-it with raw HTML turned off.
Chrome side-panel renderer using markdown-it, footnotes, maths and DOMPurify.
Find-in-answer highlighting using the browser highlight API.

guide.area: Code blocks and executable code presentation (area 021)
guide.what_it_is_for: When the assistant writes code, the person sees it as a clear block with its language name and colours, and can copy it, save it as a file, open it larger, or send it to an editor. Where the product can run code, the person can start a run from the chat, watch the output, errors, plots and generated files, and re-run or stop it. This matters because code is the thing people most often need to take elsewhere, and a run that fails silently or looks like it succeeded wastes time and trust.
guide.who_uses_it: Every chat user sees code blocks, and the copy, download and expand controls are on the web chat block for all users (no plan check seen in the block code). Running code in the cloud needs the sandbox server gate to be on (apps/web/lib/e2b/gate.ts) and a plan lookup that fails closed (apps/web/lib/e2b/runtime.ts:139-150). Running from the chat needs the code-execution toggle on and a model that reports code-execution support (apps/web/features/chat/components/Composer/ChatComposerNew.tsx:1633-1641). Workspace admins: not seen in the code. Developers use the same code path through the coding page (apps/web/features/code/components/CodeComposer.tsx).
