how_it_works.step: The reply arrives and fences are routed to the code block component
how_it_works.detail: The markdown renderer sends each finished fenced block to the CodeBlock component, passing the language class and the code text. Streaming blocks are marked so they show plain text.

how_it_works.step: CodeBlock decides what kind of block it is
how_it_works.detail: It reads the language from the class name, turns chart and diagram fences into their own components, shows inline code for unlabelled backticks, and sends other labelled blocks to the full code block.

how_it_works.step: The block draws its header and buttons
how_it_works.detail: FencedCodeBlock shows the language label, Copy, Edit (only if an editor is available and the reply is complete), Download and Expand buttons. HTML blocks also get a preview.

how_it_works.step: Highlighting runs after the block is complete
how_it_works.detail: The highlighter loads the language and theme on demand, caches the result per code and language, and renders coloured tokens. Until ready it shows the plain code.

how_it_works.step: Copy and download act on the block's own text
how_it_works.detail: Copy writes the code text to the clipboard. Download picks a file name and extension from the language and saves the text as a file on the device.

how_it_works.step: The user asks for a run from the composer
how_it_works.detail: The code-execution setting is part of the composer state. It is switched on by the toggle or the code command, and switched off automatically when the selected model does not support code execution.

how_it_works.step: The server decides whether cloud execution may run
how_it_works.detail: The sandbox gate reads the server switch and the sandbox key. The plan is looked up first and the request is refused if the lookup fails. Pricing must be known before provisioning.

how_it_works.step: The run result comes back as tool data
how_it_works.detail: The web chat shows the run result through the execution block. Mobile and VS Code keep it in a tool-call timeline. The stored form of the result is not established in this pass.

how_it_works.step: The execution block renders output, errors and plots
how_it_works.detail: It shows a spinner while running, a success or failure icon, stdout under Output, stderr under Stderr, exit code on failure, and only safe base64 images as plots.

how_it_works.step: Other apps have their own renderers
how_it_works.detail: VS Code renders its own markdown with its own copy, explain and diff classes. Mobile re-runs through a service call with its own timeout and error messages. The CLI renders in the terminal.

key_files.role: The code block itself: header, language label, Copy, Edit, Download, Expand, full-screen dialog, diff lines, shell note, chart and diagram routing.
Turns the reply markdown into React; sends each finished fence to CodeBlock (line 726).
Renders highlighted tokens, falls back to plain code while loading or when disabled during streaming.
Loads languages and the six colour themes on demand, caches highlighted lines, stores the active theme.
Maps a language name to a download file name and extension, with a plain text fallback.
Web run panel: spinner, success or failure icon, output, stderr, exit code, plots.
Code-execution toggle state, model support check, automatic turn-off, command that turns it on.
Server switches for cloud code execution: the flag, the sandbox key, and the readiness check.
Creates and runs sandbox sessions; resolves the plan first and fails closed.
Mobile re-run control and its too-long and failure messages.
VS Code chat renderer: code body, diff line classes, Copy and Explain buttons, surface copy handler.

guide.area: Rich answers and structured result widgets (Area 22)
guide.what_it_is_for: Answers show more than plain text: source chips a person can open, search-result lists, charts, maps, tables, diagrams, drafts and forms they can act on inside the chat. The goal is that a person reads the answer and acts on it in the same place. Many widgets in the brief (news, weather, sports, flights, packages, quizzes in chat, reservations) are not built yet in any app.
guide.who_uses_it: Every chat user who gets an answer with sources, charts, maps, drafts or forms, on the web, desktop (the web app), mobile, the Chrome side panel, the CLI terminal UI and the VS Code sidebar, as far as each app's status line says. how_it_works.step: 1. The model is offered the answer-card tool
how_it_works.detail: When a request streams, supports interactive cards, and tools are on, the server adds the answer-card tool to the request. Cards only arrive when this happens. The known card kinds are listed in the shared contract.

how_it_works.step: 2. Cards are stored with the message
how_it_works.detail: Cards the turn produced are saved in the assistant message's metadata, under the interactiveCards key. Stored messages come back with their cards.

how_it_works.step: 3. The web client reads the card kinds
how_it_works.detail: The web stream code lists the card kinds it can read (answer-ui, clarify, image, itinerary, map search, MCP app, places, product comparison). The answer-ui tool definition is built in one service.

how_it_works.step: 4. The client picks a widget for each card
how_it_works.detail: A registry maps each card kind to a component. Send and reply actions are blocked while the reply streams and in temporary chats.
The answer-ui card is made of typed blocks (table, chart, map, gallery and others). Each block type maps to a component. Chart and map blocks are drawn by their own components, the map loaded lazily.
Citation links in the answer text are turned into chips. Multiple citations at one spot are grouped.

how_it_works.step: 7. Charts and maps draw their data
how_it_works.detail: The chart canvas draws the values and tooltips; the chart artifact adds an expandable data view. Maps take tile addresses from configuration.

how_it_works.step: 8. Each other app draws its own version
how_it_works.detail: Mobile, the Chrome side panel, the CLI and VS Code each have their own renderer. They share the citation and card logic only where noted.

guide.what_it_is_for: A project is a named folder for one body of work. It holds its own chats, files, sources, instructions, memories, artifacts, work tasks and routines, so a person can return to a topic and keep the context together. Sharing a project lets an organisation's members work from the same instructions and files, while chats and personal memory stay with each person.
guide.who_uses_it: Signed-in users on the web, desktop, mobile, CLI and VS Code surfaces. The web API creates projects behind a plan feature gate and a plan project limit (a limit of 0 blocks creation). Sharing depends on being in an organisation (roles owner, admin, member, viewer), and the web sharing controls need the owner or an admin role. Chrome extension code only selects a project for its side panel. Workspace admins manage shared access. Developers use the CLI project commands and the VS Code active-project setting.

features.name: Create and set up a project
features.use: Make a new project with a name, optional description, instructions, colour and icon, and open it as its own workspace.
how_people_use_it: Web: open Projects, choose New project, fill the create dialog, save.
Mobile: Projects tab, create project, fill name and details.
Desktop, CLI and VS Code: create from the project list or command, then open it.
how_it_should_work: The project is saved to the signed-in account and opens as its own workspace.
Name is required; description and instructions are optional and trimmed.
Colour defaults when none is sent; icon and accent colour are stored when sent.
If the plan project limit is 0 the create call is refused with a plan message.
If the feature gate denies projects, the request returns a gate response instead of creating.
Cover image or tinted badge (S23.04) is not implemented: no code path, marked not applicable in the brief.
features.on_each_app: Web, desktop, mobile, CLI and VS Code have it (brief status done). Chrome is unverified and the brief says icon and colour are missing there. Cover or identity treatment is not applicable on any app.

features.name: Project overview and search
features.use: The overview shows a project's name, description, counts and main sections. Search finds projects by name or description.
how_people_use_it: Web: open a project from the gallery; the overview shows sections for chats, files, instructions and more.
Web and mobile: type in the project search box on the Projects page to filter by name or description.
CLI: a project listing and detail command.
how_it_should_work: Opening a project shows its overview with counts (conversations, knowledge files, members) from the server.
Search matches name and description; an empty result shows an empty state.
Loading and error states are expected on the list and overview pages; not verified in code beyond the listed files.
features.on_each_app: Web, desktop, mobile, CLI and VS Code have overview (brief done). Search is done on web, desktop and mobile; CLI, VS Code and Chrome have no search (brief missing).

features.name: Project chats, files, sources, notes and artifacts content
features.use: A project lists its chats, starts new chats filed under it, holds files and sources that chats read, and shows artifacts made in its chats. Moving, copying or adding answers to knowledge and notes are listed but are not applicable.
how_people_use_it: Web: open a project, use the chats list or start a new chat from the project.
Web: add files to the project's knowledge files, then preview, download or remove them.
Web and mobile: Sources tab, add a file, text or a connected-service source (mobile Google Drive waits on keys).
Web: Artifacts panel lists artifacts from the project's chats; open one from there.
how_it_should_work: Project chats are the conversations whose project id matches and that the user owns, not deleted and not temporary.
Project files are uploaded through the knowledge-files route; chats in the project can use them.
Google Drive picker needs the picker key and app id; until set, the picker route refuses (see switches).
Notes, move/copy conversation and add-answer-to-knowledge have no code and are marked not applicable in the brief.
features.on_each_app: Chats: all five non-Chrome apps (done); files: web, desktop, mobile done, CLI and Chrome missing; sources: web and desktop partial (Google Picker keys not set), mobile partial (files and text work, Drive waits on keys), CLI and Chrome missing; artifacts: web and desktop done, CLI done, mobile and VS Code missing; notes, move/copy, add-answer: not applicable.

features.name: Instructions, memory and project defaults
features.use: A project can carry instructions applied to its chats, its own memory, a default model, default chat tools and Skills, and a project-only context mode.
how_people_use_it: Web: Project settings dialog: edit instructions, default model field, memory.
Mobile: instructions sheet and memory sheet on the project page.
CLI: Skills and tool defaults through project commands.
how_it_should_work: Instructions saved on a project are added to the system prompt of its chats (the brief says every chat; code path not fully traced).
Memory: the project keeps its own memories; usesGlobalMemory decides whether account memory is also used.
Project-only context: usesGlobalMemory and the context service define it; no separate toggle was found in the files opened.
Default model: a project default model id is stored and applied to new chats (web and VS Code).
features.on_each_app: Instructions: web, desktop, mobile, CLI, VS Code done. Memory: web, desktop, CLI done; mobile shows a memory sheet (brief says missing); VS Code and Chrome missing. Default model: web, desktop, VS Code done. Default tools and Skills: CLI only (web, desktop, mobile missing). Project-only context: web and desktop done, mobile, CLI, VS Code, Chrome missing.

features.name: Local folders and coding sessions
features.use: Link a project to a folder on the computer so work in that folder uses the project. Coding sessions can belong to a project. Repository link is not applicable.
how_people_use_it: CLI: work in a folder; the CLI registers the folder against a project and asks for trust.
VS Code: the active project is stored and used for the workspace.
how_it_should_work: A folder is trusted per path and identity; the registry keeps trusted and revoked times.
Coding sessions listed from the project: CLI only.

features.name: Work tasks and routines
features.use: Start autonomous work tasks in a project, schedule routines in it, run parallel child threads from a coordinating chat, see blocked threads, and steer one thread.
how_people_use_it: Web: project work panel lists tasks; the project page has a schedules section for routines.
Mobile: Work tab on the project; Start work sheet; Routines tab.
CLI: background runs can be started and resumed.
how_it_should_work: The project lists the state of its work tasks.
Routines are created on the schedules page and shown on the project.
Parallel child threads (CLI background runs) run as separate prints with their own session id.
Overview of blocked child threads and steering one thread: no code found in the brief's files; only CLI background runs exist.

Parallel threads: CLI done only. Overview of child threads: missing everywhere. Thread steering: not applicable.

features.name: Sharing, members and roles
features.use: Share a project with people in the same organisation, see who has access, give each person read or edit access, get a shareable link, and see which context is shared and which stays personal. Access requests are not built.
how_people_use_it: Web: Share dialog on the project; choose who gets access (audience: invited gets no default access, others get read) and per-person access.
Web: open a shared link; the project page opens for people it is shared with.
Web: the project page explains shared versus personal context.
how_it_should_work: Only organisation owners and admins can change what is shared (a sharing-permission check refuses others).
Project-level grants have read, write or none; an editor is a member with a write grant and the share permission.
The server refuses owner-only fields (for example archive) when an editor saves; editors may change name, description, instructions and appearance.
A project that is not shared with the user returns not found.
Access-request approval is not built (brief missing); no code found.
features.on_each_app: Sharing and member list: web and desktop done; mobile, CLI, VS Code, Chrome missing. Roles and invite/remove: web and desktop done. Shared link: web and desktop done. Shared versus personal explanation: web and desktop done. Access requests: missing on every app.

features.name: Lifecycle: archive, duplicate, delete, import and export
features.use: Archive a project out of the active list and restore it, duplicate it with its settings and files, delete it, export it as a file, or import one from another assistant.
how_people_use_it: Web: Project settings dialog has Duplicate, Export and Delete project buttons.
Web: archive toggle through the project update (isArchived).
CLI: delete command with a yes flag; archive and restore commands.
how_it_should_work: Delete is a soft delete: the project row gets a deleted time; a legal hold can block it and returns an error.
Duplicate copies settings and keeps the global-memory flag; Health projects cannot be duplicated.
Archive is an owner-only field; editors get a refusal.
Export is a download route with an attachment header.
Import: the project schema stores an import source (claude, openai, manual); no import route or UI was found.
features.on_each_app: Duplicate: web and desktop done. Archive and restore: web, desktop, CLI done; mobile and VS Code missing. Delete: all surfaces. Export: web route and button exist (brief says not applicable). Import: no route or UI found (brief missing).

features.name: Project activity history
features.use: A log of what changed in a project and who changed it.
how_people_use_it: Not built in any app.
how_it_should_work: Should show added or removed files, setting and instruction edits, sharing changes and chats, with who and when. No code found.
features.on_each_app: Missing on all six apps (brief status).

how_it_works.detail: The web project page and dialogs call the managed cloud projects client, which wraps the same-origin API with session refresh and CSRF headers.

POST checks CSRF, rate limit, the projects feature gate, validates the body, reads the plan tier, refuses if the project limit is 0, then inserts the user_projects row and checks the per-user project count in the same statement. Chat membership is written in the same transaction.

how_it_works.name: List: keyset paging and shared rows
how_it_works.detail: GET checks the workspace access gate, then lists the user's own projects plus projects shared to the user's organisation, with conversation counts and a keyset cursor.

PATCH tries the update as the owner; if no row changes it resolves the caller as owner or editor. Editors may not change owner-only fields such as archive. Conditional writes use a version and return a precondition-failed response on change.

how_it_works.step: Delete: soft delete with legal-hold check
how_it_works.detail: DELETE checks CSRF and rate limit, then soft-deletes the project row in a transaction. A legal hold can refuse it. Knowledge-file retirement is a separate helper.
Every list and write resolves the user's organisation membership and the project grants. Share permission is checked on each read so a downgraded member loses edit rights.
Chat requests build the project context block from instructions, description and files and place it in the system prompt; the context block is trimmed to a size budget, keeping instruction layers.

how_it_works.step: Other clients store their own copy
how_it_works.detail: The VS Code extension keeps the active project (id, name, up to a set number of instruction characters) in extension memento storage. The Chrome side panel keeps the active project id and a name cache in chrome storage keys.

key_files.role: Project list (keyset paging) and create, with plan limit and feature gate.
Read, update (owner and editor rules, version check) and soft delete for one project.
Organisation roles, project grants (read, write, none) and the owner-or-editor write check.
Builds the project context block (instructions, description, files) for chat system prompts.
Soft delete and knowledge-file retirement, guarded by legal holds.
Web settings: edit fields, Duplicate, Export and Delete buttons.
Copies a project's settings; refuses Health projects; keeps the global-memory flag.
Downloads a project as an attachment.
Shared schema for project fields (surfaces, chat defaults, accent colours, import source).
Mobile project page: sources, work, artifacts, routines, instructions and memory sheets.
Mobile project store and source upload (cancel on account change).
VS Code active cloud project, stored in extension memento.
Chrome side panel active project id and name cache.

switches.name: Projects feature gate
switches.effect: Blocks project creation when the workspace policy denies the projects feature; returns a gate response.

switches.name: Plan project limit
switches.effect: Limit 0 refuses creation; the number caps projects per plan; a database quota check also applies on insert.

switches.name: Workspace access gate
switches.effect: Blocks listing and access when the workspace access policy denies it.

switches.name: Connectors released check
switches.effect: Google Drive picker refuses when connectors are not released.

switches.name: GOOGLE_PICKER_API_KEY and GOOGLE_PICKER_APP_ID
switches.effect: Both must be set for the Google Picker to work; the Drive source stays unavailable without them.

switches.name: Mobile memory sheet
switches.effect: Shows the project memory sheet only for cloud projects the user owns, not shared with them.

switches.name: Editor restriction on owner-only fields
switches.effect: Editors cannot change owner-only fields (including archive); the server refuses them.

switches.name: Legal hold
switches.effect: A held project or file cannot be deleted; the call is refused with a hold error.

switches.name: Global memory flag
switches.effect: Decides whether account memory is also read by the project; copied on duplicate.

switches.name: AGI_NATIVE_SEARCH_MAX_USES
switches.effect: Limits search calls per chat turn; affects research use, not projects directly.

guide.what_it_is_for: The Library is where a signed-in person finds every file and artifact they have made or uploaded in one place. They can browse by type or source, search by name, open a file, reuse it in a new chat or a project, and recover files they deleted within 30 days. It matters because generated images, documents and saved artifacts would otherwise be lost in old chats, and because deleted files must be recoverable before they are erased for good.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user on web, desktop (which shows the hosted web app, so it runs the same code) and mobile. The web and mobile Library list only files in the active workspace (organization) the user is in, through the server query (apps/web/lib/server/media-assets.ts:403, 444). Signed-out web users see a sign-in page instead (apps/web/features/library/components/LibraryView.tsx:278). Storage and download numbers depend on the user's plan. The CLI reads artifacts through a different index, not the Library. Nothing in the code I read limits Library use to paid plans or to workspace admins, but the storage and download allowances are plan-based. The CLI and the VS Code and Chrome surfaces are not in the Library.

features.name: Browse by source: All files, Uploads, Generated files, Artifacts
features.use: One place for every file, and separate views for files the user uploaded, files the assistant generated, and saved artifacts that can be opened.
how_people_use_it: Web: click a tab in the row labelled 'Filter the library' (All, Images, Videos, Documents, Artifacts, Uploads, Generated files).
Mobile: tap a filter chip (All, Uploads, Generated, Artifacts and so on) above the grid.
Web can open on a tab from the URL: ?surface=artifact opens Artifacts, ?tab=images opens Images (apps/web/features/library/components/LibraryView.tsx:137-139).
how_it_should_work: Each tab asks the server for a fresh first page of 24 items (LIBRARY_DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE, packages/contracts/cloud-contracts/src/library.ts:84).
Tab-to-query mapping lives in packages/ui/unified-chat/src/components/library/LibraryView.tsx:108-116.
Empty state: web shows a shared empty view; mobile shows a message per filter (e.g. 'Files you upload will appear here', apps/mobile/src/features/library/index.tsx:1266-1287).
Waiting: the list shows a loading state while a page loads; a failed load shows 'Something went wrong.' (LibraryView.tsx:504).

Artifacts on mobile also come from artifacts stored on the device and from the cloud, merged and filtered to the current app mode (apps/mobile/src/features/library/index.tsx:320-326). Artifacts are not in the server Library list.
Limits: none by plan on the tabs themselves.
features.on_each_app: Web: All, Images, Videos, Documents, Artifacts, Uploads, Generated tabs (done). Desktop: same as web (done). Mobile: All, Images, Videos, Documents, Uploads, Generated and Artifacts chips (uploaded view and artifact view done). CLI: artifact list only (done), no file tabs. VS Code: artifact list only (done). Chrome: artifact view not verified. Audio tab: missing on all apps (see S24.07). Brief does not state the web or desktop status of S24.01; the code has an All tab on web and mobile.

features.name: Browse by media type: Images, Videos, Documents, Audio
features.use: Quick filters by what kind of file it is, so a person can look only at pictures or only at videos.
how_people_use_it: Web: click the Images, Videos or Documents tab.
Mobile: tap the Images, Videos or Documents chip.
Open an image from the grid to see it in the viewer (web: LibraryView.tsx:1201 viewer; mobile: FileViewerScreen, index.tsx:1153).
how_it_should_work: Images are kind 'image', videos are kind 'video', documents are kind 'file' with surface 'file' (LibraryView.tsx:110-112; media-assets.ts:407-410 filters by the kind column).
Audio has no tab, no kind and no viewer on any app (not found in the code I read).
Failure: a file that cannot be loaded shows 'This file is unavailable right now. Try again later, or remove this entry.' (LibraryView.tsx:1513-1515).
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop: Images, Videos, Documents tabs (done); Audio missing. Mobile: Images, Videos, Documents chips (done); Audio missing. CLI, VS Code, Chrome: missing. The file-type filter (S24.14) is the same tabs on web and mobile; there is no finer type filter (for example by extension) in the code I read.

features.name: Recent, favourite, shared and folder views
features.use: Views that show recently added files, favourites, files shared with the person, and folders for organising files.
how_people_use_it: Recent: sort by Modified (the default) from the Sort control.
Folders: on web, the 'All' tab shows folder tiles or rows for the user's projects; click a folder to open the project page (LibraryView.tsx:849-856, 1474-1483, 1582-1602).
how_it_should_work: Recent-files: there is no separate view. The default sort is updated_at descending (media-assets.ts:367; contracts library.ts:89), which is 'recently added or changed', not 'recently used'.

Folders on web are the user's projects, read from /api/projects, and hidden when the host does not provide a list (LibraryView.tsx:160-176, 849-856). Opening one goes to /chat/projects/{id} (features LibraryView.tsx:143-146). There is no folder inside a folder.
Favourites and shared-with-me: no code found.
Limits: folders are shown only on the All tab, not while Recently deleted is on or while a search is active (LibraryView.tsx:850).
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop: recent by sort and project folders (recent done, folders not in brief status). Mobile: no folder view, no favourites, no shared view (missing). CLI, VS Code, Chrome: missing. Favourites (S24.09) and shared-with-me (S24.10) are missing on all apps. Folder hierarchy (S24.11) is missing on mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome.

features.name: Search, sort and layout
features.use: Find a file by typing part of its name, order the list, and switch between a thumbnail grid and a row list.
how_people_use_it: Search: type in the 'Search files and projects' box (web) or the 'Search library' bottom bar (mobile). Mobile debounces the query by 350 ms (index.tsx:29, 216).
Sort: open the sort menu and pick Modified, Name, Size or Type (web). Mobile has a 'Sort saved files' action with Recently added, Oldest first, Type, Name and Size.
Layout: click the grid or list icon (web, LibraryView.tsx:1043-1058). Mobile has no grid/list switch in the code I read.
how_it_should_work: Search matches the file name and also the prompt that made the file (media-assets.ts:422-426). Search characters % _ and \ are escaped (media-assets.ts:374-376).
Sort is applied on the server (media-assets.ts:366-372, 434-436). Web offers Modified, Name, Size, Type; the server also supports 'oldest', which web does not offer.
Layout choice is kept per browser in localStorage under 'agi-library-view-mode' (LibraryView.tsx:131-147). Default is grid.
Limits: none by plan.
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop: search, sort and grid/list (done). Mobile: search and sort (done), grid only, no list (grid/list missing on mobile). CLI, VS Code, Chrome: missing.

features.name: Filter by origin, owner, project or date
features.use: Narrow the list by where a file came from, who owns it, which project it belongs to, or when it was made.
how_people_use_it: Web: click the Uploads or Generated tab (these are the only origin filters).
how_it_should_work: Origin: 'uploaded' means metadata origin is upload or uploaded; 'generated' means anything else (media-assets.ts:415-421; route.ts:79).
There is no source-provider or connector filter (see things that look wrong), no owner filter, no project filter and no created/modified date filter in the code I read.
Mobile has Uploads and Generated only; it has no source filter.
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop: upload and generated origin filters only (the brief marks S24.15 done, but the code has only these two origins). Mobile: Uploads and Generated only (S24.15 missing in brief). CLI, VS Code, Chrome: missing. Owner, project and date filters (S24.16, S24.17, S24.18) are missing on all apps.

features.name: Select and act on several files
features.use: Select many files, then delete them together. Batch download and batch move are not built.
how_people_use_it: Mobile: open the action sheet and choose 'Select saved files' (index.tsx:275), tap files to select them, then tap Delete (index.tsx:1093). A confirm alert says the files move to deleted items (index.tsx:692-697).
how_it_should_work: Each deletion is a separate soft delete call; if any fail the user sees 'Some files could not be deleted. Try again.' (index.tsx:692-725).
Web has no multi-select (no checkbox or selection state found).
Limits: none by plan.
features.on_each_app: Mobile: multi-select and batch delete exist in code (the brief marks S24.20 and S24.23 missing). Batch download (S24.21) and batch move (S24.22) are missing on all apps. Web, desktop, CLI, VS Code, Chrome: missing.

features.name: Rename, duplicate and move a file
features.use: Change a file's name, make a copy of it, or put it in a folder.
how_people_use_it: Not available in any app as far as the code shows.
how_it_should_work: No rename, duplicate or move-to-folder action was found in the Library views or the mobile screen. The only 'move' is the action 'Add to project', which copies the file (see the Use a file feature).
Name shown to users comes from metadata filename, or kind plus an extension (route.ts:44-49), and is not editable.
features.on_each_app: Missing on web, desktop, mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome.

features.name: Use a file in a chat or a project
features.use: Take a Library file into a new chat, attach it to a chat, add it to a project as knowledge, or open the chat it came from.
how_people_use_it: Web: open a file's menu and choose 'Add to chat', 'Add to Work' or 'Add to project' (shown when a project list exists), or 'Ask about this file' in the viewer.
Web: open the originating chat from the menu (LibraryView.tsx:672-681).
Mobile: 'Attach to chat' sends the file to the composer (index.tsx:530-540).
how_it_should_work: Add to project: the web host reads the file's bytes and uploads them as project knowledge (features LibraryView.tsx:234-240), so the project gets a copy. Success toast: 'Added to <project>'. Failure shows an error on the row.
Add to chat or Work stages the file in a new chat (features LibraryView.tsx:217-229).
Open conversation: only for items that have a conversation_id (route.ts:86; LibraryView.tsx:672-681).
Limits: a file already larger than the monthly download allowance cannot be handed to the browser (LibraryView.tsx:563-568).
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop: add to chat, add to project, open conversation, ask about file (done). Mobile: attach to chat (done), open conversation not found in the Library screen, add to project not present (missing in brief). CLI, VS Code, Chrome: missing.

features.name: Recently deleted and restore
features.use: Deleted files stay recoverable for 30 days, then they are removed.
how_people_use_it: Web: click the Recently deleted trash toggle (LibraryView.tsx:1034-1040). Then choose Restore on a file, or Delete permanently.

how_it_works.detail: The web page builds a transport object that calls the Library API, the media delete/restore API, the project APIs and the chat staging helpers. Signed-out users get a sign-in page. Desktop shows the same web app.

The shared Library component (used by web) holds the active tab, sort, layout (grid/list), search text, the page of items, folders and the deleted toggle. The grid or list layout is saved in the browser.
The view builds query parameters (sort, surface, kind, origin, q, deleted, limit, offset) and fetches /api/library. The first page also reads storage and download numbers.

how_it_works.step: 4. API route validates and assembles the response
how_it_works.detail: The route applies the rate limit, scopes the database to the user and organization, validates the query, asks for limit plus one row to know if there is another page, and adds storage, breakdown and download meters on the first page.
listLibraryAssets reads public.media_assets for the user and active organization, excludes temporary-chat files, and applies kind, surface, origin, search, sort and the deleted window (30 days).

how_it_works.step: 6. Shape each row for the screen
how_it_works.detail: Each row becomes a LibraryItem with file name, uri (/api/files/{id}), thumbnail, surface, previewable flag, origin, provider, model, prompt, conversation id and erase_after for deleted rows.

The web host asks first (confirm dialog), then calls /api/media with a CSRF token. Soft delete and restore touch only deleted_at. Permanent delete removes stored bytes and derived records, unless a legal hold applies.

how_it_works.step: 8. Save an artifact into the Library
how_it_works.detail: POST /api/library validates the file name and content (up to 1,000,000 characters), checks CSRF, then stores the bytes as a generated file with origin saved_artifact.

how_it_works.step: 9. Add a file to a project
how_it_works.detail: The web host reads the file's bytes and uploads them to the project's knowledge files, so the project keeps its own copy.

The mobile screen keeps its own state (sort, search, filter, selection, deleted toggle), merges device and cloud artifacts for the Artifacts chip, and calls the same /api/library and /api/media endpoints through its own client.

key_files.role: The shared Library screen for web and desktop: tabs, search, sort, grid/list, viewer, row actions and confirm dialogs.
The web host. It connects the shared screen to real API calls, chat staging, project upload and artifact sharing.
GET list of Library items with paging and meters; POST saves an artifact into the Library.
Database access for public.media_assets: list query, soft delete, restore, permanent delete, and the 30-day window.
DELETE (soft or permanent), and POST (restore) for one Library file, with CSRF and rate limits.
Shared schema for list query, sort values, page sizes and the item shape used by every app.
The mobile Library screen: filters, search, sort, selection, deleted view, storage line, and the Artifacts merge.
Mobile client for /api/library and /api/media; maps items to mobile rows.
Stores generated or saved bytes as Library files and classifies them as artifact or file (classifyGeneratedFile at line 186).
Reads the workspace's file storage usage and its plan allowance for the storage meter.
CLI artifact client: the account-wide artifact index route (ARTIFACT_INDEX_PATH at line 25) and publish/show routes. It does not read the Library list.

switches.name: Plan storage allowance (file storage limit)
switches.effect: Sets the storage limit shown on the storage line; no limit means only usage is shown.

switches.name: Monthly download allowance
switches.effect: Sets the download meter; null limit means no meter. Large uploads that would exceed it are declined in the browser.

switches.name: Decline large files in chat upload
switches.effect: Upload from Library declines large files instead of attaching them inline.

switches.name: Recovery window (30 days)
switches.effect: How long deleted files stay restorable and the time shown as 'Kept until'.
switches.where: apps/web/lib/resources/deletion-policies.ts:8 (RESOURCE_RECOVERY_WINDOW_DAYS), used at apps/web/app/api/library/route.ts:60-63; the restore and deleted queries also hard-code 30 days (apps/web/lib/server/media-assets.ts:432, 723).

switches.name: Page size and max page size
switches.effect: Items per page (24 default, 100 max) for the list.

switches.name: Default sort
switches.effect: Modified (updated_at, newest first) unless the user picks another sort.

switches.name: Rate limit
switches.effect: Library list, save and file delete/restore share the chat-conversation limit.

switches.name: Mobile image generation feature flag
switches.effect: Enables the image edit action in the Library preview.

switches.name: Mobile app mode (cloud or local)
switches.effect: Delete from the preview and image edit are shown only in cloud mode; artifacts shown are only for the current mode.

switches.name: URL parameters on web
switches.effect: Preselect surface (surface=), tab (tab=), item (item=) or search text (q=).

guide.what_it_is_for: A person opens a file they saved or uploaded (in the Library, or a project's knowledge files) and sees what is inside without downloading it first. The area covers the in-product viewer for PDFs, images and video, and the text previews for plain text, Markdown, source code, spreadsheets and Word files. It matters because a file is only useful in the product if the person can check it quickly, and a failed preview must still lead to a download. Many parts the brief lists (page controls, search, audio, transcripts, presentations in most apps) are not built yet.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user who can see a Library item or a project's knowledge file. The preview routes check that the asset belongs to the caller's user and workspace (apps/web/app/api/files/[id]/text/route.ts:24-31), and the project route looks up the knowledge file by project (apps/web/app/api/projects/[id]/knowledge-files/[fileId]/text/route.ts). No plan gate on previews was seen in the code read. Workspace admins and developers are not special-cased in these files.

how_it_works.step: Pick the file and decide its preview kind
how_it_works.detail: The Library list marks each item previewable when its type has a text preview, is an image, video or PDF, or the metadata says so. A click on a previewable item opens the viewer; a click on a non-previewable item does nothing in this code path. The server also decides the kind (text, table, office) from the file name and type.

how_it_works.step: Open the viewer and choose what to show
how_it_works.detail: FileViewerOverlay picks one view: an image with zoom, a video player, a PDF frame, or a text preview. It asks for the text preview only when none of the other three applies.

how_it_works.step: Fetch the original bytes or the text
how_it_works.detail: Images, video and PDFs load through the file route (with ?preview=pdf for PDFs). Text loads through the /text route under the file's URL, through the transport the web and desktop hosts provide.

how_it_works.step: Server checks access and reads the stored file
how_it_works.detail: The text route rate-limits the request, looks up the asset for the caller's user and workspace, refuses files without a text preview or over 30 MB, then reads the stored object.

how_it_works.step: Turn the file into text or a table

guide.what_it_is_for: An artifact is a finished piece of work the assistant makes in a chat, such as a web page, document, diagram or code file. This area is the card that shows it in the chat, and the viewer that opens it beside the conversation, full screen or in its own window. It lets a person read, copy, export, version, share and reuse that work without losing it. Without it the assistant's output would be plain text that is hard to keep, change or reuse.
guide.who_uses_it: Every person who uses chat on a surface that renders artifacts (web, desktop, mobile in the code I read). The code I opened shows no plan gate for opening or viewing the artifact. Cloud save and comments are gated by code (see switches). Workspace or admin use is not established. Developers use the same viewer through the shared package.

how_it_works.detail: A reply's artifacts are passed to the inline card list. The list shows at most three cards, a '+N more' button for the rest, and a Download all button when there are two or more. Pressing a card selects the artifact in the store and opens the panel. Pressing the same card again closes the panel.

The web artifact store keeps the artifacts, their versions and the selected id. It is saved to browser storage under one key with a quota-aware writer. If the write fails for lack of space, saving is turned off and an error is logged, and the store keeps working in memory only.

The panel reads the store. When the chat changes conversation, it selects that conversation's first artifact. A deep link in the address selects the artifact and opens the panel when that artifact exists.

The panel renders nothing when closed. On the mobile layout with the panel open it becomes a modal overlay. On the desktop layout its width is set from panelWidth. Width bounds (280 to 900 pixels) live in a shared UI store that every surface that drags the panel uses.

A publish handler checks that the publication view is still open, then calls the publish service with a managed privacy mode and the origin privacy mode. A second publish on the same artifact is refused while one is pending.

The preview component gates the selection-edit, comment and changes layers. Selection-edit needs a stored artifact, the latest version, and a request handler. Comments need a stored artifact and a comment permission check. The viewer mounts the comments panel, the selection toolbar, the edit-request layer and the changes view when those are on.
An artifact flagged as interrupted shows a banner. Failed document or image rendering shows a message and a download or retry hint.
Duplicate creates a copy and shows a success toast; failure shows an error toast. Cloud save and connector actions only appear when the connectors-released check passes.
The mobile app has its own artifact store, persisted under its own name. It is separate from the web store; the mobile viewer is a full-screen sheet.

guide.what_it_is_for: A document is a written artifact the assistant makes in a chat, such as a memo, report or article. The person can read it, edit it as text or in a visual editor, keep earlier versions, select text to ask the assistant for a change, and export it as Markdown, Word, PDF or plain text. This matters because a finished draft is only useful if it can be fixed, checked against earlier versions and taken out of the app. Much of the brief's list is not built yet: no page layout, no find, no word count, no suggestion or tracked-change mode, and no live presence.
guide.who_uses_it: Every person who has a document artifact in a chat, on web and mobile, as far as the code shows. I found no plan gate in the files I read. Editing on web is only offered in the side panel view (variant 'panel'), on the latest version, and never for PDF, Word or image artifacts. Saving a document to Google Docs, Google Drive or OneDrive is hidden because the connector release state is 'coming_soon' (see switches). Workspace admins are not part of this area in the code I read, apart from the share-with-workspace control in the web viewer.

how_it_works.step: Show the title on a card and in the viewer
how_it_works.detail: The card reads the title through artifactTitle, which falls back to 'Untitled'. The store trims and length-limits titles on rename. Mobile uses a kind-based fallback instead.

how_it_works.step: Open a Markdown document in the viewer
how_it_works.detail: The viewer renders Markdown with the shared renderer, and shows an outline when there are at least 3 headings. Math, tables and checkboxes are handled by plugins in the shared renderer.

Edit document (or the Source tab) is shown only in the side panel view, on the latest stored version, for text documents. It copies the current text into a draft. If the Markdown reads back the same after a round trip, the visual editor opens; otherwise the code-style source editor opens with a notice.

how_it_works.step: Keep the draft on the device while typing
how_it_works.detail: Each change updates the draft in browser storage under a per-artifact key. The status line says 'Draft kept on this device' or 'Draft not kept'. Nothing is written as a version yet.

Save writes the draft into the store as a new version and clears the draft. Checklist ticks do the same after a 4-second pause. The store keeps versions and persists them to browser storage; a cloud push follows separately.

how_it_works.step: Ask the assistant to change a selection
how_it_works.detail: Selecting text shows the selection toolbar. The chosen action builds a request with the selected text, the surrounding text and the title, and sends it through the chat's edit-request callback. The assistant's answer comes back as a new version.
Choosing Restore asks for confirmation, then the store adds the chosen version as the newest one. Undo and Redo step through versions in an edit trail.

Web Download as Markdown, PDF or Word calls the document export service, which builds the file in the browser. Google Docs and cloud save are hidden unless connectors are released; the server refuses them too.

key_files.role: Web document viewer: reader, Source and visual editing, Save, version controls, selection actions, export menu, Google Docs and cloud save (hidden), template and brand actions.
Chooses the visual (Tiptap) editor for round-trip-safe Markdown, or the source editor with a notice.
Toolbar for the visual editor: text style dropdown, bold, italic, lists, checklist, quote, code, link, table, undo, redo.
Editor extensions (starter kit, tables, task lists) and the round-trip check that decides whether a document opens in the visual editor.
Web artifact store: versions, rename, restore, duplicate, persistence to browser storage, push to cloud.
Shared Markdown reader used by web, desktop and mobile: code, math, tables, task checkboxes, image trust, email blocks.
Markdown parser plugins; makes tables with extra cells read-only source.
The list of selection actions (rewrite, shorten, lengthen, tone, audience, translate) and the request builder.
Mobile full-screen document view: edit source, save as a new version, undo and redo, outline, export sheet, version stepper.
Mobile export options (Markdown, PDF, Word, plain text) and the export runner.
Switch that hides connected-service saves (currently set to 'coming_soon').
CLI artifact index: title fallback and output file naming by type.
CLI approval screen: lists recipients and subject from any tool's arguments before approval.

things_that_look_wrong.what: Brief says the web visual editor is missing, but a Tiptap-based visual editor exists and opens from Edit document.
Brief says Markdown mode is missing on mobile, but mobile has a plain-text source editor with Save as a new version.
Brief says the mobile outline and the web heading control are missing; both exist in code.

Brief says web selection actions (rewrite, shorten, lengthen, tone, audience, translate) are missing; the toolbar and action list exist. They send a request to the assistant rather than editing the text in place.
Brief says comments are missing; web side panel has comments with replies and API routes.
Brief says connected-service save is missing; it is built on web but hidden because the connector release state is 'coming_soon'.

Brief says autosave is done on web; text edits need the Save button. Only checklist ticks save on their own. The 'Draft kept on this device' text is local draft state, not a saving or saved indicator.
Brief says underline is done; the editor turns underline off, and no underline control exists.
Brief says images can be inserted; the visual editor has no image button, so images can only be added by typing Markdown in source mode.
A table with more cells in a row than in its header is shown as read-only source, not as an editable table.

Brief says the CLI exports Markdown from the account data export; that line is the account data export, not artifact export. Artifact export is agi artifacts show --out, which writes the raw content with an extension by type.

Brief's CLI email review refs point to the commit-message line and an MCP error message, not to email code. The review is generic: any tool's recipient and subject keys are shown. The CLI source has no email-sending tool.

Several brief code references do not match the current files (for example InlineArtifactCards.tsx has 88 lines and no line 297; mobile InlineArtifactCard.tsx:153 is an image card, and ArtifactFullScreen.tsx:310 is a style constant).
Brief says Chrome translate is done in the side panel; it is a context-menu action that fills the chat with a translate prompt.
The VS Code selection action set (Refactor, Explain, Generate Tests) applies to code selections, not to document text.

not_sure: Plan gates: no plan or entitlement check for document editing, export or selection actions was found in the files I read. I did not search the server routes for plan checks.
Desktop: I did not open desktop code. Its status comes from the brief only.
How the assistant turns an edit request into a new version: I read only the web side that sends the request (onRequestEdits), not the chat code that applies the answer.

Google Docs, Drive and OneDrive save routes: I read only the first lines of the Google Docs route and the Drive route guard. Their internals, and whether they would work once released, are unverified.
Cloud sync of artifacts: the store pushes to a cloud endpoint (artifacts-store.ts:1079-1112); I did not follow the endpoint.
Mobile email rendering: apps/mobile/src/features/chat/components/AssistantSurface.tsx refers to the email block language; I did not check how it renders.
Mobile export internals: I read the option list and the runner in artifactExport.ts, not the file creation services for PDF and Word.
CLI email send: the CLI source has no email-sending tool; the tool may come from the hosted service, which I did not read.
Chrome status: most Chrome items are marked unverified in the brief, and I did not open the Chrome document code.

Testing: this was a read-only code review. I ran no builds, tests or servers, so nothing here is verified by running the app. The relayed request asked for localhost testing with one surface at a time; that does not apply to a read-only review, and no testing was done.

guide.area: Code Canvas and application preview (brief area 028)
guide.what_it_is_for: When the assistant writes an HTML page, a React component, a diagram or a multi-file project, the person can look at it running, read or edit its source, and keep, download, publish or continue it. This area is the panel that shows those generated artifacts. It matters because a generated app is only useful if the person can see it work, change it, and share it safely.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in person who has a generated artifact (web, desktop and mobile show it in chat; VS Code and the CLI open artifacts from the account index). Publishing needs a signed-in person. A viewer of a published app can run it, but its AI and saved data need a signed-in viewer (infrastructure/sandbox/index.html:242-243). Workspace-level sharing is an option on publish (apps/web/features/chat/components/artifacts/ArtifactPreview.tsx:1317-1350). The brief names no plan gate for this area. The only plan value read in the AI path is the account's plan entitlement (apps/web/app/api/artifacts/runtime/artifact-completion.ts:252). Whether that gates paid plans only was not established.

Type in the code editor. The editor opens as a lazy-loaded component.

how_it_should_work: Edits are saved through the same store path as Restore, so each save becomes a new version rather than an overwrite (ArtifactPreview.tsx:935-939, 1124-1136).
Unsaved text is kept in browser storage under agi.artifact-draft:<artifact id> so a reload does not lose it (ArtifactPreview.tsx:395-425).
Source editing is offered only for text artifacts and only on the latest version (ArtifactPreview.tsx:937-942).

Syntax highlighting, diagnostics and completion are required by the brief for the web and desktop apps (S28.05 to S28.07 are marked missing there). The code shows an editor component with a language prop (ArtifactPreview.tsx:3333-3340), but the editor internals were not read, so the real language support is unknown.
No empty-state or failure text for the editor was found in the brief.

how_it_works.step: Show the artifact in the panel
how_it_works.detail: The web panel decides whether to show the preview or the source. For HTML, React, SVG and Mermaid it renders the preview. For text it shows the source. A preview payload is built and passed to the sandboxed frame component.

how_it_works.step: Pick the frame: separate sandbox origin or local fallback
how_it_works.detail: If NEXT_PUBLIC_SANDBOX_ORIGIN is set to an allowed https or localhost origin, the artifact loads from that origin in a frame with allow-scripts and allow-same-origin. If not set, or if the sandbox does not connect in time, the artifact is written into a local frame with allow-scripts and allow-modals only.

how_it_works.step: Send the artifact to the renderer
how_it_works.detail: The parent posts a render message to the renderer. The renderer accepts messages only from its own parent and only from allowed origins, then picks a renderer by kind (html, react, svg, mermaid, text, code).

how_it_works.step: Render HTML as a real document
how_it_works.detail: HTML is put in a nested frame with srcdoc, so the artifact's own load events and viewport work. The nested frame has no sandbox attribute, so it inherits the renderer's content policy. A blocked frame falls back to plain markup.

how_it_works.step: Run artifact code and report errors
how_it_works.detail: Errors and rejected promises in the artifact are sent back to the parent as render errors and shown in an error block. Runtime requests from the artifact (AI and storage) are sent to the parent with an id and the parent sends the answer back.

how_it_works.step: Server handles app AI and storage
how_it_works.detail: The renderer's storage calls go to the storage route, which checks the token, the value size and the connector rule, then writes to the published-app storage table. AI calls go to the completion route, which checks the AI switch and the connector release gate.
A source edit is written to the artifact store as a new version. Drafts are also kept in browser storage until saved or restored.
The client checks that the artifact kind can be published, then posts to the publish route. The route checks the CSRF token and a rate limit, then prepares and stores the publication.

key_files.role: The one renderer used by web (separate origin) and desktop (built into the app). Runs HTML, React, SVG, Mermaid and text, the error reporting, the element picker and the runtime bridge.
Reads the sandbox origin from NEXT_PUBLIC_SANDBOX_ORIGIN, checks the message source, and parses the render, picker and runtime messages.
Parent-side frame component. Chooses the separate-origin frame or the local fallback, and handles timeouts and render errors.
The web side panel: preview and code tabs, source editing, reload, version restore, download, Library and cloud save, publish and audience controls.
Server route for an app's saved values (get, set, delete, list), with size and connector checks.
Server logic for an app's storage and AI calls, including the AI switch and the token-based access.
Server route that publishes an artifact to a shareable link.
Mobile preview in a WebView. Runs script only for HTML and React, and shows the error panel with Retry and View source.
VS Code commands: open an artifact read-only, copy its content, save it into the workspace, open the published page.
CLI client for the account's artifact index, publish, audience and unpublish.
Single-file download and zip export of artifacts in the browser.
Shared limits: prompt size, connectors, storage key and value sizes.

switches.name: NEXT_PUBLIC_SANDBOX_ORIGIN
switches.effect: When set to an allowed https or localhost origin, artifacts run on a separate origin. When unset, they run in the local fallback frame. It is read at build time, so changing it needs a rebuild. Audit notes say it is unset in production (apps/web/lib/artifact-sandbox.ts:159; audit/prior-audits/chat-security-audit-2026-10-26.md:62).

switches.name: AGI_ARTIFACT_AI_ENABLED
switches.effect: Turns on the AI call for apps. When off, AI calls are refused with artifact_ai_off.

switches.name: CONNECTOR_RELEASE_STATE (released or coming_soon)
switches.effect: While not released, any AI request that asks for connectors is refused with connectors_coming_soon.

switches.name: Account plan entitlement
switches.effect: Passed into the AI and connector plan. Which plans get what was not established.

switches.name: Publish rate limit (share-create)
switches.effect: Limits how often an artifact can be published.

switches.name: Artifact storage limits
switches.effect: Maximum 4 MiB per saved value, 20 MiB per scope, prompt 100,000 characters, at most 10 connectors.

switches.name: Cloud save size limit
switches.effect: Maximum 3,000,000 bytes for a cloud save.

switches.name: Parent origin allowlist in the renderer
switches.effect: Only the listed parent origins can drive the renderer. Developer origins (localhost) are added only when the renderer itself is served from localhost.

switches.name: Mobile script switch
switches.effect: Only HTML and React artifacts run script on mobile. Diagrams get script for drawing.

guide.shared_code: Shared: the renderer in infrastructure/sandbox/index.html is the same file for web (served from a separate origin) and desktop (built into the desktop app and served from a special address, per the comment at index.html:11-13; the desktop Rust file was not opened). Shared limits and message rules live in packages/contracts/cloud-contracts and packages/contracts/types (the content policy string is generated from packages/contracts/types/src/artifact-csp.ts per index.html:48-53). Web-only: ArtifactPreview.tsx, SandboxedIframe.tsx, artifact-sandbox.ts, and the web API routes. Separate per app: mobile uses its own WebView preview (SafeArtifactPreview.tsx, sandboxedArtifactHtml.ts). VS Code and CLI have their own code that reads the account artifact index and never runs an artifact (VS Code opens artifacts read-only).

The brief's switch-on step for HTML and React sets that origin, so the flaw becomes live when it is turned on.

The brief's switch-on for HTML and React preview says to set NEXT_PUBLIC_SANDBOX_ORIGIN. The code says the same, but the known flaw above must be closed before that switch. The brief does not mention it.

guide.area: Spreadsheet and data-analysis workspace (brief area 029, 40 items)
guide.what_it_is_for: Most of this area is not built. The working part is that a person asks the assistant in chat for a spreadsheet, Word, PowerPoint, PDF or CSV file, and gets a real file to download. The assistant calls one server tool, which builds the file, can add a simple chart, and can edit an attached Word or Excel file in place. The in-app grid, formula bar, sorting, cleaning, SQL and connected-data features in the brief have no code in the places I read, so a person cannot yet work in a sheet inside the product.

I found no plan gate on this tool in the code I opened, so whether paid plans only is not established. Workspace admins and developers are not specifically involved in the code I read.

how_it_works.step: Chat request asks for an office file
how_it_works.detail: When the chat request has the office-creation flag, the server removes any old copy of the tool and adds a fresh one, with the output format and the attached Word or Excel files offered as editable sources.

The tool is named create_office_file. Its description and fields tell the model which fields belong to which format. Attached Word and Excel files are listed with name and checksum, so the model can ask to edit them.

The arguments are checked with a schema per format. Unknown fields are rejected. A file name must be a bare name with no folder parts. Sheet and cell limits apply. A failure is sent back to the model as a message.

how_it_works.step: Run the tool in the chat loop
how_it_works.detail: The tool loop checks that the tool is available and that a user is signed in. It calls the generator, passing attached files and a sandbox executor that is only started when needed.

For spreadsheets the sheets are turned into workbook parts. Text that starts with = becomes a formula. A numeric-looking text becomes a number. Other text becomes an inline string. A chart is added as a drawing part. The zip is written with DEFLATE compression.
If any worksheet holds a formula, the sandbox recalculates the workbook. Without a sandbox the request fails. Optional render checks need the sandbox too. The file is then checked as a package.

how_it_works.step: Return the file to the client
how_it_works.detail: The result has the data, filename, file type and verification. Errors come back as a message. The web app shows a spreadsheet artifact and offers CSV download; the extension saves server-made files.
When an attached workbook is the source, the server applies explicit cell edits. Each edit first checks that the old value matches the expected one. Parts not touched are kept. A receipt is returned.

guide.what_it_is_for: A presentation (called a deck) is a chat artifact of type "presentation". The person opens it beside the chat, reads and edits slides, asks the assistant to change one slide, presents it full screen, and exports it as HTML, PDF or PowerPoint. It matters because a deck the assistant writes is only useful if the person can fix, reorder and present it without starting over.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user who has a presentation artifact in a chat. The code shows no plan gate on the workspace itself. Older (non-latest) versions of a deck are read-only. The brief lists most items as missing on every app, but the code has a working web workspace and a mobile deck view, so the brief is out of date for those apps.

guide.what_it_is_for: Lets a person attach a PDF, Word, spreadsheet or slide file to a chat and ask about it, and get back a file the product made. Working today: reading PDFs into text and page images for the model (web and mobile), and creating a simple PDF from text in the web app. Most other document work (merge, split, redaction, annotation, form filling, comparison, compression, e-signature, PDF-to-PDF editing) has no code in the parts read, so it is missing.
guide.who_uses_it: The code shows no plan or role gate on the PDF reading path in the files opened, so any signed-in chat user who can attach files reaches it. Office-type attachments are allowed on mobile only when the send goes to the cloud (apps/mobile/src/features/chat/utils/attachmentValidation.ts:113-115). The PDF creation tool is a model-callable managed office format on the web (apps/web/lib/services/managed-office-file-service.ts:192-197). The LibreOffice template build is run by the owner with a secret key, not by end users (apps/web/scripts/build-e2b-office-template.mjs:28-31). Project knowledge extraction is used by project members (apps/web/lib/server/project-knowledge-extraction.ts). Plan gates were not traced in the files read.

features.name: Ask about an attached PDF (summary, questions, page questions)
features.use: The person attaches a PDF to a chat and asks for a summary, an answer, or an answer about one page. The product sends the PDF's text, and page images for scanned pages, to the model with the turn.
how_people_use_it: Attach a PDF to the chat composer (click the attach control or drag the file in; exact composer gesture not traced).
Type a request such as 'summarise this' or 'what does page 4 say about fees'.
Send. The answer appears in the chat.
how_it_should_work: Text of each page is marked with a [Page n] label so the model can refer to pages (apps/web/lib/server/pdf-attachment-content.ts:283-292).
Up to 250 pages are read as text. Pages beyond that are flagged as omitted (apps/web/lib/server/pdf-attachment-content.ts:9, 229).
Up to 30 scanned pages are sent as PNG images, with a total image budget of 8 MB (apps/web/lib/server/pdf-attachment-content.ts:10, 16, 252-268).
A file that does not start with the PDF header is refused as unreadable (apps/web/lib/server/pdf-attachment-content.ts:225-227).
A password-protected PDF is refused with a message asking the user to remove the password and upload again (apps/web/lib/server/pdf-attachment-content.ts:44-47, 296-297).
The model is the only summariser; no separate summary code path was found, so summary quality depends on the model.
Limit by plan: not established in the files read.

Mobile: done per brief; mobile reads PDFs into text on the device (apps/mobile/services/docParser.ts:416-428) and sends the turn through the chat store (apps/mobile/stores/chat/chatExecutionStore.ts). how_it_works.step: Attach and admit files in the chat turn
how_it_works.detail: When a turn is sent, the server finds every attachment slot in the messages. The turn being sent goes first, so older history cannot use up the file budget. Too many files in the current message is refused with a 413 error. Each file is checked against its recorded size before bytes are read.

how_it_works.step: Read the PDF into text and page images
how_it_works.detail: The PDF bytes are checked for the PDF header, then the PDF library reads every page up to the 250-page cap. Pages with no text get an image render, up to 30 pages and 8 MB. The result is text with [Page n] labels, plus page images.

how_it_works.step: Send text and images to the model
how_it_works.detail: The hydrated text and images become part of the model request for that turn. The model writes the summary or answer. No separate summariser was found.

Project files keep extracted text. Retrieval picks passages for a request and keeps page markers so the model can cite pages. Scanned pages in project files go to a transcription routine. A file over the page cap is refused with a message to split it.
On the phone, the parser checks the file, then reads its text. A file with a bad header or password is refused. A file with no readable text is refused as empty.

how_it_works.step: Create a PDF from text on the server
how_it_works.detail: The model can call the managed office tool with format pdf, a filename, a title and content. The server validates the input with a schema, lays out the text on A4 pages with jsPDF, and returns the bytes. Optional render verification needs a sandbox.

how_it_works.step: Store files the model or sandbox made
how_it_works.detail: When a provider or code run makes a file, the server fetches it and saves it with the file store, then returns a link under /api/files/. Files are saved only when storage is configured and the file has an ID. Failures are logged and skipped.
The web preview reads slides into text and workbooks into sheets, with size limits that show a message instead of a broken view.

Server tool that creates Word, slide, workbook, PDF and CSV files from validated input; the PDF creator is generatePdf at line 796.

Keeps page positions in extracted text so retrieved passages can name their page.
Builds the knowledge block for a request from stored project files, choosing passages and adding page markers.
Reads slide decks and workbooks for the web preview, with preview size limits.
Saves files that a model provider or code run created, so they can be downloaded later.
On-device reader for PDF, text, Markdown, CSV and code files; extracts text and reports empty or encrypted PDFs.
Decides which file types a phone can attach, per destination (on device or cloud), and their size limits.
Connector list; holds the e-signature (DocuSign) OAuth entry.
Owner-run script that builds the sandbox template with the LibreOffice packages for office rendering.

guide.what_it_is_for: A person can turn a short brief (what the design is for, its format and style) into a visual design, then select parts of it and ask the model to change them, replace images, compare versions, and export the result. The code that exists today is mostly the general artifact panel and preview (web and mobile), with a brief dialog, a selection-based change request, image replacement and a version-changes view. Most of the brief's design-tool items (canvas, layers, alignment, tokens, Figma, breakpoints, prototypes) have no code found. This matters because the brief is the contract for a design tool that is not yet built.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user who opens the artifacts panel in the web app, and the same panel in the mobile app. The brief dialog is reached from the new-artifact menu, so no plan gate was seen in the files opened. Developers maintain the code. No workspace-admin or paid-plan gate was seen in the files opened for this area. Not verified for the desktop, CLI, VS Code or Chrome apps (see not_sure).

guide.what_it_is_for: A person builds a page or small app in the assistant (HTML, React, SVG, diagram, Markdown, text or code), then publishes it to a link that other people can open. The owner can change who may open it, roll it back to an earlier version, unpublish it, copy it, or download its source. This is how a finished result becomes something others can use or see.
guide.who_uses_it: Any signed-in user who has an artifact in chat can publish it on the web, desktop (through the web feature), mobile and the CLI. Viewers are anyone with a public link, or signed-in people when the audience is invited people or the workspace. Workspace admins are not special here: the code checks the publisher's workspace only for the workspace audience. AI calls from inside a published app depend on the person's plan and on a server switch. Developers use the CLI and the shared contract package.

how_it_works.detail: The person taps Publish. The web menu item calls handlePublish, which sends the artifact to the publish client. The client posts JSON to the publish route with artifact id, kind, title and content.
The route checks the CSRF token, applies the share-create rate limit, parses the JSON and checks the schema. Failure returns a validation error.
The publication policy checks the title with the content moderation rules and runs the outbound sharing gate. A refused sharing gate returns a response to the caller.

The service checks the conversation belongs to the person, takes a per-user lock, counts published apps against the 200 limit, and inserts or updates the row. A linked live artifact makes the audience invited. A new version is added only when the content changed.

The shared page first looks for a public row. If none, it checks the signed-in organization grant and the invited list. If none fits, the page shows invite-only or unavailable. Scripted kinds render in a sandbox.

The app's prompt goes to the runtime. The server first checks the AI switch and estimates cost, then refuses connector tools on public pages and Google user-data tools on the wrong model, then reserves usage through the managed usage request.

The settings section loads the published sites page by page. Unpublish opens a confirm dialog; on confirm the client calls the publish token route, which deletes the row for that owner. Cascades remove storage, viewers and versions.
Restore reads the chosen version for the owner and writes it into the live row, then records it as a new version and moves the live pointer.

guide.what_it_is_for: When an answer uses outside material, the person can see which source backs each claim. They can read the source's title, site, dates and a short quoted passage, and open the original. This lets a reader check an answer instead of trusting it, which is the main reason a research or search answer is worth more than a bare reply. Most of the area is built and working on web, desktop and mobile. The CLI, VS Code and Chrome side panel show only part of it, and the corrections, conflict and notice features are mostly missing.
guide.who_uses_it: Every person who gets an answer that has web sources or project-file sources, on each app that renders them. Research reports are used by people who run deep research and then open the report. The code I opened does not show a plan gate on citation display. I did not establish which plans can run web search or deep research, because that gate lives in server code I did not open. Project-file citations are for people who have a project with uploaded files. The brief does not name workspace admins or developers as separate users for this area.

features.name: Inline citation markers
features.use: Puts a small source chip at the claim it supports, so the reader sees which source backs which sentence. A claim that uses several sources shows one chip with a count.
how_people_use_it: Read the answer. Small chips with a site name (for example a domain) and a "+N" count sit at the end of claims.
Click a chip to open the first source in a new tab.
Hover a chip (mouse) to see a card that lists every source for that claim.
On mobile, tap a chip to see a native alert with the source title, site, dates, snippet and an Open page button.
how_it_should_work: Each marker in the answer text (for example a bracketed number) becomes a chip linked to the matching source in the list.
A run of markers with no words between them (for example [1][2]) becomes one grouped chip.
If the marker number has no matching source, no chip is drawn (the text is left as it was).
On web and desktop, the chip is a link to the first source. On mobile, a chip with no openable URL is disabled.
Limit: the number of sources is capped by the server-side source list, not by plan (not verified).
features.on_each_app: Web: done, inline chips via the shared markdown renderer with a tooltip card. Desktop: done, same shared renderer. Mobile: done, chips in MessageContentRenderer with a native alert. CLI: missing (the terminal renderer only lists links; it has no chips). VS Code: missing. Chrome side panel: done, with its own chip and hover card built in sources.ts (the brief marks Chrome as missing for this item, but the code has the chip, so the brief and the code disagree on Chrome for S36.01).

features.name: Source card details
features.use: Shows what a source is: its title, the site it came from, when it was published, when it was retrieved, and the excerpt that supports the claim.
how_people_use_it: Hover a chip on web or desktop to read the card. Focus it with the keyboard to read it too.
On mobile, tap the chip to read the same fields in the alert.
In the Chrome side panel, hover or focus the chip, or tap it on touch, to open its card with every source for that claim.
how_it_should_work: The title is shown; if there is no title, the site name is used.
The site is the publisher's domain, not the redirect host of a search provider. Where a source is a routing redirect, the domain is taken from the site name or title when that looks like a domain.
The published date is formatted as a date when it parses; a non-date phrase is shown as given, if it is 32 characters or fewer.
The retrieved date is shown as "Retrieved <date>" when the value parses.
The snippet is cut to 180 characters and ends with an ellipsis.
Empty state: fields that are missing are left out of the card, so a source with only a URL still shows its domain.
features.on_each_app: Web: done, card in the shared tooltip (CitationChip.tsx), plus the research panel rows (ResearchPanel.tsx). Desktop: done, same shared card. Mobile: done, the alert in CitationChip.tsx and the source row in WebSearchResultCard.tsx. CLI: missing for these fields. VS Code: missing. Chrome: partly done. The card has title, host, snippet and a raw publishedDate string, with no retrieved date (sources.ts:28-38). guide.area: Notebook and knowledge-workspace product (code calls these "projects")
guide.what_it_is_for: A notebook is a named workspace that holds the user's own sources (uploaded files, typed notes) and its own instructions. Chats inside it answer from those sources, and the user can click a citation to see the cited place. Studio buttons turn the sources into a briefing, study guide, FAQ, timeline, mind map, table or slide deck in one click. It matters because the answers stay tied to the user's own material, with a visible trail back to where each point came from.
guide.who_uses_it: Any signed-in account user, as the code shows: the project routes are scoped to the user, to the user's organization, and to projects shared with them (apps/web/lib/server/project-knowledge-files.ts:221-245). Adding sources needs an owner or an editor role (project-knowledge-files.ts:221-245; ProjectSharingControls.tsx:43-70). Viewers see sources and notes read-only (apps/web/app/chat/projects/[id]/page.tsx:1330). Paid plans affect file size and storage limits (project-knowledge-files.ts:255-263, plan tier from resolveFileStorageAllowance). Workspace admins are not singled out in the code I read.

how_it_works.step: Register the source on the server
how_it_works.detail: The POST route checks the body against the shared register schema, then registers the file. The route is scoped to the user and the organization.

The capacity check refuses archived projects, adds past 40 files without a same-name replacement, duplicate checksums, files over the plan size, and no storage left. It also checks that the user may add sources.
After save, the server extracts text and records index states. The panel polls the index state while indexing runs and offers a retry for failed files.
The GET route returns the project's live files (not deleted, not superseded), their index states and the storage meter.
When a chat belongs to a project, the turn loads the project row and up to 40 files, then renders them as capped system-context blocks with citations.
A Studio button sends a fixed prompt into a new chat in the project. No output is stored outside the chat.
A citation URL carries a cite parameter that opens the cited page. Notes are saved as the Notes.md source file.
Mobile decides whether a project is local or cloud, then picks files with the document picker and adds each one through the cloud source client.

key_files.role: Web API: lists a project's sources (GET) and registers a new one (POST), with the user and organization scope.
Server rules for sources: access checks, the 40-file cap, duplicate checks, plan size, storage, registration and index states.
Loads a project's instructions and source text for chat and renders it as capped context blocks with citations.
