how_it_works.step: 1. Press the microphone in the web composer
how_it_works.detail: The composer renders the mic button, which calls the dictation start function. The start function is wired from the dictation hook.

how_it_works.step: 2. The hook checks whether dictation may run
how_it_works.detail: It stops if the Voice setting is off, if the billing data switches dictation off, or if the chat is Local or own-key. It then creates a request owner so late results from an old recording are dropped, and asks the store to start.
The store asks for the microphone with echo cancellation and noise suppression, then records in short 100 ms chunks. The stream also feeds the waveform (use-dictation.ts:263-297).

how_it_works.step: 4. Stop and upload the whole recording
how_it_works.detail: Stopping ends the recorder, joins the chunks into one audio blob, and posts it as a form with the model and the language code to the web transcription endpoint.
The web endpoint checks the dictation switch, then the shared handler checks region, CSRF token, rate limit, sign-in, organisation policy and workspace spend cap, and the file size (25 MB).
Free plans draw from a monthly voice-second grant; paid plans reserve managed usage first. The transcription is sent to the provider, then usage is settled with the actual cost.
An empty result shows a message. Otherwise the text goes to the composer (insert) or is appended and sent (send). Send runs on the next render after the message is set.
Each failure code is mapped to a message. A plan or allowance refusal shows Upgrade and drops the recording; other failures keep the recording for Try again.

how_it_works.step: 9. The other apps take their own paths
how_it_works.detail: Phone: on-device speech recognition only, with a 60-second cap, no upload. Chrome extension: the browser's speech engine, text appended to the box. Command line: records to a WAV file, asks for consent, then sends to the managed account, a provider key, or a local program. VS Code: records, base64-encodes, posts to the same web endpoint with surface=vscode. Desktop shortcut: a separate floating window and typing path.

key_files.role: State machine for web dictation: start, stop, send, retry, cancel; checks switches; drives the waveform.
Microphone capture, upload to the web endpoint, failure messages, retry, language code handling.
Web entry point for dictation; checks the dictation kill switch and reuses the shared transcription handler.
Shared server handler: limits, sign-in, policy and spend gates, allowance and billing, provider call.
The recording bar: waveform, stop, send, discard, transcribing spinner, error with retry or upgrade.
Connects dictation to the composer: insert and send handlers, Local and own-key gate, desktop hotkey, mic button.
Phone speech capture using the device's own recognizer (on-device only), 60-second cap, file transcription.
Phone mic button: tap or hold, first-use intro, finish and cancel, error handling.
Command-line recording (120 s cap), consent notice, backend choice and privacy gate, retry and confirm prompts.
Chrome extension mic using the browser's speech engine and a first-use notice.
VS Code recording with a 3 MB and 120-second limit; sends audio to the shared endpoint through dictationClient.ts.
Desktop dictate-into-other-apps: front-app checks, guarded apps, text cleaning, 10-minute limit.

switches.name: Dictation setting (on or off)
switches.effect: Turns the microphone button off; the button shows 'Dictation is off in Voice settings'.

switches.name: Dictation kill switch (capability 'dictation')
switches.effect: Server and client turn dictation off for everyone for a release or incident, with an optional version reason.

switches.name: Plan voice-minute allowance
switches.effect: Free plans get a monthly number of voice minutes (converted to seconds); the value is set per plan in the model catalog file, one plan shows 10.

switches.name: Paid plan managed usage
switches.effect: Paid plans reserve and check voice minutes against their tier unit quota before transcribing.

switches.name: Organisation policy and spend cap
switches.effect: Blocks transcription when the workspace policy or spend cap refuses it.

switches.name: Rate limit 'audio-transcription'
switches.effect: Limits how many transcription requests one user can make.

switches.name: Upload size limit 25 MB
switches.effect: Refuses larger audio files.

switches.name: Phone voice on or off, and first-use flag
switches.effect: Turns phone dictation off; the first tap shows the intro sheet until it is seen.

switches.name: Phone 60-second listen cap
switches.effect: Stops a phone recording after 60 seconds.

switches.name: Command line 'voice' build feature
switches.effect: Builds without the voice feature refuse dictation with a message. Linux release builds leave it out.

switches.name: Command line 120-second cap
switches.effect: Stops a command-line recording.

switches.name: Command line privacy gate and provider key
switches.effect: In Local mode, an environment variable (AGIWORKFORCE_VOICE_ALLOW_CLOUD) must be set before audio goes to the provider. The provider key is read from an environment variable and selects the provider backend.

switches.name: Chrome extension browser speech and language
switches.effect: Button is disabled when the browser has no speech recognition. Language comes from the stored choice, else the browser languages.

switches.name: VS Code 3 MB and 120-second limits
switches.effect: Stops or refuses an overlong or oversized recording.

switches.name: Desktop 'dictate into the app you are using'
switches.effect: Turns on the dictate-into-other-apps path; turning it on asks for confirmation and needs accessibility access.

switches.name: Desktop dictation session limit
switches.effect: Ends a dictate-into-other-apps session after 10 minutes.

guide.shared_code: Shared: the web composer dictation code (use-dictation, voice-input-store, DictationStrip, the transcription route) is used by web and by the desktop window, which loads the hosted web app. The desktop dictation-bar window (apps/desktop/electron/dictationBar.ts) is desktop-only. The web transcription endpoint is also used by the VS Code extension (surface=vscode) and by the public API. The dictation state names and messages come from apps/web/features/chat/lib/dictation-machine (imported, not opened). Separate per app: phone speech capture (on-device, apps/mobile/src/features/voice), command-line recording (apps/cli/src/voice.rs, Rust), Chrome extension speech (apps/extension/src/features/side-panel/voice.ts, browser speech engine), VS Code recording (apps/extension-vscode/src/webview), and desktop dictate-into-apps (apps/desktop/electron). Live voice conversations use a separate server path (apps/web/app/api/voice/live/sessions).

guide.area: Audio overviews, speech generation, and music (brief area 50, 32 items)
guide.what_it_is_for: A person can have an assistant reply read aloud. Only the read-aloud part exists in code: it is done on web, desktop and mobile, and missing on the CLI, VS Code extension and Chrome extension. Everything else in the brief (audio overviews, music generation, voice cloning) has no feature code in the repository. Read-aloud lets a person listen while doing something else, and makes the app usable for people who cannot easily read the screen.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user on web and mobile can use read-aloud on a reply. how_it_works.step: Person taps Read aloud on a reply
how_it_works.detail: Web: the message list toggles speech for one message and passes a check that the message is still eligible (ChatMessageList.tsx:1785-1791). The web button is disabled for Local or own-key replies (MessageBubble.tsx:3981). Mobile: the handler checks the speech owner, then starts speech with the saved voice settings and server mode for Cloud (apps/mobile/src/features/chat/components/MessageBubble.tsx:2002-2023).
Markdown is stripped so the voice does not read symbols or raw code. Empty text stops here.

Text longer than 3,800 characters is cut at a sentence or line break. Each chunk is posted to the speech route with the speed and an Idempotency-Key header. The request uses the signed-in session; if there is no session, the browser voice is used instead.

how_it_works.step: Server checks before any provider call
how_it_works.detail: The route checks, in order: CSRF token, per-user rate limit, age gate, managed-compute gate, request shape (up to 4,000 characters), that the speech model slot is a live speech model, that the privacy setting allows this provider, and the model policy gate.

Cost is estimated from character count and the model's price. The route checks the account's access and reserves usage under the Idempotency-Key, so a retry does not charge twice. A quota or access failure returns an error body.

how_it_works.step: Call the speech provider and settle usage
how_it_works.detail: The server calls the provider's speech endpoint with the server key and a 60-second timeout. On failure, the reservation is released and an error is returned. On success, usage is finalized, delivery is marked, and the audio is returned as audio/mpeg with no-store caching.

how_it_works.step: Decode and play in the browser (web)
how_it_works.detail: The browser resumes its audio context, decodes each chunk, and plays chunks one after another. If the first chunk cannot be fetched or decoded, the device voice speaks the text. If a later chunk fails, the person sees the playback error.
The browser's own speech engine speaks with the chosen backup voice and speed. Starting a new device utterance cancels only the one this hook owns.

In Cloud mode, the text is split into 3,800-character chunks and fetched from the same speech route with a read-aloud Idempotency-Key. Each chunk is saved to a temporary file, played, then deleted. In Local mode, or after a server failure, the phone's voice speaks in 500-character chunks.

guide.what_it_is_for:
This area is meant to let a person build a voice bot that holds phone calls or talks on a website, for example to answer questions, book, or hand a caller to a human. The owner would give it a name, a role, instructions, a voice and knowledge sources, then attach it to a phone number or a web widget. Calls would leave transcripts, outcome labels, and metered minutes for billing.

The code does not do this yet. All 25 items are marked missing on web, desktop and mobile, and the API is missing where the brief lists it. Nothing in the repository creates a voice agent, a phone number, a SIP connection, a call or a call record. The nearest existing feature is live voice conversation in chat, which is a different feature.
guide.who_uses_it: Today: nobody, because no screen or route exists. The brief describes the intended users as the owner of a voice agent and the owner of a phone number. The brief does not say which plans may use it. Workspace admins and developers are not named in the brief or the code for this area.

guide.area: 052 Custom-assistant builder (assistants, called agents in the code)
guide.what_it_is_for: A custom assistant is a saved setup: a name, instructions, a preferred model, on/off switches for tools, optional reference files and sharing rules. Each time the person chats with it, the same setup applies. The brief lists 41 items and marks most of them missing for web, desktop, mobile, VS Code and Chrome. The code shows that web and desktop already have much of this area, and the CLI has its own version built on markdown files. This guide describes what the code does.

Desktop: the settings screen lists and edits agent files stored on the device. CLI: anyone who runs the CLI; project agents load only when the folder is trusted (apps/cli/src/agents.rs:255-257). how_it_works.detail: The Agents page calls the agents client, which calls the list route. The route checks rate limits and gets a user-scoped database handle, then reads the rows and returns them with a no-store header.
The editor starts from a blank draft or the saved assistant. The form checks the draft locally before saving. The server schema applies the same limits.
A write checks the CSRF token, then the server validates the body and inserts a row in user_agents. Defaults fill in any field left out.
Publish copies the current config into user_agent_versions with the next version number. Restore copies an old version back into the draft.

how_it_works.step: 5. Start a chat with the assistant (web)
how_it_works.detail: The conversations route checks the assistant can be read, then inserts a web chat row that stores the agent id.

how_it_works.step: 6. Apply the assistant on each turn (web)
how_it_works.detail: When a chat has an agent id, the chat request loads the assistant config. It stops if the assistant is paused, retired or over its daily turn limit, and returns a message.
An upload goes to the files route, which checks the owner and the file count, hashes the text and stores it in user_agent_files.
The desktop settings list reads agent markdown files from the Claude agents folders in the home and project directories. Writes go to the same folders.

The /agents command parses the subcommand. Create from words asks the session model for a draft and writes a file. Discovery reads markdown files from the home and project agent folders, with project folders only when trusted. When a session starts with an agent, its fields are applied to the session.

guide.what_it_is_for: A skill is a short instruction file (SKILL.md, with optional reference files and scripts) that teaches the assistant how to do one kind of task. This area lets a person find skills in a catalogue, turn them on or off, write their own, import or export them, and use them in chat by picking one or by letting the assistant match one to the request. It matters because the same skill works the same way across the apps, so a person's own method for a task can be reused without retyping it.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user for browsing, installing and using skills on web, desktop and mobile (Cloud mode). Writing or importing personal skills is gated by a server environment flag and a workspace feature gate, so it is not open to every account. CLI and VS Code users work with skill folders on their own machine (CLI global, account and project folders; VS Code personal and project folders). No code path for organisation admins or organisation-wide skills was found (brief items 05 and 25 are missing). Developers use the SKILL.md format and the skills packages; no separate developer-only surface was found.

how_it_works.detail: The screen asks the server for the skill list. The server returns the account's installed skills, or the whole catalogue when asked, merged with personal skills and plugin skills, each with origin, lifecycle, install count and required tools or connections. The list is checked against per-account install overrides.

how_it_works.step: 2. Install or turn off a skill
how_it_works.detail: Install and uninstall send a request with a CSRF token. The server writes a per-account override under the skills.installs key of the account's settings row inside a database transaction that locks the row. Authored skills are deleted rather than switched off.
The screen loads the skill body and file list, then shows provenance, version, required tools and connections, and a file viewer. Files that cannot be shown offer a download.

how_it_works.step: 4. Create or upload a personal skill
how_it_works.detail: A JSON body or a multipart upload (zip or Markdown) is read. Zip files are read for one skill folder; the content is checked by an upload scan and parsed for a valid draft. The name is checked against built-in names. The skill and its files are saved and an audit event is written.

how_it_works.step: 5. Pick a skill for a message
how_it_works.detail: The chat request may name one skill. The server validates the name, checks it exists in the catalog, adds the skill's instructions and the skill tool to the request, and reports a missing requirement when a tool or connection is not offered.

When no skill is named, the server picks skills whose descriptions fit the prompt, up to a fixed character budget, and offers them through the skill tool. This is skipped for the VS Code, CLI and API surfaces. Install overrides are read first; if that read fails, skills are withheld.

how_it_works.step: 7. Load a skill during the model turn
how_it_works.detail: When the model calls the skill tool with a load or read action, the tool returns the skill text, a file inventory and a note. Skills that ship scripts are copied into the code sandbox when code runs for the first time in the turn.
Personal skills live in a skills table with one row per skill and a child table for its files. Install overrides live in the settings row. Desktop and CLI read skill folders on disk.

guide.area: Plugin marketplace and customization (brief area 54, 40 items)
guide.what_it_is_for: A person finds add-ons (plugins) that add skills, connectors, agents, commands or hooks, installs them, and turns them on or off. It sits under one Customize area that also holds Skills and Connectors. A company can also run a private plugin marketplace for its members. Plugin use is the main way the product gets new abilities without a new app release.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in web or desktop user can browse and install plugins (installs are stored per user). Workspace admins assign plugins to an organization, its groups or members. Publishers submit plugins for review. Platform staff moderate listings. Command-line users manage plugins from the terminal, both on disk and from their account's marketplaces. Mobile and the Chrome extension have no plugin install path in the code I read. Plan-level limits were not established (not sure).

how_it_works.detail: The Customize group in the settings navigation lists Skills, Connectors and Plugins. The chat customize route only redirects to the matching settings section.

how_it_works.step: Load the directory and install state
how_it_works.detail: The directory hook loads the catalogue and the user's installs in one place. It keeps the plugin page state and the settings target.
The install route checks the request token, applies a rate limit, validates the plugin id, and then runs the workspace and dependency gates before it plans and writes the install.

how_it_works.step: Gates decide if the install is allowed
how_it_works.detail: The workspace feature check for plugins (and skills for authored plugins) runs first. Then each plugin is checked against the organization policy.
The service works out required dependencies, then writes the install row for each one. The write upserts the row, turns it on, and records the approved permissions and skills.

how_it_works.step: Turn a plugin on or off
how_it_works.detail: The enable route checks unmet dependencies when turning on. When turning off, it refuses if other plugins depend on it, unless withDependents is set, in which case those dependents are turned off too.
Versions move only along allowed steps (draft, in review, published, deprecated, suspended). The installed view lists only published versions.
The customize route checks the request token, applies a rate limit, runs the authored-skill gate, and copies the installed plugin's skills into an owned editable copy.
The marketplace route accepts a public GitHub address, registers the source, and writes an audit event.
The command-line tool has its own plugin commands. Marketplace installs go to the account (cloud); plugin installs from a path or git address are kept on disk in the plugins folder.

guide.area: Connector setup and account management (brief area 55, 32 items)
guide.what_it_is_for: Connectors let the assistant read and act in outside services such as Gmail, Google Drive, Linear or Notion. This area is where a person browses the connector catalogue, reads what a connector can read and change, connects it (sign-in or API key), checks that it still works, reconnects it when access expires, and disconnects it. It matters because the assistant can only use a connector that the person has connected, and every write it makes depends on the approval settings chosen here.
guide.who_uses_it: Signed-in users on web, desktop (which shows the same hosted web settings), mobile, the VS Code extension and the CLI. Workspace admins use the organization-shared connector settings (apps/web/app/workspace/sharing/page.tsx:10-20) to authorize a connector once for members. Plan tiers limit tool counts (apps/web/app/api/connectors/[connectorId]/credentials/route.ts:190, assertConnectorToolCapacity). Connectors are gated by a release state: by default only a short list of connector IDs is released (see switches), so most catalogue entries cannot be connected yet.

Type in the search box to match name, publisher, tools or description.
Pick a category chip to filter (for example Productivity or Developer).

While loading, show a waiting state; on failure show an error notice rather than an empty list.
Search and category filtering run on the loaded catalogue.
Connectors that are not released show as not yet available, not as connectable.

how_it_works.step: 1. The person opens a connector and presses Connect or Reconnect
how_it_works.detail: The shared detail view decides which primary action to show. A reconnect state shows Reconnect and a reconnect message; otherwise a connect or open action is shown.

how_it_works.step: 2. The web app loads the catalogue and the person's connections
how_it_works.detail: The settings adapter fetches the managed connectors list and the directory in parallel. The list API merges connections from custom servers, GitHub, OAuth grants and the directory, and adds a health marker from recent calls.

how_it_works.step: 3. The connect request is checked by policy and routed by connector type
how_it_works.detail: POST /api/connectors checks CSRF, rate limit, the workspace access gate and the connector policy. It then routes: device-only connectors are refused on web, GitHub uses its own install flow, regional and account-URL connectors are refused or sent to custom setup, bank accounts go to Plaid, and OAuth connectors return an oauthStartPath with a 409 that tells the client to start sign-in.

how_it_works.step: 4. Sign-in start builds the provider request
how_it_works.detail: The OAuth start route checks token storage (503 if unavailable), runs the workspace access and connector policy again, reads existing accounts, detects scope widening (scopes above the reviewed list are dropped and re-consent is requested), then builds the provider's authorization request.

how_it_works.step: 5. The provider returns to the callback
how_it_works.detail: The callback checks the state value; a malformed state returns invalid_state. It then calls the shared finish step, which exchanges the code and stores the grant, and redirects back to Connectors with a status.

how_it_works.step: 6. The token is exchanged and the account label is read
how_it_works.detail: The OAuth client exchanges the code for tokens and takes a display label from the identity token's email, preferred username or UPN claim.
Grants are written to the connector OAuth tables with an account key ('default' for every grant written before multiple accounts). Listing reads accounts by connector and user.

DELETE removes the connector's stored grant (and custom connector rows and tool permissions) and asks the provider to revoke the token. The result is reported as revoked, nothing to revoke, or not revoked with a manage link.

how_it_works.step: 9. Health, test and tool permissions at call time
how_it_works.detail: The health endpoint returns each connector's health state. The capability catalogue for one connector lists its tools with read-only flag and risk tier. The credentials route probes an API-key connector before saving it and maps failures to 502 messages. Per-tool levels Allow, Ask and Deny are set in the permissions panel.

key_files.role: Release gate. Sets the default state to coming_soon and lists the 13 connector IDs that are released selectively.
Main connector API: list (GET, line 233), connect (POST, line 530) and disconnect (DELETE, line 880).
Starts the provider sign-in, runs policy checks and scope-widening checks, and builds the consent request.
Receives the provider redirect, checks state, and hands the code to the shared finish step.
Stores and lists OAuth grants and accounts (tables connector_oauth_grants and connector_oauth_authorizations).
Refreshes grants, marks expired or revoked ones as needing reauthorization, and revokes tokens at the provider.
Account key normalisation and the readable account label taken from the sign-in token.
Shared detail page: primary action (Connect, Reconnect), operation list and read/write copy; used by web and desktop.
Web settings state: loads the catalogue and connections, and runs connect, disconnect, test and reconnect calls.
Per-tool Allow, Ask and Deny, grouped into read-only and write categories, with reset to default.
Mobile connector detail, disconnect and write-action settings.
CLI connector commands (connect, API-key entry, disconnect, reconnect); Rust, separate from the web code.

guide.area: Concrete integration families (connectors to outside apps such as Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Slack, GitHub, CRM, banks)
guide.what_it_is_for: This area lets the assistant work inside the apps a person already uses: search and read email, draft or send mail, look at calendars, edit cloud files, post to team chat, update tickets and CRM records, and read bank or health data. Writes (sending, creating events, posting) are meant to wait for the user's approval. It matters because it moves real work out of the chat window and into the user's own accounts. how_it_works.step: Operator sets up each connector's OAuth client
how_it_works.detail: The server reads CONNECTOR_OAUTH_PROVIDERS_JSON, validates each provider entry (HTTPS URLs, scopes, an enabled flag that defaults to true), and reads the client id and secret from CONNECTOR_OAUTH_<ID>_CLIENT_ID and _CLIENT_SECRET.

how_it_works.step: Connector is declared in the catalog and directory
how_it_works.detail: Each connector has a capability record (Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Contacts, Slack, GitHub-MCP, Outlook, HealthEx and others) and a directory entry with its hosted server address (Gmail's server is listed there).

how_it_works.step: Release gate decides whether the connector may be used
how_it_works.detail: A single constant sets the whole family to coming soon. Only a short list of connectors is released by name. A connector outside that list is refused before any MCP connection is opened.

how_it_works.step: OAuth scopes are capped by a per-connector ceiling
how_it_works.detail: Requested scopes are filtered to the connector's allowed list; scopes outside it are dropped and reported. Connectors whose ceiling is still under review get no filter.

how_it_works.step: A request-scoped MCP client is opened
how_it_works.detail: For an allowed connector, the server opens a client to the connector's hosted MCP server for this one request, runs the operation, and closes it before returning. Discovery is also checked against the user's policy first.

how_it_works.step: Gmail-specific tools are declared in code
how_it_works.detail: The Gmail actions (read attachments, create draft with attachments, send draft) are defined as tools with qualified names. The draft tool says the draft is not sent until the user has seen it and send_draft is called.

how_it_works.step: Approval decides whether a write runs
how_it_works.detail: Tool approval is decided by the user's policy and the organization's policy. The chat route also accepts an approval_mode=auto query that skips prompts. Each approval is recorded as a pause in the run.

how_it_works.step: Model tool call is streamed back to the app
how_it_works.detail: The LLM crate turns the model's tool calls into a tool handoff that the desktop and CLI show to the user. The tool result is returned to the model; I did not trace the full return path.

key_files.role: Validates the operator's OAuth provider list and resolves client ids and secrets per connector.
Holds the release state (currently coming soon) and the short list of released connector ids; the gate for every connector.
Per-connector scope ceilings (what each connector is allowed to request).
Filters requested OAuth scopes against the ceiling and reports dropped ones.
Opens the per-request MCP client for a connected connector and applies the release and discovery checks.
Capability records for each connector (actions, surfaces, risk class).
Gmail-specific tool definitions: attachments, drafts, send_draft.
Directory entries with hosted server addresses (for example the Gmail MCP URL) and tool lists.
Decides whether a tool call runs without asking, using user and organization policy.
CLI side of approvals: records the pause when a tool needs approval and prompts the user.
Bank link records (Plaid items) and the carry-over from an older single bank link.

guide.what_it_is_for: A tool is an action the assistant can take during a reply, such as searching the web, reading a file, running code, creating a document or saving a memory. This area is how the assistant calls those tools, how the person sees each call and its result, and how the person finds out which tools exist. It matters because the assistant is only as useful as the actions it can actually take, and the person must be able to see and trust each action.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in person on the web, desktop, mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome apps sees the tool calls in a chat. Web search, page fetch and memory are offered by the server to the chat as a whole, with per-turn limits that depend on the mode of the turn (ordinary or agent work). Scheduled tasks are blocked in temporary chats and limited by plan tier. Sandbox execution tools are off unless the server has the sandbox switch on and the account passes the code-execution policy check. Desktop device steps need the desktop app and a folder or screen the person has granted. Workspace admin rules were not established in the code I opened.

how_it_works.detail: A result too big for the reply is saved under the user and conversation with a random reference, kept 24 hours, and the reply gets a reference. A reader tool pages through it 40000 characters at a time.

Memory tools save one sentence or delete matching memories; deletion waits for the person's approval. The schedule tool checks temporary-chat status, takes a database lock, checks the plan quota, and creates the task.
The web transcript shows each call as a timeline with a retry control for the whole turn. Each shared card shows the arguments and the result preview and can expand.

guide.area: MCP and interactive extension products (brief area 058: MCP server management, MCP app panels, site-provided tools)
guide.what_it_is_for: This area lets a person connect outside tools to the assistant using MCP (Model Context Protocol, a shared standard for giving an AI access to outside tools, resources and prompts). A person can add a remote server by web address or a local server on their machine, see what it offers, and switch it off without deleting it. Some tool results also show a small interactive panel (an "MCP App") inside the chat, and the browser extension can use tools that a web page itself publishes.
guide.who_uses_it: Signed-in users of the web app and desktop can manage their own custom servers; adding one is gated by the workspace access check and the organization policy flag allowCustomConnectors (apps/web/app/api/connectors/custom/route.ts:94-112). Workspace admins control the organization-approved catalog and can publish or retire servers (role check "policy.manage", apps/web/app/api/settings/organization/mcp/route.ts:240-245). Developers use the CLI to add local servers and project-level config files. Chat users see MCP App panels when a tool returns one. The browser extension uses site-provided tools on pages it runs on. A per-plan cap on connector tools exists (apps/web/lib/user-connector-tools.ts:177-179); the exact paid-plan rules were not traced.

how_it_works.detail: The web app and desktop request the user's custom connectors. The route checks the user, rate limit and workspace access, then returns the user's connectors with a sign-in flag from their OAuth grants.

The route checks CSRF, rate limit, workspace access and the allowCustomConnectors policy. If allowed, it reads the body and creates the connector, then records an external resource reference and returns 201.

The capabilities route validates the connector ID, loads the user's capability catalog, and returns tools, resources, prompts, apps and discovery errors. Text from the server is cleaned before display, and each tool gets a read-only flag and risk tier.
When a tool returns an app, the payload (tool input and result) is saved for 30 days. Payloads over 2 MB are not saved.
The tool loop turns a tool result that carries an app into a card of kind mcp-app.v1, with a text fallback for clients that cannot show it. A failed task binding returns a message instead.

The web card registry maps the kind to McpAppCard. The card builds a sandbox URL on a separate origin (required in production), waits for the sandbox to be ready, then passes the resource with its security policy. Device requests from the app need approval per device name.
An admin's publish or retire request checks the policy.manage role and the connectors-released gate, then updates the server, checks the workspace revision and writes an audit event.
The content script discovers page-published tools and reports them to the background worker, which sends change updates. The browser agent's discover action takes no arguments.

Runs an MCP App in a sandboxed frame in the web chat and handles tool-call approval and resizing.
Creates the mcp-app.v1 chat card from a tool result and saves its payload.
Admin catalog: publish and retire approved servers with role, release gate, revision and audit checks.
Mobile client that fetches a saved MCP App payload from the web payload route.
Mobile chat card switch; renders McpAppCard for kind mcp-app.v1.
Finds tools a web page declares (declarative and imperative) and watches for changes.
Extension browser agent; has the discover_site_tools action.
CLI MCP runtime; reads project and global .mcp.json and mcp.json config files.
Builds the user's connector tool catalog, applies the plan tool limit and the connectors-released gate.

guide.what_it_is_for: When the agent wants to do something that can change data, send a message, spend money, or touch files on the person's computer, it stops and waits for the person to approve or deny it. This area is the set of prompts, buttons, saved rules and modes that let the person decide each action, remember that decision, or choose how often the agent should ask. It matters because it is how the person stays in control of what the agent does on their behalf.
guide.who_uses_it: The code I opened shows approval prompts for signed-in people on the managed Cloud path (the chat completions routes), and for local desktop and CLI sessions. I found no paid-plan gate on approvals in the files I opened. Workspace admins have one control: the server reads a workspace setting named allowAutonomousToolApprovals (packages/contracts/types/src/tool-approval-policy.ts:80). features.name: Approve or deny one action
features.use: A tool call that needs a decision waits. The person allows it so it runs, or denies it so it does not run.
how_people_use_it: Web and desktop: read the card in the chat, then press Approve or Deny on that card.
Mobile: press Allow once or Deny on the tool row in the chat.
CLI: press Yes or No in the approval overlay (the keys are shown on the buttons).
VS Code: press Allow once or Deny in the notification.
how_it_should_work: While the call waits, the card shows the waiting state and the run pauses.
Allow runs the call and the run continues. Deny stops that call and the model is told it was denied.
If the approval has expired, the card shows it as expired and the action cannot run from it (see the timing feature).
If the server cannot resume the run, the person sees an error and the lease on the checkpoint is released.
features.on_each_app: Web, desktop, mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome: done (per brief). API: done.

features.name: Approve several calls at once
features.use: A run can ask for several tool calls together. The person can answer them all in one action.
how_people_use_it: Tasks page on web, desktop and mobile: use the batch approval control on the pending run.
how_it_should_work: All pending calls of one run are decided together, and the run then resumes once.
The brief does not say what happens when one call in the batch fails; not verified.

features.name: Remember a decision, review saved rules, and see history
features.use: The person can allow a tool for this chat or session, set allow, ask or deny for each connected app and tool, keep those choices, see past decisions, and revoke a saved choice.
how_people_use_it: Web chat: choose Allow for this chat (session scope) on the approval card; manage saved rules in the connectors panel (ToolPermissionsPanel) and the approval history panel in settings.
Mobile: Allow for chat and Always allow buttons on the approval row; saved rules in connector settings; history in settings.
CLI: Allow Session (until the session ends) or Always allow (saved in the config file) in the overlay; the /permissions command edits rules.
Desktop: the permission prompt offers the choice, and the review list shows saved decisions.
how_it_should_work: A session allow stops asking until the session ends. A saved allow stays across sessions and devices until the person changes it.

A standing allow is refused for a critical tool (one that can delete or send data that cannot be recovered). That tool always asks. The server raises CriticalStandingAllowError (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/lib/connector-tool-permissions.ts:45).
Revoking a saved choice makes the next call ask again.
If the workspace forbids the skip-approvals mode, a stored skip choice drops back to the default ask mode, not to the read-only mode.

features.name: Permission modes
features.use: One switch decides how every tool runs: ask every time, run reads without asking, or skip approvals. Read-only and ask-before-writing are variants of the same idea.
how_people_use_it: Web settings: the action approvals panel (ToolApprovalDefaultsPanel) lists the three modes.
Mobile: Settings, then Action approvals (auto-approve screen) with the same three options.
CLI: press Shift+Tab to cycle Default, Plan, Auto, Bypass and Full Auto modes.
Web connector panel: a bulk preset marks all read-only tools as one level and writes as another.
how_it_should_work: Ask before every action (ask_every_time) is the default. Reads, searches, page fetches and sandboxed code run on their own under the read-only mode; writes, sends, purchases and unknown tools still ask.
Skip approvals (autonomous) runs tools without waiting, but destructive actions, unknown connector tools and some sends still ask. It is only used when the workspace allows it.
Read-only mode should refuse write, send and execute tools. The code I opened only sets saved levels per tool in the connector panel; it does not refuse them globally (not verified).

features.name: What the approval shows, and stronger checks for risky actions
features.use: Each approval says what the tool will do: who gets a message, the amount of a purchase, the destination, the exact command, the files or records that change, and the diff for an edit. Risky actions get a stronger prompt.
how_people_use_it: Read the stakes list on the card (recipient, amount, item, path, command, destination) and the request block (the command, diff or JSON arguments).
For a file edit, read the diff shown in the request block.
For a risky action, read the warning, then choose Allow once. A permanent allow is not offered for it.
how_it_should_work: The stakes are derived from the tool's arguments (send tools show recipients, payment tools show amount and item). A value too long is cut and shows how many more there are.
The card shows a plain summary and why it needs approval. Destructive and irreversible actions show a warning and do not offer a permanent allow.
If the request has no readable parameters, the card says so rather than hiding the request.

features.name: Approval timing and resuming a run
features.use: An approval waits for a limited time. After the person decides, the same run continues and the transcript shows what happened.
how_people_use_it: Answer the approval while it is shown as waiting. If you come back later, the card says it expired.
After a decision, watch the same chat: the action should show as ran, or denied, with its result.
how_it_should_work: Cloud approvals stay open for 24 hours (APPROVAL_CHECKPOINT_TTL_HOURS). Device approvals stay open for 15 minutes. CLI prompts expire after 10 minutes.
If a checkpoint is past its time, the server answers 410 with the message 'This approval request expired and can no longer be resumed.' and the action does not run.
A run that is already resuming holds a lease; the lease expires on its own if the resume stops.

how_it_works.step: 1. The agent wants a tool. The gate ranks the rules and decides allow, ask, deny, or escalate.
how_it_works.detail: Each tool call is checked against nine ranked rules, in order. Rule 1 denies a call the person blocked. Rule 4 allows a call the person always allowed. Rule 5 asks when the person chose ask. Rule 7 asks in manual mode. A 'lethal trifecta' (untrusted content, a sensitive source and an egress path together) escalates. Rule 9 allows when nothing else applies. 'escalate' asks and, when unattended, denies unless the run can pause.
The stored policy is read per request from the user's settings row. An autonomous choice is downgraded to the default when the workspace forbids it. Unknown stored values fall back to the default.
Saved allow, ask and deny levels for each connector tool are loaded and combined with session grants, workspace rules and lockdown. A standing allow for a critical tool is refused when saved.

how_it_works.step: 4. The run pauses and a checkpoint is saved.
how_it_works.detail: When a call must wait, the run's messages and pending calls are saved as a checkpoint with a time limit. Cloud checkpoints last 24 hours and device checkpoints 15 minutes.

how_it_works.step: 5. The card shows the request and its stakes.
how_it_works.detail: The stakes (recipients, amounts, items, paths, commands, destination) are built from the tool arguments and shared by all apps. The web card shows Approve and Decision buttons, the request block and the stakes list.
The client collects each call's decision (approved or rejected, with session or always scope) and posts tool_approvals to the resume path. Mobile sends the same shape from its execution store.

how_it_works.step: 7. The server checks and saves the decision.
how_it_works.detail: The approve route claims the checkpoint (410 if expired), checks each scoped approval against the offered tool and its generation, and saves session or always grants. A stale permission returns 409.

how_it_works.step: 8. The run resumes from the checkpoint.
how_it_works.detail: The saved request is rebuilt with the same messages and the decisions. Denied calls return a denial to the model. The lease on the checkpoint is released on failure.

how_it_works.step: 9. Local desktop and CLI keep their own prompts.
how_it_works.detail: The desktop app asks through its own permission manager and stores decisions in a file in the app data folder. The CLI overlay answers the broker's request and stores rules in its config file.

Defines the resume path that the apps post approval decisions to.
Server side of a decision: claims the checkpoint, checks expiry, saves session and always grants, resumes the run.
The ranked rules that decide allow, ask, deny or escalate for each tool call.
Loads and saves per-tool allow, ask and deny levels, and the lockdown and disabled-connector checks.
Checkpoint lifetimes (24 hours cloud, 15 minutes device) and the claim and release of approval checkpoints.

Web approval controls: Approve, the decision group (allow with scope, or reject) and the always-allow confirmation.
Mobile approval controls: allow once, allow for chat, always allow, and the text box to tell the agent what to do instead.

switches.name: Default policy: ask every time

switches.name: Cloud account default: skip approvals
switches.effect: Cloud accounts start on the skip mode unless the user changes it.

switches.name: Workspace setting allowAutonomousToolApprovals
switches.effect: When not true, a workspace forbids the skip mode; members fall back to the default. Absent means allowed.

switches.name: Autonomy availability check in settings
switches.effect: The settings panel asks whether skip mode is allowed for this user and hides the option if not.

switches.name: Connector lockdown
switches.effect: A locked-down account uses the locked-down permission set, which refuses tools.

switches.name: Unattended escalation pause
switches.effect: When a run is unattended and cannot pause, an escalation is denied instead of allowed.

switches.name: Device checkpoint lifetime

switches.effect: How long a CLI approval waits (600 seconds).

switches.effect: Changes the permission mode for the CLI session; skip modes appear only when the session was launched with them.

guide.area: Agentic work product (AGI Work tasks: Cloud runs the user starts, watches, steers and reviews)
guide.what_it_is_for: A person describes a goal in plain words, and a managed agent runs it as a task in the background, with a plan, visible steps, and a result they can open, change, pause, or stop. The point is to get finished work (a report, a file, a set of actions) instead of a single chat reply. Because the task runs on the server, it can continue when the person closes the app, and the person can follow it from another device.
guide.who_uses_it: Only users whose plan grants the agi_work capability and whose account has the canUseAgiWork switch on. The handshake removes canUseAgiWork when no agentic model is in the catalog or when the plan lacks agi_work (apps/web/lib/services/capability-handshake-service.ts:101, :121). Which plans grant agi_work was not established. Admins and developers were not seen as a separate group in this area. The Tasks list shows only runs made in agiwork mode (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/runs/route.ts:67).

Optionally add constraints and the deliverable they want (for example a report or a file).
Press send. On mobile the same fields are in a start-work sheet, then the run starts.
how_it_should_work: The goal is required and limited in length. Constraints and deliverable are optional and limited in length (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/lib/agiwork-plan.ts:27 AgiWorkGoalSchema).
Empty optional fields are dropped, so an empty field and a missing field are stored the same way.
The run record stores the goal. A readable title is the goal cut to 60 characters (apps/mobile/src/features/tasks/startWork.ts:33).
Failure: if the request is refused, the person sees the refusal and no run is created (not verified in the UI).
No plan-specific limit beyond the capability gate was seen for starting a task.

features.name: Steer, pause, resume and stop
features.use: Lets the person send new guidance into a running task, pause it, resume it, or stop it for good.
how_people_use_it: Type a message in the steer box on a running task and send. A queued message can be withdrawn.
Press Pause on a running task; press Resume on a paused or stopped one; press Cancel (Stop) to end it.

how_it_should_work: Steer: the message is queued on the run. If the queue is full the request fails (cloud-agent-run-service.ts:2850). A message the task can still read cannot be withdrawn; the server says it stays queued (steer/[steerId]/route.ts withdraw error).

Pause: allowed only while the run is in an executor-held state; otherwise HTTP 409 with the text Only a task that is still working can be paused (pause/route.ts). The pause is recorded and the run stops at a step boundary (step boundary not traced).
Cancel: marks cancellation on the server (runs/[runId]/route.ts:81). A run waiting on the person is cancelled at once (route.ts:84 cancelHumanHeldCloudAgentRun).
Resume: a paused run resumes from its checkpoint (resume route).
Failure: each route returns an error; the steer box keeps the draft and shows the error.

how_it_works.step: Turn on the mode and check the switch
how_it_works.detail: The composer sends the goal only when the agiwork mode is on and the account has canUseAgiWork. The server checks the same capability before it runs the turn. The kill switch maps canUseAgiWork to the 'work' subject.
The request carries agi_work_goal. It is parsed for goal, constraints, deliverable and excludedTools, with length limits and empty fields dropped.
The mobile app builds the goal input, picks a cloud model, and starts a run. The run id is passed back so the app can follow it.

how_it_works.step: Run the agent loop and emit steps
how_it_works.detail: The server runs the agent turn. Steps, plan and progress are emitted as events. A clarify question can pause the run and resume it with the answer.

how_it_works.step: Store run state and follow it
how_it_works.detail: Runs are rows in a server table. Listing filters by agiwork mode and active states. Follow-up reads the snapshot and its events by sequence number.

Pause sets pause_requested_at only while the run is executor-held, else it returns 409. Steer queues a message on the run. Cancel marks a cancellation, and a human-held run is cancelled at once. Each write is CSRF-checked and audited.
A paused run is claimed by a lease, then re-run from its saved checkpoint. The lease is released when done or on error.
The shared Tasks page renders the list, detail panel, steer box and actions. Each app renders its own detail view.

guide.what_it_is_for: This area lets a person run more than one AI at once in three ways. A main task can start child agents that work on parts of a job, and the user can see each child's role, status and result. A user can watch many running cloud tasks in one overview and answer the ones waiting for them. A user can also send one prompt to two or three models and read the answers side by side, to pick the better one.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user can open the model comparison on web and mobile. The code gates it by the plan's model list and by cloud access, not by a workspace role. The command-line child-agent tools run in any session where the model may call the task tool; the code refuses nested children beyond a depth limit. The cloud task overview lists runs produced by the AGI Work mode. No workspace-admin-only path was seen in the code read.

how_it_works.detail: The model calls the task tool, or the user runs a task. The manager checks the depth limit, the session spend cap and the concurrent-child limit, then gives the child an id and a role (general-purpose or a named agent). The child runs on its own thread. The parent keeps an entry with status, result and usage.

how_it_works.step: 2. Child route stays inside the parent boundary
how_it_works.detail: A child is built on the parent route (model, provider, privacy mode). If the route would leave the parent's trust boundary, the spawn is refused.
The child's status changes to completed, failed or cancelled as the run ends. Usage and the transcript are saved on the entry, and an audit record is written.
The /task or /tasks command calls the manager, prints the list (id, role, status, description), and prints a detail or transcript for one id.

The /advisor command returns a request. The REPL or full-screen view runs the advisor tool, which returns JSON with the answer and the model used. The output is shown with the model label and is not added to the conversation.
The user sends a prompt. The page uses up to three models, starts workers limited by the plan concurrency number, and each worker streams one answer into its own panel.
Two streaming requests run from the compare screen. If the plan allows one answer at a time, the second waits for the first. Local mode is refused before any request is sent.

how_it_works.step: 8. Cloud task list and needs-you grouping
how_it_works.detail: The cloud runs endpoint lists runs for the AGI Work mode. The shared overview groups runs into filters, and runs in awaiting-input, awaiting-approval or paused states count as needing the user.

how_it_works.step: 9. Inline reply to a waiting run
how_it_works.detail: The run detail sends a steer answer through the cloud transport. The page replaces the run with the server copy. The resume route releases and checks the pause lease before continuing.
A branch request posts to the managed conversation branches route for one message. The hook blocks a second branch while one is being made.

how_it_works.step: Person asks from the web composer
how_it_works.detail: The Use the browser row in the composer opens the browser tools dialog. The dialog lists actions and each one calls a desktop command.
Each browser action is described as a shared step with its command, capability and description. The desktop plan for a command sets the confirm title and text.
The bridge server checks the origin and the token for each route. Browser commands are refused unless the browser is paired, except open tab.

how_it_works.step: Website rules check each landing page
how_it_works.detail: After an action that may land on a new page, the desktop reads the tab address and checks the workspace allow and deny lists. A refused page is left by going back.
The desktop pane is an Electron view in its own persistent session. Permission requests are denied. Back, forward and reload check history before they move.

how_it_works.step: Chrome side panel runs the agent
how_it_works.detail: The panel shows Stop and Take over buttons during a run. The agent loop waits when the person takes over and resumes when they hand back.
Downloads always ask for approval. Each click is checked after it settles, and typed fields are read back.
The CLI offers browser tools only when a browser is paired. Each call asks for approval with a message that names the action, and navigation checks workspace website rules first.
Shared text is cut to a size limit and the first link is found. Summarize sends a fixed prompt with the shared text. Nothing is read from the open browser page.
Pane cookies live in a persistent Electron session that the clear action wipes. Consent is kept in extension storage. History is read only when asked for each search.

guide.area: Coding-workspace frontend (the /code coding surface on web, plus its desktop, mobile, CLI and VS Code counterparts)
guide.what_it_is_for: A coding session lets a person ask the AI agent to read, change and test code in a project folder or a git repository. The person picks the folder or repository, watches the agent work, sees the changes and checks, and decides what it may do without asking. This area is the screens and controls for that: starting a session, the session list, the file and terminal panels, the change review, checkpoints, plan and approval modes, usage, previews, pull requests, and sharing. It matters because it is the part of the product where the agent touches real files and runs real commands, so the controls for permission and review carry the trust.
guide.who_uses_it: Local sessions (on the person's own computer) run only inside the desktop app, because the web page only reaches a local folder through the desktop host bridge (apps/web/features/code/hooks/use-local-sessions.ts:121, apps/web/features/desktop-host/lib/host.ts:34-36). Cloud sessions (in a managed sandbox) need the deployment flag and a paid plan that includes coding (apps/web/app/api/code/sessions/route.ts:57-64). Sharing a cloud session is limited by the person's role in a workspace (apps/web/lib/services/cloud-code-session-sharing.ts:32-35). Mobile is a remote control for sessions that run on a desktop, not a separate runner. Developers use the terminal CLI and the VS Code extension directly.

features.name: Start a session in a folder, branch or worktree
features.use: Chooses where the session runs: a folder or repository, which git branch it starts from, whether it runs in its own worktree (a second working copy of the repository), and whether it runs locally or in the cloud.
how_people_use_it: On web /code, open the composer; choose the repository from the list or paste a repository URL, then choose a branch.
In the composer, open the 'Run the session in' radio group and pick 'This folder', 'New worktree' or 'New worktree with my changes'.
In the desktop app, pick a folder with the folder picker, then start a session.
In the terminal, add --worktree (or -w) with an optional name to start in a worktree; without a name one is made up.
In VS Code, the active editor's folder is used; if there is only one folder it is used without asking; otherwise a quick-pick asks which folder.
how_it_should_work: Before a session starts, the person sees which folder or repository it will use.
The worktree choice must keep parallel sessions from editing the same files.
Empty state: with no repository or folder available, the picker must say so and offer a way to add one (not verified in every app).
Waiting state: the list of repositories and branches loads first; a failed load shows an error and a Retry button (CodeComposer.tsx:1443-1450 region).
Failure: if a session cannot start, the person sees a message and no half-started session is left (not verified).
Limits by plan: cloud sessions are capped by the plan's maximum number of active sandboxes (apps/web/lib/services/cloud-code-session-service.ts:1243-1256).
features.on_each_app: Web: repository picker and placement radio work for the local side inside the desktop app; for cloud, the repository picker exists, but cloud sessions stay off unless the deployment flag and sandbox key are set (brief status: partial). Desktop: folder picker, local or worktree start, and branch switching exist (done). Mobile: no picker; it shows the folder list and branch name of sessions from the desktop (missing for start). CLI: --worktree flag exists; there is no branch picker in the brief (worktree done, branch missing). VS Code: picks the folder from the active editor (done); no worktree picker (missing).

how_it_works.detail: On web, the composer lets the person choose the runtime, folder and placement (folder, new worktree, or new worktree with changes). The placement values are fixed in one list.

The web page treats itself as a desktop host only when the desktop bridge exists. Without it, the local side is off and only cloud sessions can be listed. The cloud list reports whether the deployment and the plan allow coding.
The web page asks the desktop shell to start a session. The shell checks the request, then starts the bundled CLI agent in the folder (or in a worktree) with the chosen start point.
The server first checks that the deployment has the sandbox flag and key and a price rate, then the private-beta gate, then the plan's active-sandbox limit. Only then is a cloud session created.

how_it_works.step: Check the permission for each action
how_it_works.detail: Each desktop action is listed with the capability it needs and a plain reason. Running programs, computer use and remote control each need their own grant. The agent's approval policy is set in the composer and sent with each turn.
The desktop forwards events from the CLI. The web page turns each event into a row marker: running, needs approval, needs input, or failed. A turn that ends normally clears the marker.

how_it_works.step: Read and edit files and git state
how_it_works.detail: File reads and saves go through the desktop bridge. The change list and diff come from git commands run on the folder. Editing refuses non-UTF-8 and very large files.

how_it_works.step: Keep queued messages in the page
how_it_works.detail: Follow-up messages, a draft and attached context files for a local session are kept in a memory map in the page. They are lost on a full reload.
The mobile app sends session commands (list, attach, detach, steer) over the remote link. The desktop host controller receives them and acts on the session.
The owner changes the sharing state; the server checks the workspace role first. A teammate opens the shared page, which loads the session read-only.

switches.name: AGI_E2B_EXECUTION (set to 1)
switches.effect: Turns on the cutover to cloud execution. Without it, cloud session provisioning is refused.

switches.name: E2B_API_KEY
switches.effect: The sandbox provider key. Its presence alone enables the execution check; provisioning also needs the flag and a priced rate.

switches.name: Sandbox rate card
switches.effect: Cloud provisioning is allowed only when a rate can be resolved.

switches.name: AGI_MANAGED_COMPUTE_PRIVATE_BETA
switches.effect: Private-beta gate for managed compute. On when unset; setting it to 0, false or off turns cloud sessions off.

switches.name: Plan includes coding and active-sandbox limit
switches.effect: Decides whether the coding feature is offered and how many cloud sessions can run at once.

switches.name: Tool approval policy default
switches.effect: Sets the starting approval policy (ask every time) and the cloud account default (autonomous).

switches.name: Desktop capability grants per folder
switches.effect: Running commands, computer use and remote control each need a grant; the list of sessions is hidden until command access is allowed.

switches.name: CLI worktree flag
switches.effect: Starts the session in its own git worktree.

switches.name: CLI permission mode
switches.effect: Chooses default, plan, auto, bypassPermissions or dontAsk.

switches.name: Desktop CLI capability advertisement
switches.effect: Shows or hides worktree, checkpoint, approval and thread features based on what the bundled CLI reports.

switches.name: Local context file attach
switches.effect: Off for remote SSH sessions and when the capability is missing.

guide.what_it_is_for: This area lets a person hand a coding task to the AI agent: read a project, answer questions about it, change files, run the project's checks, review changes, and turn the result into a branch, a commit or a pull request. It matters because the agent does the reading, editing and checking inside the person's own folder or a managed sandbox, and the person stays in control of each change. Most of the work runs on the user's computer (Desktop app and CLI); the managed cloud version is gated and mostly off.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user who opens a coding session on a folder (Desktop, Web via the paired desktop host, CLI, VS Code and Mobile as a remote view). The managed cloud coding path is for users on a plan, and it is off unless the deployment switches are set (see switches). Workspace admins and developers are not separately gated in the code read for this area; GitHub actions need a connected GitHub account (apps/web/app/api/code/local-pull-requests/route.ts:63). The brief's "developers" framing is not a separate role in the code.

how_it_works.step: 1. The person starts or continues a session in the UI
how_it_works.detail: The coding panel on Web is a local-folder session panel. It takes the composer text and sends it through the local session pipeline.

how_it_works.step: 2. The desktop host or the cloud route receives the command
how_it_works.detail: On Desktop the command is a developer_* command handled by the dispatcher. On Web for a Cloud session, the request first passes the cloud gate; if the gate is off the request is refused with a message to use the desktop app.
code: apps/web/lib/services/cloud-code-session-open.ts:44-53 (refusal when the switch is off or the beta is unavailable)

how_it_works.step: 3. The permission check decides what is asked first
how_it_works.detail: Each command has a capability (for example git.read, git.write, shell.execute, filesystem.read). Most developer commands ask for the agent grant first; git-only commands on this app's own git are answered without starting an agent.
code: apps/desktop/electron/runtime/dispatcher.ts:954-960 (commands answered by the app's own git)

how_it_works.step: 4. The agent runs in the folder
how_it_works.detail: The folder's CLI runs the agent. Its tools are read, write, edit, glob, grep, bash and git tools; mutating tools ask for approval by permission class.

how_it_works.step: 5. Instruction files and memory are loaded into the prompt
how_it_works.detail: The CLI reads the folder's instruction files, always-on rules, and the skill catalog and builds the system prompt.
code: apps/cli/src/agent/prompt.rs:390-405 (instructions, memory, skills, rules into the prompt)

how_it_works.step: 6. Device steps for the desktop and browser
how_it_works.detail: Screen, shell and browser actions are described as named steps, each with a capability and a short reason shown to the person. The shell steps are: run one command (wait for exit) or start one that keeps running, read its output, and stop it.
code: apps/web/features/desktop-host/lib/device-steps.ts:392-410 (start and read command handlers on Web)

how_it_works.step: 7. Changes are shown and applied only when chosen
how_it_works.detail: The agent's file changes are listed in the changes panel. The person picks the changes to keep; discard needs a git-write grant.
Branch, commit and push go through the app's git service. Opening a pull request on Web calls the local pull request route, which requires a connected GitHub account and records an audit event.

how_it_works.step: 9. GitHub mentions start a task later
how_it_works.detail: The GitHub webhook checks the mention, answers at once, and schedules the review or task in the background. The task itself checks the cloud switch and the beta.
The transcript shows the agent's messages, command output and review findings. Mobile shows the same session as a remote view through the remote control controller.

guide.area: Session continuity and remote-session product (brief area 068)
guide.what_it_is_for: A person starts a coding task on one device and carries on with it on another: the web app, the desktop app, the phone, the command line or the editor extension. The same session keeps its history, branch, repository and model, and an approval waiting in the session can be answered from any attached client. Cloud execution runs the session on a managed machine, and Remote Control lets a phone drive a computer the person owns, so the work does not depend on one device being open. This matters because a coding session is only useful if the person can pick it up where they left it.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in person can open a session that exists for their account. Remote Control needs the paid-plan capability 'remote_control' and the screen-share switch (apps/web/lib/feature-flags/remote-control-gate.ts:57-78, :97-113). Cloud execution needs the cloud switch and managed-compute access (apps/web/lib/e2b/gate.ts:20-28; apps/web/app/api/code/sessions/[sessionId]/agent/approvals/route.ts:98-106). Workspace admins are covered by a workspace feature gate and audit events (apps/web/lib/feature-flags/remote-control-gate.ts:104-111; apps/web/app/api/pair/claim/route.ts:161-170). Developers use the command line and the VS Code extension, which hand sessions to and from the cloud. Which plan tiers hold 'remote_control' was not established.

how_it_works.detail: The /code/<session id> route passes the id to the Cloud Code page. The path prefix /code is one of the product route prefixes shared with the desktop shell.

how_it_works.step: Phone loads the session and its approvals together
how_it_works.detail: The phone reads the session and the pending approvals in one step. It reloads when the app comes to the foreground, and polls on a fixed interval only while a turn or the session is busy.
The approvals route checks the cloud switch, validates the turn id, step index and decision, then checks the account's managed-compute access and plan. Only then does it apply the decision.
Cloud execution is on when the environment flag is set to 1 and the sandbox key is present and the rate card is priceable. The private-beta flag is a separate, broader gate.

how_it_works.step: Phone to computer commands through the relay
how_it_works.detail: The phone sends typed requests (start, steer, interrupt, answer, read transcript) to the computer through the relay. On the computer, every request is checked against the folder's allowed agent scope before it runs. The dispatcher maps each file command to a capability.

An approval the policy reserves for the person at the computer opens a native dialog that names the phone. Without an answer in two minutes, or with the screen locked, the allow is dropped and the agent keeps waiting.

The web claim route checks the relay settings and the signed-in account, then asks the relay to claim the code for that account. The relay refuses a code that belongs to another account, or a role already in use. The result is audited.

Creating, claiming and checking a live pairing all ask the same question: workspace policy, the plan's remote_control capability and the screen-share switch. A failed plan lookup is a temporary refusal (503), not a permanent one.

how_it_works.step: Command line hands a session to the cloud
how_it_works.detail: The hand-off reads the git checkout, refuses unpushed commits, checks the session, builds a review of what moves and what stays, asks for confirmation (or needs the yes flag), submits the session, and runs the first cloud turn.
A device posts a local session event. The server checks the device, builds the notification if the account's push preference is on, and reports whether a push was sent.

key_files.role: Web route for one cloud session; passes the session id to the Cloud Code page.
Lists pending approvals and applies an approve or reject decision; gated by the cloud switch, plan and managed-compute access.
The cloud execution switch: reads the environment flag and the sandbox key.
Decides whether an account may hold a Remote Control pairing (workspace policy, plan capability, screen-share switch).
Lets a phone claim a pairing code for the signed-in account; talks to the relay with the internal secret.
The relay: looks up pairing codes, mints pair tokens and forwards messages between the computer and the phone.
The computer side of Remote Control: checks each phone command against folder permission and holds sensitive approvals for a native dialog.
Phone hook for one cloud session: loads it, polls while busy, sends turns and decisions.
Phone-side wrappers that send session commands (start, steer, interrupt, answer, transcript) to the computer through the relay.
Command line entry for the hand-off to cloud (handle_code_handoff) and the first cloud turn.
Builds the review of what moves to the cloud and what stays on the machine, and checks GitHub access.
Receives activity events from a device and asks the notification service to alert the account's other clients.

data_kept.where: Read from the request by readRequestingDeviceId and readRequestingDevice (apps/web/app/api/pair/claim/route.ts:99; apps/web/app/api/code/local-sessions/activity/route.ts:26).
