guide.area: Area 81: Free / Basic / Pro / Max 5x / Max 15x plan structure (brief title says "Max 20x")
guide.what_it_is_for: This area is the set of plans a person can be on, and what each plan gives: how much cloud AI usage, which features, which limits, and what it costs. It decides what a person sees on the pricing page, what happens when they upgrade or downgrade, and whether a request to the managed cloud is allowed. It matters because one account plan must mean the same thing on every app, and the server (not the app) must enforce it.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in person sees a plan (Free if they have none). Paid plans (Basic, Premium/pro, Max, Ultra/max_15x) unlock more usage and features. Team and Enterprise plans are per-seat and are managed by workspace admins. Developers reach the same plan rules through the API, CLI and VS Code extension. Local-only and BYOK (own key) modes are free of charge and are not managed-cloud plans.

features.name: Plan catalog and plan lineup
features.use: One list of plans with prices, labels and versions. It drives the pricing page, checkout and the plan a person is shown. Each subscription records the catalog version it was sold under, so old buyers keep their terms.
how_people_use_it: Open the pricing page on web (apps/web/app/pricing/page.tsx) and compare the plan columns
Open plan settings on mobile (apps/mobile/src/features/settings/plans/index.tsx) or desktop and read the plan list
Open the upgrade chooser (apps/web/app/upgrade/UpgradeChooser.tsx) from a blocked feature
how_it_should_work: Every plan shows its own price, label and what it adds over the plan below it
Free, Basic, Premium, Max and Ultra exist in the catalog; Team, Team Premium and Enterprise are seat plans
A subscription stores plan_catalog_version and keeps the terms it was sold under when the catalog changes
A retired plan keeps working for existing buyers; new buyers go to the successor
Unknown or unsupported plan values fall back to a known tier rather than crashing (not fully traced)
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop: done. Mobile: done (plan screens and paywall sheet). CLI, VS Code and Chrome read the same plan through their own usage and plan views (see the feature-access and generation-settings features). Mobile in-app purchase is not switched on, see the upgrade-timing feature.

features.name: Usage allowance and the multiplier baseline (5x, 15x)
features.use: Each plan gets a managed-usage allowance counted in credits over a 5-hour window, a weekly window and a monthly window. Higher plans state how many times more usage they give than a named baseline plan, and some model classes have their own weekly cap.
how_people_use_it: Read the 'x more usage than' line under a plan on the pricing page
Open the usage section in settings (apps/web/features/settings/sections/UsageSection.tsx) to see used and remaining credits per window
Hit a model-class cap and read the message about the flagship weekly allowance
how_it_should_work: Premium (pro) is 5x Basic (baseline). Max is 5x Premium. Ultra (max_15x) is compared with Premium, and its number must match the real ratio of its allowances
Plan copy names the window being multiplied (session and weekly) and says 'for every seat' on team plans
The flagship weekly cap applies only to Premium and higher, as a share of the weekly budget
A plan whose allowance is unlimited shows no multiplier
Over the limit the request is refused with the reset time (reset logic not traced)
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop: done (pricing and usage section). Mobile: done (plans screen reads the same comparison). CLI and VS Code: done, they show their own usage summary. Chrome: pricing copy unverified, the Chrome panel shows usage through its own code.

features.name: Per-plan limits
features.use: Each plan has its own project count, knowledge storage, context size, number of answers that can run at once, and upload size for chat files. These are set in one product-limits table and enforced when a file is added or a request runs.
how_people_use_it: Add files to a project (knowledge files) until the storage limit is reached
Attach a large file to a chat message; large files need a paid plan
Start several answers at once and see the concurrency limit
Read the limits list on the pricing page under context and concurrency
how_it_should_work: Free: 5 projects, 500 MiB knowledge storage, 1 answer at a time, 5 daily uploads, no large chat files
Basic: 4 GiB storage, 3 answers, larger chat file limits; Premium: 20 GiB, 3 answers; Max: 50 GiB, 5 answers; Ultra: 100 GiB, 10 answers
Each limit is refused with a clear message when reached (message text not traced)
Context size comes from the model catalog, not from the plan table
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop: done (storage, context, concurrency). Upload-size: the brief marks it missing on web and desktop, but the catalog defines per-plan chat-file sizes (see things_that_look_wrong). Mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome: not listed in the brief for this group.

features.name: Feature access by plan
features.use: Plans differ in which features they include (for example Connectors, Remote Control, image generation, Cloud API access, Cloud in the CLI and VS Code). Each feature is a named capability in the catalog and is checked on the server for each surface.
how_people_use_it: Click a locked feature and read the upgrade message that names the plans that include it
Use Cloud API access with an API key, which needs a plan that includes it
Sign in on any app and see the same plan
how_it_should_work: Capabilities are listed per plan (for example Connectors from Basic up, Deep Research and image generation from Premium up, video generation only on Ultra and Enterprise)
A locked capability says which plans include it, in plain words
Each surface (web, desktop, mobile, Chrome, CLI, VS Code, API) is checked server-side; the app only hides or shows controls
Surface rules are separate from plan rules: for example a surface may not run managed cloud chat at all
features.on_each_app: Web, desktop and API: done. Mobile, CLI and VS Code: done for feature explanations and gates. Chrome: done for cross-platform sharing; feature-explanation copy unverified.

features.name: Shared or dedicated usage pools
features.use: A team plan can pool usage across members or give each seat its own allowance. The plan states which one, and the ledger follows it.
how_people_use_it: Admin opens the workspace spend limit screen (apps/web/features/workspace-console/components/WorkspaceSpendLimit.tsx) to set a limit
Members see their own allowance on the usage section
how_it_should_work: Seat plans state whether usage is per seat (perSeat) and the usage line says 'for every seat'
A seat member gets a monthly credit ledger that is created on first use
If the ledger cannot be created the error is logged and the request continues with no ledger (see entitlement-resolution.ts:198-207)
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop: done. The brief marks the handler as unfinished on both.

features.name: Pricing, billing cadence, upgrades and downgrades
features.use: People choose monthly or yearly billing where both are offered, see the charge and new renewal date before confirming an upgrade, and see when a downgrade takes effect. A failed renewal follows a grace rule and the person is told what access remains.
how_people_use_it: Pick Monthly or Yearly on the pricing page; the yearly saving is shown
Upgrade in the upgrade chooser, then read and confirm the charge in the confirm dialog
Downgrade in the review dialog, which shows the end-of-period date
When a renewal fails, read the notice banner and fix the payment
how_it_should_work: Upgrades take effect immediately; the charge and new renewal date are shown before confirming
Downgrades take effect at a stated time and access stays until then
A lapsed paid plan is served as Free and a billing notice header is sent with the response (auth-gate.ts:68)
Mobile in-app purchase must show the same charge and renewal date before purchase; this is not switched on yet
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop: done. Mobile: partial. Mobile billing is switched off in the feature list (apps/mobile/lib/v1FeatureFlags.ts:6), so purchase, receipt and restore code is built but not shown. CLI, VS Code and Chrome: grace-period notices done.

features.name: Trials, promotions, credits and overage
features.use: A plan can be granted as a time-limited trial that ends on a set date. Promo codes and invite grants give bonus entitlements. Purchased credit top-ups form a separate balance from the plan allowance. Overage lets a person spend purchased credits past their plan limit, off by default.
how_people_use_it: Enter a promo code on the upgrade or billing screen (apps/web/features/billing/components/UpgradePromotionCode.tsx)
Buy a credit top-up from the billing section
Turn overage on or off in the billing section; the preference is saved through the overage API
how_it_should_work: Trials show as trials with an end date and revert to Free or bill when the period ends (expiry runs on a scheduled job)
Overage is off by default; when on, overage use is counted apart from the plan windows
Purchased credits carry over and show apart from the plan allowance
Invalid promo codes show an error without changing the plan (message not traced)
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop: done for all four. Chrome: trials done. Mobile, CLI and VS Code: not listed in the brief for this group.

how_it_works.detail: The plan list lives in code: id, label, monthly and yearly price, and whether a plan is per seat. Basic is 7 USD, Premium (id pro) 20, Max 100, Ultra (id max_15x) 200, Team 25 per seat, Team Premium 125 per seat, Enterprise is contract priced. Free, Local Mode and Local Mode plus own key cost 0.

how_it_works.step: Which surfaces may pick a plan
how_it_works.detail: Each plan lists the surfaces (web, desktop, mobile) where it can be selected. Currently every plan lists all three.

A table lists, for each capability (for example managed chat, connectors, image generation, team admin), the plans that include it. The check function is canUseBillingPlanCapability. Labels and upgrade messages are built from the same table.

Credit allowances per plan (monthly, weekly, five-hour, unlimited flag) are in one table. A separate map keys the table by catalog version; versions 1 to 3 and the current version all use the same table today. Multipliers are computed as the ratio to the baseline plan (Premium to Basic, Max to Premium, Ultra to Premium, Team to Premium, Team Premium to Team).

how_it_works.step: Who the person is entitled to
how_it_works.detail: Entitlement is resolved in one place. For a seat member the code finds the workspace subscription first, then any other seat. The bundle says which plan, catalog version and source apply. The usage window subject is the paid plan while it is entitled, and Free after it lapses.
For a seat member with a budget above zero, a monthly credit account is created for the subscription period, tagged with the catalog version.

The managed cloud gate checks the signed-in surface against the plan. The response header that tells the app its paid plan lapsed is named here. Surfaces are mapped to capabilities (web, mobile, desktop and chrome all map to managed chat).

One table holds per-plan limits: projects, storage, download bytes, concurrent turns, artifact AI calls, sandboxes, connector tools, scheduled tasks, chat file sizes and daily upload bytes. Free daily caps (messages, conversations, egress, email, vector queries) are separate constants.
The pricing page builds the comparison columns from the plan prices and capability table. It shows the baseline-relative multiplier lines through the managed-usage comparison helpers.
The overage endpoint reads and writes the person's overage on/off setting, then returns the saved row.

key_files.role: Plan list, prices, surfaces, capability table, per-plan product limits and free daily caps. Central source.
Credit allowances per plan, catalog-version table, baselines and multiplier wording.
Single place that works out a person's plan, seat source and usage window subject; creates seat ledgers.
Server gate on managed chat requests: surface check, terms check and billing-lapsed notice header.
Maps each signed-in surface (web, desktop, mobile, chrome, CLI, VS Code) to the plan capability it needs.
Public pricing page: comparison columns, prices, capability rows and multiplier copy.
Mobile feature switches; billing is off here.
Read and write the overage on/off setting.
Usage meter and per-window allowance display in settings.
Upgrade choice screen and plan explanations.

data_kept.what: Plan price list, capability table, per-plan limits, credit allowances, free daily caps
data_kept.where: Code constants in packages/contracts/types/src/billing-catalog.ts and managed-usage-limits.ts (not database)

data_kept.what: Subscription row with plan tier, catalog version, period dates, Stripe ids, Apple and Google purchase ids
data_kept.where: Database, read by apps/web/lib/services/entitlement-resolution.ts:133-167 (table name not traced)

data_kept.what: Monthly seat credit account (budget and period), tagged with plan catalog version
data_kept.where: Database via CreditService.getOrCreateAccount, apps/web/lib/services/entitlement-resolution.ts:189-197

data_kept.what: Overage on/off preference per person
data_kept.where: Database via db.query, apps/web/app/api/billing/overage/route.ts:94 (table not traced)

data_kept.what: Managed usage periods and windows
data_kept.where: Not traced in this pass

switches.name: BILLING_PLAN_CATALOG_VERSION and the version table
switches.effect: Picks which allowance table a subscription uses; versions 1 to 3 map to the same table today.

switches.name: PLAN_SURFACE_VISIBILITY
switches.effect: Which surfaces can select each plan.

switches.effect: Brief says this must be on, with App Store and Play products live, before mobile purchase works. Not opened in this pass.

guide.shared_code: Shared across apps: the plan list, prices, capability table, per-plan limits and multiplier wording (packages/contracts/types/src/billing-catalog.ts, managed-usage-limits.ts); the server entitlement resolver and chat gate (apps/web/lib/services/entitlement-resolution.ts, auth-gate.ts). Separate per app: the pricing and upgrade screens (web), the plans screen and paywall sheet (mobile, apps/mobile/src/features/settings/plans and cloud-billing), the CLI usage summary (apps/cli/src/usage_summary.rs, apps/cli/src/plans.rs), the VS Code plan comparison (apps/extension-vscode/src/features/account-auth/planComparison.ts), and the Chrome side panel and free-trial client (apps/extension/src/side_panel.ts, apps/extension/src/features/cloud-bridge/freeTrialClient.ts).

things_that_look_wrong.what: The brief's area title says Max 20x, and the brief's item S81.06 says Max 15x, but the code has no 20x plan. The plan id is max_15x and its label is Ultra.

The Ultra (max_15x) allowance is 10 times Premium on the monthly and weekly windows (20,000 vs 2,000 monthly; 5,000 vs 500 weekly), and the five-hour window is unlimited. The code's own ratio is therefore 10x, not the 15x name. Pricing copy was not opened to confirm what it says.

The brief says upload-size limits are missing on web and desktop, but the catalog defines per-plan chat-file sizes and daily upload bytes. Whether the upload route enforces them was not traced. Every plan also uses the same maxAttachmentBytes value.
The team knowledge storage limit is a hard-coded byte number, while other team-style limits are computed from prices.
Mobile billing is switched off, so the upgrade-timing item is partial on mobile.

not_sure: Rate-limit concurrency enforcement (apps/web/lib/rate-limit.ts:1223, 1234 and apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/lib/turn-slot.ts:35) was not opened.
Upload route and knowledge-file storage check (apps/web/app/api/projects/[id]/knowledge-files/route.ts:227) was not opened.

Checkout, upgrade and top-up routes (apps/web/app/api/checkout/route.ts, apps/web/app/api/upgrade/route.ts, apps/web/app/api/billing/top-up/route.ts) and the trial-expiry job (apps/web/lib/services/code-trial-expiry.ts, apps/web/app/api/cron/expire-code-trials/route.ts) were not opened.
Stripe webhook plan-version storage (apps/web/app/api/stripe-webhook/lib/db.ts:773) was not opened, so grandfathering is only partly seen.
Mobile in-app purchase server flag and product catalog (apps/web/lib/server/mobile-iap-catalog.ts:26) were not opened.
Exact wording of the pricing copy for 5x and 15x (apps/web/app/pricing/page.tsx:741-818 covers rows, not all text) was not read in full.
Per-window reset logic and the exact refusal messages when a limit is reached were not traced.
Chrome status for S81.07 and S81.08 (marked unverified) was not checked; the Chrome copy source was not opened.
Mobile app plan screen (apps/mobile/src/features/settings/plans/index.tsx) and the image generation route (apps/web/app/api/media/image/generate/route.ts:223) were not opened.
The database table names for subscriptions, credit accounts and overage were not confirmed.
Test coverage for this area was not examined (read-only task, no tests run).

guide.what_it_is_for: This area shows a person how much of their plan they have used, when each limit resets, and how many credits they have left. When a limit is reached, it explains which limit was hit and offers a way forward: wait for the reset, buy extra usage, change model, or upgrade. It matters because a user who cannot see their limits either runs out without warning or cannot tell why a request was refused.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user sees their own usage on every app, from the server's account data. Free-plan users see the upgrade path and no meters, and paid-plan users can also buy credits and turn on auto-reload (apps/web/app/api/billing/top-up/route.ts:160-163 requires an active paid plan with a payment source). Workspace owners and admins set a monthly spend cap (apps/web/features/workspace-console/components/WorkspaceSpendLimit.tsx). Developers read the same numbers through the API with the usage:read key scope (apps/web/app/api/usage/limits/route.ts:59).

features.name: Plan and billing period
features.use: Shows which plan the account is on and when the current billing period starts and ends or renews.
how_people_use_it: Open Settings, then Usage (web, desktop) or Settings, then Cloud usage (mobile).
Read the plan name and the period dates at the top of the page.
On the CLI, run the usage command to see the plan line in the terminal.
how_it_should_work: The plan comes from the server on every read, never from a saved copy.
Paid plans show the period start and end dates. Free plans show the next reset time instead.

While the summary loads, the page shows a loading state. If the read fails, it shows an error message and a retry action, and the last good reading stays on screen marked as stale (apps/web/lib/hooks/useManagedUsageSummary.ts:76-82).
Plan labels follow the server's plan tier and seat type (apps/web/app/api/usage/route.ts:27-31).
features.on_each_app: Web, desktop (hosted web app), mobile, CLI, VS Code extension and Chrome extension all show the plan. Each reads the same endpoint (web and mobile: /api/usage; CLI: apps/cli/src/usage_summary.rs; VS Code: apps/extension-vscode/src/utils/api.ts:1545; Chrome: apps/extension/src/features/cloud-bridge/freeTrialClient.ts). Their layouts differ.

features.name: Usage meters and reset times
features.use: Shows how full each usage window is, as a percentage, and how long until it resets.
how_people_use_it: Open the usage page and read the bars for the session window, the weekly window, the flagship weekly window and the period.
Read the reset time under each bar. On web it reads as a time today or a weekday and time later.
Tap a bar on mobile to open the limit explainer sheet.
how_it_should_work: Each window shows a percentage used and a reset moment. A window with no cap is shown without a bar.
A status line summarises the state: none used, on track, getting close (90 percent or more), or limit reached (100 percent or more) (apps/web/features/settings/sections/UsageSection.tsx:159-174).
Refreshes every 5 minutes while the app is active, and when the user returns to the page (apps/web/lib/hooks/useManagedUsageSummary.ts:22, 91-108).
On failure during a background refresh, the meter keeps its last value and is marked stale, so it does not go blank.
Free-plan usage uses a separate free-trial reading and its own reset times (apps/web/lib/services/managed-usage-summary-service.ts:92-97).
features.on_each_app: Web, desktop, mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome show the windows (see the Status lines for S82.03 and S82.17). Mobile has the sheet with the explainer text (apps/mobile/src/features/settings/cloud-usage/index.tsx:736-746). The CLI renders the reset as text (apps/cli/src/usage_summary.rs:146, 295, 338).

features.name: Usage by model, feature, work and project
features.use: Breaks usage down by model, by product area (chat, work, research, code, browser), by coding or agent work, and by project.
how_people_use_it: On the usage page, pick a granularity (days, weeks or months) and read the rows in the breakdown.
Use the workload filter in the history query to show one area only (apps/web/app/api/usage/history/route.ts:23-27 accepts a known workload name).
Look at the per-model rows in the usage history table.
how_it_should_work: Rows come from the usage history for the chosen window. An unknown workload name is rejected with a validation error.
The project breakdown is available on web and through the API only. Mobile does not show it yet.
Empty history shows an empty state for the chosen window, not an error.
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop show all four. Mobile shows model, feature and task, but not project (S82.19 is missing on mobile; apps/mobile/src/features/settings/cloud-usage/index.tsx has no project breakdown). The CLI shows model and task (apps/cli/src/usage_summary.rs:727, 740). The VS Code extension shows model and task (apps/extension-vscode/src/data/usagePresentation.ts:120, 123). Chrome shows none of them.

features.name: Usage by task and by device or surface
features.use: Shows the cost of each agent run or work session, and (where built) usage per device or app.
how_people_use_it: Open the Tasks page, pick a task, and read its usage in the detail panel.
On mobile, open a cloud run and read its cost in the run detail sheet.
how_it_should_work: Each task shows its own usage, including the cost once the run has finished.
A device or surface breakdown is not built on any app or in the API. Do not present one.
features.on_each_app: Per-task usage is on web, desktop, mobile, CLI and VS Code (packages/ui/unified-chat/src/components/tasks/TasksPage.tsx:591; apps/mobile/src/features/tasks/components/CloudRunDetailSheet.tsx:179). Per-device or per-surface usage is missing on web, desktop, mobile and API.

features.name: Voice, image, video, research, storage and running jobs
features.use: Shows usage of the non-text allowances: voice minutes, image count, video seconds, research usage, file storage, and the number of jobs running now.
how_people_use_it: Read the Allowances card on the usage page or the cloud usage screen on mobile.
Read the Storage card for files and project sources used against the plan limit.
Read the running count to see how many responses are active.
how_it_should_work: The limits endpoint returns voice minutes, image count, video seconds, responses and storage in one reply (apps/web/app/api/usage/limits/route.ts:85-101).
Voice minutes on a free plan come from the free voice allowance (route.ts:79-96). If the running-count read fails, the count is shown as unavailable instead of as zero (route.ts:44-54).
Storage is read from the file storage meter for the user or organisation (route.ts:73-77).
features.on_each_app: Web, desktop and mobile show these (voice, image, video, storage, running jobs on web and mobile). The API route is used by web and mobile. CLI, VS Code and Chrome do not show them (see Status lines). Research usage is only in the history data and is shown on web and mobile.

features.name: Credit balances: included, purchased, bonus and expiry
features.use: Shows how many credits remain, and keeps the plan's included credits apart from purchased credits and promotional (bonus) credits, with the date each one expires.
how_people_use_it: Read the Credit balances card on the usage page.
Read the included and purchased rows, then the bonus row with its next expiry date.
On the CLI, read the purchased and included lines in the usage output.
how_it_should_work: Included plan credits reset with the plan period. Purchased credits have their own balance and expiry. Bonus credits lapse after a set number of days (BONUS_CREDIT_EXPIRY_DAYS = 90, apps/web/lib/services/bonus-credit-service.ts:7).
If the purchased-credit read fails, its balance is reported as unknown (null), not zero (apps/web/lib/services/managed-usage-summary-service.ts:195; bonus-credit-service.ts:164).
Each kind of credit shows its own expiry: plan reset, purchased lifetime, or bonus lapse (apps/web/lib/services/managed-usage-summary-service.ts:198-207).
features.on_each_app: Web, desktop, mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome show the balances in their own layout (see Status lines). Promotional credits and expiry are on web, desktop and mobile only.

features.name: Usage history, export and discrepancy report
features.use: Shows usage by day, week or month, lets the user download it as a CSV file, and lets the user report a billing or usage mismatch.
how_people_use_it: Pick Days, Weeks or Months above the history table (web: UsageSection.tsx granularity options; mobile: a history picker).
Click the Download link to get a CSV file for the window shown.
Open the discrepancy form, describe the problem, and optionally add a charge or invoice reference, then send.
how_it_should_work: History is grouped in UTC. A day is a UTC day, a week runs Monday to Sunday, and a month is a calendar month (UsageSection.tsx:126-130).

The CSV has one row per request with request ID, workload, operation, model, project, tokens and credits, and is served as an attachment with no caching (apps/web/app/api/usage/export/route.ts:81-88).

The discrepancy report needs a message and the usage window. It creates a support ticket that includes the usage record, and staff are notified (apps/web/app/api/usage/discrepancy/route.ts:182-195). Successful creation returns status 201.
Export and history return an error message with a retry option if the read fails.
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop have all three. Mobile has history but no CSV download and no discrepancy form (Status lines). The API has history and export. CLI has history (apps/cli/src/usage_summary.rs:158).

features.name: Task cost estimate and actual cost
features.use: Shows what a task is expected to cost before or while it runs, and what it actually cost when it finishes.
how_people_use_it: Before a research run, read the estimated credits on the research activity card (ResearchActivity.tsx:284).
After a run finishes, open the task detail to read its real cost.
how_it_should_work: The estimate for a research run is calculated in the browser from the number of rounds and searches (apps/web/features/chat/components/research/ResearchActivity.tsx:284).

The estimate endpoint takes a model and a messages body and returns a minimum and maximum credit range (apps/web/app/api/usage/estimate/route.ts:97-106). It refuses models with no per-token price (route.ts:77-81).
Actual cost appears only after the run is settled. A turn that is not settled does not show a cost.
features.on_each_app: Web, desktop and the API have the estimate endpoint. Mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome show the actual cost (Status lines). No app caller of the estimate endpoint was found (see things_that_look_wrong).

features.name: Limit warnings and blocked state
features.use: Warns the user before a limit is hit, shows a clear blocked state when it is hit, offers an alternative model, and offers to wait until the reset.
how_people_use_it: Watch for the warning banner above the chat composer on web and mobile, or the warning line in the CLI, VS Code panel or Chrome side panel.
When blocked, read the paywall card: it names the limit and shows its reset time.
Choose Use another model, or choose to wait for the reset, or choose an upgrade or top-up action.
how_it_should_work: A blocked request returns a machine code (for example insufficient credits or organisation spend cap reached) and a message (apps/web/lib/services/managed-usage-request-service.ts:399, 426).
The response carries the reset time and an alternative model when one exists (createManagedUsageErrorBody, managed-usage-request-service.ts:106-124).

The recovery action depends on the plan: top-up for a self-serve paid plan billed by a payment processor; contact support for contract-priced plans; upgrade when a higher tier exists; otherwise a link to the usage page (managed-usage-request-service.ts:86-104).
The waiting option shows when the limit resets, in the UI text: Credits past your plan limits resume on that date (UsageSection.tsx:753).
The warning appears before a limit is reached, and the blocked state shows one clear message, not a silent failure.
features.on_each_app: Web, desktop, mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome all have the warning and blocked state (Status lines). Mobile uses a bottom sheet (apps/mobile/src/features/chat/components/PaywallBottomSheet.tsx). The CLI maps the error to text (apps/cli/src/errors.rs:373, 602).

features.name: Buying extra usage and auto-reload
features.use: Lets a paid user buy more credits when they run out, and turn on automatic top-ups when the balance drops below a set amount.
how_people_use_it: On web or desktop, at a limit, click the buy extra usage action in the paywall card, or open the billing settings.
Open the auto-reload panel in billing settings, set the threshold and amount, accept the consent text, and save.
On the CLI, the extra-usage command prints the pricing page link. Credits are bought on web.
how_it_should_work: Buying is allowed only on an active paid plan with a payment source (apps/web/app/api/billing/top-up/route.ts:160-163).
Auto-reload runs only when the payment processor is enabled: the check reads STRIPE_CHECKOUT_ENABLED and the secret key (apps/web/lib/services/auto-reload-service.ts:159-166).
The consent text is versioned and the user must accept it before saving (auto-reload-service.ts:411 saveAutoReloadSettings).
A failed top-up is recorded with a failure reason so it can be shown and retried (auto-reload-service.ts:761 failAutoReloadPayment).
Upgrade-waitlist gate: a first-time buyer without access is refused (see things_that_look_wrong).
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop have both. VS Code's Add credits opens the web billing page (apps/extension-vscode/src/features/sidebar-webview/ChatStateManager.ts:1088 area). Chrome opens web usage and billing pages. The CLI prints a link only (apps/cli/src/tui/tui_app.rs:6698-6700).

features.name: Workspace spending cap
features.use: Lets an owner set a monthly spend limit for the workspace that stops managed usage once reached.
how_people_use_it: An owner opens the workspace console, sets the monthly cap or mode, and confirms the change through the confirmation dialog.
Members see the request refused with the organisation spend cap message when the cap is reached.
how_it_should_work: Modes are off, notify and block. Only block refuses requests; notify and off always allow (apps/web/lib/services/spend-limit-service.ts:150-154, 183).
Decisions are cached for 60 seconds, so the cap is enforced with a small delay and can overshoot by about one window of spend (spend-limit-service.ts:53-60 comment).
If the spend cannot be read, the request is allowed (spend-limit-service.ts:175-179). This is deliberate.
Each refused request writes an audit event (managed-usage-request-service.ts:381-397).
features.on_each_app: Web and desktop only (the workspace console). Other apps show the refusal message when a request is blocked.

features.name: Resume-after-reset preference
features.use: Lets a user ask to be told when their limit resets, so they can resume blocked work.
how_people_use_it: On mobile, when a usage warning appears, tap Notify me when it resets.
If the device has no notification permission, the app asks for it first.
how_it_should_work: Mobile asks the server to set a reminder for the reset time, after notification permission is granted (apps/mobile/src/features/chat/services/usageResetReminder.ts). The reminder is a notification, not an automatic resume.

The server route is rate limited under usage-reset-reminder (apps/web/app/api/usage/reset-reminder/route.ts:66). A workflow sends the reminder only if the user's preference allows it (apps/web/lib/workflows/steps/send-usage-reset-reminder.ts:20).
Automatic resume of blocked work is not built.
features.on_each_app: Mobile has the Notify me when it resets action (UsageLimitBanner.tsx:66). The server route exists but no web UI caller was found. Desktop, web and the CLI do not have it (Status lines: missing).

how_it_works.step: 1. The screen asks for the summary
how_it_works.detail: The web usage page and other shared views call one hook. Its state lives at module level, so the four copies on a chat route share one read and one timer. The hook fetches /api/usage and refreshes every 5 minutes while the app is active.

how_it_works.step: 2. The summary route checks the caller
how_it_works.detail: The route authenticates the user through the user-scoped database. An API key needs the usage:read scope. Failure to authenticate returns an unauthorized error.

how_it_works.step: 3. The summary is assembled from several reads
how_it_works.detail: The service reads the credit balance, the entitlement (plan), spendable credits and prepaid balances in parallel. Free plans skip promotions and rolling windows. Rolling windows are read for the session (5 hour), weekly and flagship weekly limits.

how_it_works.step: 4. Reset times and percentages are computed
how_it_works.detail: Each window gets a percentage used and a reset moment. Plan allowance values are shown as credit windows (monthly, weekly, five hour, flagship weekly, purchased, bonus, purchase expiry).

how_it_works.step: 5. The limits route adds allowances, jobs and storage
how_it_works.detail: A second route returns the per-unit allowances (voice, video, computer-use), image count, running responses, storage meter and the voice-minute credit value. Its reads run in parallel and the running count can fail to null.

how_it_works.step: 6. History and export are built from the usage ledger
how_it_works.detail: The history route takes granularity, workload and a time window, then reads grouped usage. The export route reads the same records and returns a CSV attachment.

how_it_works.step: 7. A request is checked before it runs
how_it_works.detail: Before a managed request, the server checks the organisation spend cap (block mode only refuses) and reserves an idempotency key. A refused request returns a code, a message, the reset time and an alternative model, plus a recovery action.

how_it_works.step: 8. The client shows the warning or the blocked card
how_it_works.detail: Web shows the paywall card inside the chat. Mobile shows the usage limit banner and bottom sheet. The CLI prints a message. Each app turns the returned code into its own text.
A top-up creates a payment through the payment processor for a paid plan. Auto-reload settings are saved with a consent version, and a reload runs when the balance falls below the threshold.

key_files.role: Web usage page: meters, status line, credit cards, history, export and discrepancy form.
Shared client read of /api/usage with a 5 minute refresh and stale marking.
Builds the usage summary: plan, windows, reset times, credit balances and expiry.
Returns allowances, image count, running jobs, storage and voice minute value.
Decides the error code, reset time, alternative model and recovery action for a blocked request.
Owner spend cap decision: off, notify or block, cached for 60 seconds.
Auto-reload settings, consent, top-up payments and failure recording.
Upgrade access gate: a global switch or a beta redemption row.
Mobile cloud usage screen: meters, allowances, storage, history, overage and the limits sheet.

guide.shared_code: The web usage routes and services under apps/web (summary, limits, history, export, discrepancy, estimate, reset reminder) are used by the web app. The desktop shows the hosted web app, so it uses the same routes and page (per AGENTS.md section 5). The shared contract types (parseManagedUsageSummaryResponse, AccountUsageLimitsResponse, ManagedUsageSummaryResponse) come from @agiworkforce/types under packages/contracts. The mobile app calls the same endpoints through its own services/usage.ts (fetchUsageSnapshot, fetchUsageHistory, fetchUsageAllowances, applyLimitReset). The CLI parses the same JSON in apps/cli/src/usage_summary.rs (parse_account_usage, parse_usage_history). The VS Code extension reads /api/usage and /api/usage/history (apps/extension-vscode/src/utils/api.ts:1545, 1555). Separate per app: all rendering code (web components, mobile screens and banners, CLI text, VS Code webview, Chrome side panel), the mobile usage store, and the mobile reminder service.

things_that_look_wrong.what: Brief says the estimate endpoint backs the task estimate on web, desktop and API. No app caller of /api/usage/estimate was found in the web app. The composer has no estimate for chat turns. The only pre-run estimate is the browser-side research estimate.

things_that_look_wrong.what: Brief says resume-after-reset is missing on web, desktop and mobile. Mobile has a Notify me when it resets action, and the server has a reset reminder route with no web UI caller found. The action is a notification, not an automatic resume.

Upgrade-waitlist gate: first-time buyers without a beta redemption row are refused for upgrades. The brief says this blocks buyers on CLI, VS Code and Chrome. I did not confirm the gate on the top-up path. Top-up checks only the plan and payment source.
Spend cap fails open. If the spend state cannot be read, the request is allowed. This is deliberate, but it means the cap is not a hard stop when the read fails.
Spend cap is eventual. Decisions are cached for 60 seconds, so a workspace can overshoot its cap by about one window of spend. The console states this.
CLI extra-usage command only opens the pricing page and does not offer a purchase.
The mobile usage store and the project breakdown are missing. S82.19 is marked missing on mobile, which matches the code.

guide.what_it_is_for: This area holds the settings that decide how AGI Workforce looks and behaves for one person: theme, accent colour, text size, motion, code display, display language, what a new chat starts with, how the Enter key sends, notifications and quiet hours, and a few desktop launch options. A person gets an app that matches their eyes, their language and their habits, and on web and mobile those choices follow them to other devices after sign-in. It matters because the same preferences are read in six different apps, so a setting that is saved but not read by an app looks like a broken control to the user.
guide.who_uses_it: Every user on every surface, as far as the code shows. Only signed-in users get their choices copied to the account on web and mobile (CloudSettingsSync.tsx:194-199 stops when no one is signed in); signed-out users keep device-only values. Some defaults are plan-gated: on web, models above the user's plan show "Upgrade to use" and higher reasoning-effort levels are shown disabled (GeneralSection.tsx:361, 460). Workspace admins and developers have no separate path in this area. Desktop uses the same web settings screens, because the desktop window shows the hosted web app.

how_it_works.step: The person changes a setting on a screen
how_it_works.detail: On web, the Appearance screen shows theme, accent, contrast, motion, font, text size, code wrap and code theme. The General screen shows display language, defaults, composer and sidebar rows. Each control reads and writes one value through a hook or store.

how_it_works.step: The value is saved in the web settings store on the device
how_it_works.detail: Most web appearance and composer values are fields of one zustand store that is persisted to browser storage under one key. Each field has a setter.

how_it_works.step: Theme is handled by the theme provider
how_it_works.detail: The theme hook calls the theme library, which stores the value under the key 'theme' and sets the theme class on the page. The provider then sets data-theme and data-theme-preference on the page root. A stored value that is not valid falls back to dark.
A component mounted at the root of the settings and app runtime reads the store and sets or removes one attribute per setting on the page root. It also hands the code theme to the syntax highlighter.
CSS rules keyed on those attributes change the accent colour, text size, font, contrast, code wrapping and motion. The reduced-motion rule for the OS setting is separate.

how_it_works.step: Signed-in users: the values are copied to the account
how_it_works.detail: A sync component reads the values, builds one appearance record, and after a 400 ms pause writes the changed fields to the server. Language and custom commands are written the same way. Nothing syncs when no one is signed in. On sign-in it pulls the account copy and applies it to the store.
The web and mobile names for accent and font are translated to one shared vocabulary. Unknown names from another app are ignored on load.

The preferences route validates the patch with a schema, then writes the namespace inside a database transaction with a version check. The client calls the path defined in the shared contract package. Rows live in the user settings table as a JSON column.

how_it_works.step: Display language is applied at once
how_it_works.detail: The language selector calls the i18n library. The library stores the choice in a cookie and in browser storage, and sets the document language and direction.

how_it_works.step: Desktop and Chrome keep their own copies
how_it_works.detail: The desktop shell stores its window theme and launch options in a settings file in the app data folder. Chrome stores the theme in extension storage and follows changes to it.

how_it_works.step: CLI reads its config at startup
how_it_works.detail: The CLI keeps theme and reduced-motion values in its config. The theme is restored before the first frame and applied to the palette. Reduced motion, or plain output, turns off animation.

key_files.role: Web Appearance screen: theme, accent, contrast, motion, font, text size, code wrap and code theme controls.
Web General screen: display language, default model, effort, mode, composer send key, sidebar items, read-aloud and shortcuts link.
The persisted store that holds most web appearance and composer values, under one browser storage key.
Turns stored values into page attributes that the stylesheet reads, and sets the code theme.
Copies signed-in users' appearance, language, sidebar and composer values to the account and back.
Maps web and mobile names for accent and font to one shared vocabulary.
Server read and write for account settings namespaces, with a version check and a database transaction.
Per-event notification channel choices, with channels hidden when a surface is not released.
Quiet hours form (days, start and end, save) and the read-only timezone line.
Mobile Appearance screen: theme choice for the current mode (Local or Cloud).
Desktop preference writes: window theme, launch at login, shortcut changes and menu-bar choice.
CLI startup: restores the saved theme and applies reduced motion.
Chrome Options page Theme select with load and save status text.

guide.shared_code: Shared across apps: the web settings screens and stores (apps/web) are the source for web and desktop, since the desktop window shows the hosted web app. Shared packages used by these screens: @agiworkforce/types (time-focus preferences, effort labels, cloud work modes), @agiworkforce/cloud-contracts (the preferences path and sync schemas), @agiworkforce/unified-chat/shiki-highlighter (code themes), @agiworkforce/i18n (languages). The web and mobile appearance namespace is one shared vocabulary, written as a comment in appearance-namespace.ts:53-55. Separate per app: mobile has its own settings screens and stores (apps/mobile/src/features/settings and apps/mobile/stores); the CLI keeps its own config and terminal palette in Rust (apps/cli/src/config.rs, apps/cli/src/tui); Chrome has its own options page and theme module (apps/extension/src/options.ts, apps/extension/src/features/appearance); the desktop shell has its own Electron code for window theme, launch at login, menus and shortcuts (apps/desktop/electron); VS Code declares its own settings in its package.json.

guide.area: Personalization and data settings (brief area 85, 26 items)
guide.what_it_is_for: This area is where a person controls what the assistant knows about them and what happens to their chats and data. It covers profile, custom instructions, reply style, saved memory, using past chats, keeping or not keeping chat history, deleting and exporting data, sharing links, and privacy choices about training and crash reports. A person needs it to trust the product: they decide what is remembered, what is kept, and how to remove it.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user on web, desktop, mobile, CLI, the VS Code extension and the Chrome extension, as the brief's per-app status shows. Some controls depend on plan: the web privacy screen reads the subscription and treats Free plan users differently (apps/web/features/settings/sections/PrivacySection.tsx:219-220, and the managedOnly flag on toggles). Workspace owners and members see workspace-scoped bulk delete (apps/web/features/settings/components/BulkConversationControls.tsx:95-100). Developers read the server routes and the turn-context code. The brief does not list a separate admin screen for this area.

how_it_works.step: 1. The person changes a setting on a surface
how_it_works.detail: On web, the privacy screen reads the stored value and the subscription tier. Toggles save through a request authority that checks the owner and the screen is still current. Free plan users see the toggles marked for all plans, while some toggles are managed-only.

how_it_works.step: 2. Chat settings are held in the browser store
how_it_works.detail: The 'start new chats temporary' flag and other web settings live in a client store with a default of off.

how_it_works.step: 3. A chat turn is built with context
how_it_works.detail: For each message, the server decides which sources may be used: project files, past chats, and account memory. Temporary chats and organization policy remove sources. Memory is used only when memory is on and the chat is not temporary.

how_it_works.step: 4. Custom instructions and style are added
how_it_works.detail: The server reads the general and personalization settings, checks whether the project opts out, and writes a block of instructions into the prompt.
code: apps/web/lib/server/user-identity.ts (readProjectPersonalizationScope and formatPersonalizationBlock, below line 226; exact lines not re-read)

how_it_works.step: 5. Temporary and history rules apply when saving
how_it_works.detail: A chat marked temporary is not written to history on the free-plan save path. Search filters out temporary chats.

how_it_works.step: 6. Bulk and single deletes write soft deletes
how_it_works.detail: Delete all sets deleted_at on the account's active and archived chats in one statement. Restore clears it within 30 days. Single delete and restore go through the conversation data service.

how_it_works.step: 7. Memory import runs in two passes
how_it_works.detail: The import route first runs a dry run, then a commit if asked. It checks the CSRF token and a rate limit first.
The delete route checks for an active paid subscription and for sole-owned workspaces. If either check cannot run, it stops and deletes nothing.
A background call that would send content to a provider checks the opt-out. A provider that keeps inputs out of training is always allowed. If the opt-out cannot be read, the call is blocked.
The local wipe signs out, withdraws provider sharing on this device, and deletes local rows in one transaction.

key_files.role: Web privacy screen: toggles, temporary-chat switch, training choices, recently deleted, export row.
Decides per turn which memory, past chats and project context are sent, and removes temporary chats and withdrawn sources.
Builds the custom instructions and reply style block from stored settings and project opt-outs.
Archive all and Delete all chats controls with the confirmation text.
Server route for bulk archive and delete (soft delete with deleted_at).
Client calls for restore, archive restore and delete of a single chat, and shared-link list.
Memory import endpoint with dry-run and commit modes.
Account deletion endpoint with billing and workspace checks.
Decides whether background provider calls may run given the training opt-out.
Mobile local data wipe and the export transcript builder.
Mobile delete-all controls and confirmations for local and cloud chats.
CLI client for the account data export archives.

guide.shared_code: Shared across apps: the server routes under apps/web/app/api (for example bulk chat actions, memory import, data export, account deletion) are the same routes the desktop and mobile Cloud clients call. The turn-context and user-identity services under apps/web/lib/ build the prompt for every Cloud chat, whichever surface sends it. The Cloud data export route is used by the CLI (apps/cli/src/cloud/data_export.rs). The privacy UI in apps/mobile/src/features/settings/ is separate code from the web screen. Desktop reuses the web settings components (PrivacySection.tsx and BulkConversationControls.tsx) and adds the browser pairing screen. The VS Code and Chrome extensions each have their own settings code and storage. Whether mobile calls the same bulk-delete route is not verified.

guide.what_it_is_for: This area is where a signed-in person checks how their account can be reached and what AGI may touch. It lists sign-in methods, passwords, passkeys, second sign-in codes, signed-in sessions and linked devices, and lets the person end any of them. It also holds the rules for what the agent may do without asking: default approval level, per-tool rules, and permissions for folders, websites, apps, clipboard and screen on each device. It matters because a sign-in that someone else can still reach, or an agent that acts without consent, is the main account risk.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user on the web, desktop and phone settings screens. Developers use the API key rules (web and the CLI). Workspace admins set limits that bind members: a workspace can require two-step sign-in (apps/web/lib/mfa-policy-gate.ts:93-104) and can refuse skipping approvals (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/lib/tool-approval-policy.ts:37-44). Local permissions (folders, apps, clipboard, screen, websites) are granted by the person on their own device. I found no paid-plan gate in the files I read.

features.name: Sign-in methods and password
features.use: Shows every way the account can be signed in to, lets the person remove one, and lets them change the password.
how_people_use_it: Web: open Settings, Security, then the Sign-in methods panel (SecuritySection.tsx:241-244). Remove a method with its button, then confirm.
Web: Change password opens a form. Type the current password (if one is set) and the new one, at least 8 characters.
Phone: Account security lists the methods. The row Add or remove a sign-in method opens the web Security page in the browser.
how_it_should_work: Every method is listed with when it was last used.
The last sign-in method cannot be removed, and the primary sign-in method cannot be removed (apps/web/app/api/settings/identities/route.ts:26-31).
Removing a method needs a recent re-check of the person (step-up, 300 seconds, apps/web/lib/server/step-up/actions.ts:35-38).
Password change: with a password set and no second factor, the current password is enough. Otherwise a recent re-check is also needed (apps/web/app/api/settings/password/route.ts:50-71).

After a password change, every other session and device credential is signed out. If that partly fails, the person sees a 503 message asking them to end other sessions in Settings (password/route.ts:107-114).
Empty state, waiting state and plan limits: not seen in the files read.
features.on_each_app: Web: full. Desktop: same web screens, shown inside the desktop app (brief status done). Phone: lists methods, but add and remove happen on the web (account-security/index.tsx:629-635). CLI, VS Code and Chrome: no settings screen for this in the code I opened (brief status: missing).

how_people_use_it: Web: Settings, Security, Passkeys panel (SecuritySection.tsx:246). Add a passkey, rename it or remove it.

Phone: in cloud mode, the Account security screen shows a Passkeys section that opens a list of passkeys; changes ask for a re-check first (account-security/index.tsx:495-509, 637-650; PasskeysSection.tsx:143).
how_it_should_work: Add, see, rename and remove passkeys for the account.
Each change needs a recent re-check (step-up action account_security.change, actions.ts:57-60).
Empty state, failure text and limits: not verified (PasskeysPanel.tsx body not opened).
features.on_each_app: Web: full. Desktop: same web panel. Phone: brief says missing, but the phone code has a Passkeys section in cloud mode, so the brief status is out of date. CLI, VS Code, Chrome: not verified.

features.name: Two-step sign-in and recovery codes
features.use: Adds a second check, a code from an authenticator app, at sign-in. Recovery codes are one-time backup codes for when the authenticator is lost.
how_people_use_it: Web: Security, Two-factor panel (SecuritySection.tsx:250). Start setup, scan or type the setup key in an authenticator app, enter the 6-digit code.
Regenerate backup codes: confirm, re-check, then view the new codes.
Turn off: a re-check is required (action two_factor.disable, 300 s, actions.ts:27-30).
how_it_should_work: Setup is only possible when the environment switch AGI_AUTHENTICATOR_ENROLLMENT is 1. Otherwise the server answers that authenticator apps and backup codes are temporarily unavailable (lib/authenticator-enrollment.ts:5-18).
The setup key stays usable for 30 minutes (apps/web/app/api/settings/2fa/verify/route.ts:63-68). A wrong code is logged and returns unauthorized.
If the identity provider refuses the change, the server says nothing changed.
Regenerating backup codes makes the old codes stop working at once, and the person is told (backup-codes/route.ts:47-72).
A workspace that requires two-step sign-in can refuse actions for members who have not enrolled (mfa-policy-gate.ts:97-104).
Phone hides the section when enrollment is unavailable (TwoFactorSection.tsx:129).
features.on_each_app: Web: full. Desktop: same web panel. Phone: full, with the availability check. CLI, VS Code, Chrome: not verified.

features.name: Advanced Account Security
features.use: An optional stricter mode for people at higher risk. Sign-in needs a passkey or security key, and email recovery stops working.
how_people_use_it: Web: Settings, Security, Advanced Account Security panel (SecuritySection.tsx:248; panel in apps/web/features/account-security/components/AdvancedAccountSecurityPanel.tsx).
Turn on: add at least two passkeys or security keys, save recovery keys, then enter a code emailed to the account address and confirm with a passkey.
Turn off: confirm with a passkey. The emailed link to undo within 48 hours works without a passkey.
how_it_should_work: Turning on signs out every other device and emails a notice.
Recovery keys start a recovery that unlocks 48 hours later. Each works once.
Undo link cleanup runs under a 120-second lease, and a partly finished cleanup tells the person to open the link again (apps/web/lib/server/account-security/undo.ts:26-35).

The support copy says it is not available to organisation-managed accounts or verified-domain accounts (apps/web/lib/support/agent/corpus.generated.json, Advanced Account Security entry). I did not find that check in the route code I read.
Empty and waiting states: not verified.
features.on_each_app: Web: full. Desktop: brief says done, via the web screens. Phone: a row that only opens the web Security page (account-security/index.tsx:592-598), so it cannot be turned on in the app. CLI, VS Code, Chrome: brief says done; not verified in code.

features.name: Active sessions and sign-out
features.use: Shows signed-in sessions with device, place and last activity, ends one, ends all, and signs out this device.
how_people_use_it: Web: Settings, Security or Account. Each session has an end button. The current session is listed first.
Web: Log out of all devices (SecuritySection.tsx:120-135), then Log out everywhere in the confirm dialog.
Phone: Account security lists sessions; revoke one or all, with a confirm (account-security/index.tsx:315, 358). Profile has Log Out behind an Alert (profile/index.tsx:117-125).
CLI and extensions: sign out of this device (see code in the notes below).
how_it_should_work: List: sorted with current session first, then last active. Each row shows device, OS, browser, location and times (apps/web/app/api/settings/sessions/route.ts:72-102, 158-163).
Sessions older than the account lifetime policy are ended automatically when the list loads (sessions/route.ts:151-155, 108-141). This is a side effect of a read.

Sign out all needs a re-check (300 s, actions.ts:61-64). It ends every other session and device credential. If some fail, it returns 502 with counts and asks the person to try again (sessions/route.ts:213-236). Success writes an identity event (sessions/route.ts:252).
Sign out this device is done by the extension (freeTrialClient.ts:504 signOutOfAccount, called from side_panel.ts:12089-12110) and by the CLI (app_server/account.rs:635-694).
Empty state, waiting state, plan limits: not verified.

Each notice is recorded once per dedupe key, then emailed (apps/web/lib/services/account-activity-notifications.ts:35-54).

how_people_use_it: Web: Tool approvals panel with three radio options: Ask before every action, Run read-only actions without asking, Skip approvals (ToolApprovalDefaultsPanel.tsx:125-160). Choices save at once.

If the default cannot be read, the agent falls back to Ask before every action (tool-approval-policy.ts:63-68).
Skip approvals is offered only where the workspace allows it. Members cannot skip approvals by switching workspace (tool-approval-policy.ts:34-44; panel copy at ToolApprovalDefaultsPanel.tsx:20).
A critical tool cannot get a standing allow; the server answers 422 critical_tool_always_asks (connectors/permissions/route.ts:103-109; connector-tool-permissions.ts:45-80).
Removing a per-tool rule advances a generation and revokes that connector's session grants in the same transaction (connectors/permissions/route.ts:131-163).

how_it_works.step: 1. Person opens the security screen on the web
how_it_works.detail: The Security section mounts the sign-in methods, passkeys, Advanced Account Security and two-step panels. Log out of all devices sits here with a confirm dialog.

how_it_works.step: 2. Person asks for a change, and a confirm dialog appears for risky actions
how_it_works.detail: Ending all sessions, unpairing a browser and unlinking a device each ask first. The panel then calls the server route and updates its list.
Each write route checks the security token (CSRF), applies a rate limit, and resolves the signed-in person. Password change checks the current password and the second-factor state.

Removing a sign-in method, ending all sessions, changing the password (in some cases) and regenerating backup codes need a fresh re-check. The required freshness and the consequence text come from one table.
The external identity provider sets the password, unlinks the method, or ends other sessions. Device refresh credentials are revoked in the app's own database.
If some sessions could not be ended, the route returns 502 with counts and asks for another try. Password change returns 503 and says to end other sessions in Settings.

how_it_works.step: 7. Change is recorded and the person is told
how_it_works.detail: Audit records are written. Identity security events and two-step change notices are sent to the account holder, even when they made the change.

how_it_works.step: 8. Default approval level is saved and applied on every turn
how_it_works.detail: The approvals panel saves the default in account settings. Each agent turn reads it fresh, bounded by the workspace's permission, and falls back to Ask before every action if the read fails.

key_files.role: The web Security page. Mounts the sign-in, passkey, Advanced and two-step panels and the log out everywhere button.
Lists signed-in sessions, ends sessions past the lifetime policy, and revokes all other sessions after a re-check.
Changes the password, ends other sessions and device credentials, and tells the person.
Lists sign-in methods and removes one, refusing the last or the primary method.
Completes two-step sign-in setup from the authenticator code; gated by the authenticator environment switch.
Single table of risky actions: how fresh a re-check must be and the consequence text shown to the person.
Per-tool approval rules for connectors: read, save, and remove, with the critical-tool refusal.
Reads the saved approval default on each turn, applies the workspace ceiling, and falls back to asking.
The approval default radio group in settings; saves on change and reverts on failure.
Desktop permission decisions: reviews them for the settings list and asks the person when needed.

switches.name: AGI_AUTHENTICATOR_ENROLLMENT
switches.effect: Must be 1 for authenticator apps and backup codes to be set up or regenerated. Otherwise the server answers that they are temporarily unavailable.

switches.name: Organization requires two-step sign-in
switches.effect: Members of a workspace with this policy are refused until they enroll.

guide.area: Enterprise administration screens (workspace console: overview, people, roles, identity, policy, data, audit, usage, billing, compliance)
guide.what_it_is_for: A workspace administrator uses this area to run a shared team workspace: see who is in it, invite and remove people, decide what they may use, sign them in through the company's identity provider, control where data is kept, and read the audit trail and spend. It matters because a company cannot adopt the product for staff without these controls, and each control has to be enforced on the server, not only shown on screen.
guide.who_uses_it: Workspace owners and admins use the console (apps/web/app/workspace/*). Owners are the only role that can transfer ownership. Members are affected but do not use the console: policy refusals reach them in chat requests, CLI runs and the extension. Developers and automations use the scoped admin API keys and service accounts (S87.12, S87.40). Platform operators, not workspace admins, use the support-access grant flow (S87.35). Plan gates apply: the code checks enterprise plan tiers for some controls (apps/web/lib/services/managed-compute-access.ts, apps/web/app/api/settings/organization/data-region/route.ts).

features.name: Overview and policy diagnostics
features.use: One page that summarises the workspace security posture, and a view that explains why a member's request was allowed or refused.
how_people_use_it: Sign in as an owner or admin and open the Workspace section in the console (Overview link).
Read the posture summary (name, plan, members, identity, provisioning, data settings) and its recommendations.
Open the policy diagnostics panel and choose a member or request to see the decision and its reason.
how_it_should_work: Only owners and admins see the posture; members get a refusal from the server, not just a hidden page.
Live data: the summary is read from the database on each open, not from a cached copy.
Diagnostics shows the decision code and a plain reason for each refused action.
Failure: if the policy cannot be read, requests are refused rather than allowed (fail closed, as the code's policy-unavailable path does).
Plan limit: not established in the code read.
features.on_each_app: Web: done (console pages). Desktop: done per brief (Electron shows the hosted web app, so it is the same screens). Mobile: S87.01 done in apps/mobile (WorkspaceAdministration). CLI: S87.01 and S87.39 missing (CLI shows policy in its own output only, not a console).

features.name: Members, invitations, seats and ownership
features.use: List people in the workspace, invite them by email with a role, track seats, and hand the owner role to another member.
how_people_use_it: Open Members in the console (Workspace > People > Members).
Type an email, pick a role (admin, member or viewer), and send an invitation. Pending invitations appear in the list.
Renew or revoke a pending invitation from its row.
Invitee opens the email link and accepts (accept path not read in this pass).
Owner opens Transfer ownership, picks a successor, confirms in a dialog that says what is lost, and the owner role moves.
how_it_should_work: Listing needs members.manage permission; invitations are created only for roles admin, member or viewer (the schema in the invitations route has no owner role).
Seats: the screen shows licensed, used and available seats. A seat is used by a member and released when the member is removed.
Expired invitations are marked expired on each list call.
Removing a member also tries to revoke that person's device tokens and API keys; the response reports any cleanup problems.
Ownership transfer must be atomic on the server (the brief's Should). Confirmation is required because the action cannot be undone by the owner alone.
Empty state: not established. Failure: create and remove return server errors shown on the screen.
features.on_each_app: Web: done. Desktop: done (hosted web screens). Mobile: S87.02, S87.03, S87.05 (role change) and S87.08 done in apps/mobile (team and settings screens). CLI: missing for all four.

features.name: Roles, custom roles and groups
features.use: See roles and their permissions, change a member's role, make custom roles from permission sets, and group members for shared role grants.
how_people_use_it: Open Roles in the console (Workspace > People > Roles).
Read the list of roles and what each permission allows.
Change a member's role from the member row or role picker (web and mobile role picker).
Create or edit a custom role by ticking permissions and saving; assign it to members or groups.
Groups: view members of a group, rename, create or sync a group, and grant a role to it.
how_it_should_work: Role changes are enforced by the server: the member-role route accepts owner, admin, member or viewer and checks the actor's permission.
A role-ceiling check stops an actor from granting more than their own role (membership-role-ceiling helper used by the invitations route).
Custom roles take effect for the members and groups that hold them; the code path that proves this was not read.
Groups can also be synced from the identity provider over SCIM (see the directory provisioning feature).
Empty state and failure states: not established in this pass.
features.on_each_app: Web: done (roles and groups panel). Desktop: done (hosted web screens). Mobile: S87.05 role change only (role picker). CLI: missing for groups and custom roles. API: groups are also served by the SCIM Groups endpoint (S87.04 API done).

features.name: Sign-in, domains and directory sync
features.use: Claim a company domain by proving a DNS record, connect a single sign-on (SSO) provider for that domain, and let the identity provider create, update and remove members through SCIM.
how_people_use_it: Open Identity (Workspace > People > Identity).
Enter the company domain; the console shows a DNS TXT record to publish.
Click verify after the DNS record is published.
Create an SSO connection (SAML or OIDC) for the verified domain and paste the provider's metadata.
Create a directory-sync (SCIM) connection and copy the bearer token once into the identity provider.
how_it_should_work: A domain is verified only when a TXT record at the domain carries the expected token. Records with a different token are reported as token_mismatch, and no record as no_record.
Verify on an already verified connection returns success without re-checking.
A connection with no challenge is told to reissue one.
SSO sign-in is used only for verified domains; the just-in-time (first sign-in) provisioning reads only verified domains.
SCIM: the provider creates, updates and deprovisions members through the SCIM Users and Groups endpoints.
The brief says sign-in is routed by domain; the routing code was not read, so this is unconfirmed.

Revoked keys stop working on the next request (not verified in code read).

features.name: Sharing, publishing and memory

features.name: Data retention, region, keys, network and managed client settings
features.use: Set how long conversations are kept and enforce it, choose the region where data is stored, connect a customer-managed encryption key, restrict access to listed IP ranges, deploy managed settings through device management, and control client release channels.
how_people_use_it: Open Data (Workspace > Data) to choose the data region, connect or rotate an encryption key, and see the region move status.
Open Policy to set the retention period and whether it is enforced, and to enter allowed IP ranges.
IT deploys a managed configuration file to the browser extension or CLI through device management (no console for it in web, desktop or mobile).
how_it_should_work: Retention: a scheduled sweep deletes conversations older than the period, in small batches, skips conversations under a legal hold, and records each sweep in the audit trail. A dry-run mode exists.
Region: a move request is refused with a conflict while the region is not provisioned; the region must be provisioned by the owner before data can move there.
Encryption key: rotating or revoking the key is done from the console; data is sealed under the key when one is connected.
IP ranges: requests from outside the allowed ranges are refused and the refusal is audited.
Managed client settings (S87.27): the extension reads a managed schema, and the CLI reads a server-issued effective policy.
Rollout settings (S87.38) are missing in web, desktop and CLI.

The compliance export is recorded.

how_it_works.detail: The workspace page renders the posture overview. The left navigation groups links as Workspace, People, Controls, Data and so on. Each link is a page under /workspace.

how_it_works.step: Page loads its data through an admin route
how_it_works.detail: Each console panel calls a settings API route. The posture route checks the rate limit, opens a user-scoped database connection, requires workspace membership, requires team admin access, and requires the audit.read permission. It then reads the posture and writes an admin data-access log row.

how_it_works.step: Changing people: invite, change role, remove
how_it_works.detail: Invitations need the members.manage permission and a CSRF token on writes. Invitable roles are admin, member and viewer. Role changes accept owner, admin, member or viewer. Removing a member drops the membership, then deprovisions device tokens and API keys, and writes an audit event.

Admin saves are stored as an organization policy. The evaluator turns a question (for example managed compute, privacy mode, audit export, external sharing, MFA or spend cap) into an allow or refuse decision with a code and a reason.

The chat route first runs the product-wide kill switch, then asks the workspace policy gate. If the policy cannot be read, the request is denied. A denial returns a 403 response; an allowed request continues.
After the policy check passes, a managed request is checked against the monthly spend limit for the selected workspace and for the enterprise funding workspace, if there is one.
Bearer-token and API requests call the IP allow-list check. A request from outside the allowed ranges is refused, and the refusal is written to the audit trail.
The admin requests a challenge, publishes the TXT record, then calls verify. The DNS lookup compares each TXT value with the expected token and returns verified, token_mismatch or no_record.

An audit export is checked against the export policy, recorded before the file streams, and streamed in batches. A scheduled retention job deletes old conversations one organization at a time, skips held data, and writes a sweep audit event.

how_it_works.step: CLI and extension read the same policy
how_it_works.detail: The CLI fetches the effective workspace policy about once an hour, caches it sealed in the OS credential store, and treats an old or unreadable cache as not allowed. The Chrome extension reads a managed site-policy file from browser managed storage.

key_files.role: Groups the console links by the question an admin asks (Workspace, People, Controls, and so on).
Turns each policy question (managed compute, feature, privacy, audit export, spend cap, billing state) into allow or refuse with a code and reason.
Runs the product kill switch and then the workspace policy check for managed compute requests; denies when the policy cannot be read.
Lists and creates invitations; requires members.manage and checks seat state.
Changes a member's role, removes members, and deprovisions their device tokens and keys.
Checks the DNS TXT record for a claimed domain against the expected token.
Checks the export policy, records the export, and streams the audit trail.
Scheduled sweep that deletes old workspace conversations, one organization at a time, and audits each sweep.
Applies the workspace spend limit to managed compute, including the enterprise funding workspace.
Reads each workspace's data region and whether the target region is provisioned.
CLI copy of the effective workspace policy: hourly refresh, sealed cache, fails closed when stale or unreadable.
Admin-only read of the workspace security posture, with a data-access log row.

switches.name: Managed compute kill switch (product-wide)
switches.effect: When off, every managed compute request is refused with a 403 and the message says to use Local or BYOK.

switches.name: Workspace policy (governed flag and per-rule values)
switches.effect: Turns feature, privacy, audit export, external sharing, memory and other rules on or off for the workspace. An absent policy means the workspace is not governed and everything is allowed.

switches.name: Feature exceptions
switches.effect: Lets one person or group keep a switched-off feature.

switches.name: Monthly spend limit and alert threshold
switches.effect: When spent, managed usage is refused (spend_cap_exceeded). Threshold sets the alert percent.

switches.name: Enterprise plan tier check
switches.effect: Some controls are offered only on enterprise plans.

switches.name: Data region provisioning
switches.effect: A region is usable only after its database, bucket, log sink and key are set up. A move to an unprovisioned region is refused with a conflict.
switches.where: Environment variables AGI_DATA_REGION_EU_* read through resolveDataRegion in apps/web/lib/server/data-region.ts:20-25

switches.name: Retention sweep schedule and batch size
switches.effect: Runs the retention job on a schedule and caps the number of organizations per run.

guide.area: Support, trust and policy product (brief area 88)
guide.what_it_is_for: This area gives a person a way to get help and to be heard. It covers the help centre, contacting support, sending bug reports and feedback, and getting a reference id when something fails. It also shows service status and notices, and it lets people report content or appeal a block. Public pages such as privacy, cookies, security, subprocessors and the trust page make the company's promises easy to check.
guide.who_uses_it: Every visitor uses the public pages: help, status, privacy, cookies, security, subprocessors, terms archive and copyright form. Signed-in users use tickets, feedback, diagnostics and content reports. A suspended user uses the appeal form, signed in or signed out. Support staff read and answer tickets through staff routes in apps/web/lib/support/tickets/service.ts. Paid plans change only the support priority, read from the organisation's billing contract (apps/web/lib/support/handoff/priority.ts:72). The code I read has no other plan gate on these features.

how_it_works.step: The person opens a support or help screen
how_it_works.detail: The help page renders the search box. The Help section in settings shows the support tickets panel, the status link and the release notes link.
The search box calls the help search API. The API is rate limited and returns matching articles and whether the index is available.
The panel asks the server to prepare a diagnostic bundle. The browser collects platform, locale, time zone and release details, and the server checks and redacts them.
The ticket route checks the user, the anti-forgery token and the rate limit, then validates the body. It asks for a reply email and re-checks the diagnostics before saving.

how_it_works.step: Save the ticket and notify the team
how_it_works.detail: The service looks up the support tier from the organisation contract, clamps the subject and message length, inserts the row and tells the team.

how_it_works.step: Send feedback from a chat message
how_it_works.detail: The feedback dialog sends the type, text and context. The feedback route checks the fields for each type (rating, task, safety refusal) and inserts a row.
The app mounts the product notice stack. The notice component fetches the notice list every 5 minutes and filters out dismissed notices.

how_it_works.step: Decide which notices apply on the server
how_it_works.detail: The server reads a health check with a 3 second limit. It turns blocked services into incident notices, and it reads the maintenance window from configuration.

how_it_works.step: Show a reference id on failure
how_it_works.detail: The server error handler carries a request id with each error. The chat turn notice shows it as 'Reference' only when the turn failed.

how_it_works.step: Report content, copyright or appeal a block
how_it_works.detail: Content reports are saved to the content report table. Copyright notices are saved and do not remove content. Appeals are saved as support tickets; signed-out appeals need a human check first.

Decides which incident and maintenance notices apply, with the 3 second health read and the maintenance window.
Client component that polls the notice list every 5 minutes and shows dismissible banners.

Stores feedback and reports in the feedback table with per-type field checks.

Collects browser-side diagnostic facts for a bug report.

Shared schema and path for the service notice list (SERVICE_NOTICES_PATH, ServiceNoticeListSchema).
