guide.what_it_is_for: This area lets a person connect outside services (mail, calendars, files, chat, tickets, and similar tools) and lets the assistant use them with the person's permission. It also covers MCP (a standard way for AI tools to talk to outside servers), add-on packages called plugins, skills (bundles of instructions and files), and hooks (commands that run at set moments). Together these let the product grow without changing its core code. The brief's status is "platform" only, so these parts are judged on the server and runtime side, not on each app's screens.
guide.who_uses_it: Signed-in people connect their own accounts (per-user OAuth grants, see apps/web/lib/connectors/oauth-store.ts). Workspace admins distribute approved plugins, skills and servers to members (apps/web/lib/services/organization-plugin-service.ts, apps/web/app/api/settings/organization/plugins/route.ts). Developers author plugins and skills (apps/web/app/api/plugins/authored/route.ts, apps/web/app/api/plugins/uploads/route.ts) and write hook files (~/.agiworkforce/hooks.json, apps/cli/src/features/hooks/hooks.rs:3). Outside providers send signed webhooks in. Other AI clients connect to this product as an MCP server (apps/cli/src/app_server.rs:132). Plan gates were not found in the files read, so who may connect by plan is unknown.

features.name: Connect a service account
features.use: Lets a person sign in to an outside service once, so the assistant can act in that service. A person can link more than one account of the same service, such as a work and a personal mailbox.
how_people_use_it: Open the connectors page, pick a service in the directory, and choose Connect.
Approve the service's sign-in and consent screen in the browser.
Return to the app; the new account appears with its label.
Set one account as the default, or pick an account for a task.
how_it_should_work: The catalog lists each service with its auth scheme, risk class and release state (catalog.ts:161).
The callback checks the state value and rejects a missing or malformed one (callback/route.ts:66-68).
A second account of the same service is kept as its own grant, not overwritten (migration 0253 lines 4-19).
If one account is the default, an unqualified call uses it; a call scoped to an account never resolves to another (oauth-store.ts:500-504; migration 0253 line 86).
A wider scope set than the person consented to needs fresh consent (scopes-escalation.ts:48-54).
Empty state: the directory shows services with a connect mode or a needs-setup mode (directory/connectable.ts:13-24).
Failure: a bad or expired state, or a failed exchange, returns the person to /connectors with an error code (callback/route.ts:68).
Limit by plan: not verified in these files.
features.on_each_app: The brief gives platform status only. Cloud connectors use the web backend (catalog.ts:100 surfaces cloud-web). Connectors marked desktop-local run on the device and are not enumerated by the cloud (catalog.ts:207-211, 125-137).

features.name: Keep connections working
features.use: Stores tokens safely, refreshes expiring tokens, and tracks whether each connection is healthy.
how_people_use_it: Nothing to do in normal use.
When a connection needs attention, the person is asked to reconnect (reauthorization).
how_it_should_work: Tokens are encrypted at rest and decrypted only when used (oauth-store.ts:516-543; custom-connector-crypto.ts:64-87).
Concurrent requests for the same expiring token share one refresh (oauth-access.ts:37, 136-149).
Refresh holds a lock; a slow refresh is reported as a failure that needs reauthorization (oauth-access.ts:173-188).
Health comes from the recent call log within a time window (health.ts:300-310); a gate decision uses the same log (health.ts:312-323).
Empty state: no call history means no health entries yet.
Failure: a token that cannot be decrypted raises a grant decryption error (oauth-store.ts:540-541).

how_it_works.detail: Each service has an id, auth scheme, scope source, risk class, release state and the surfaces it runs on. Services can be cloud-web or desktop-local. Services that are not built in declare no action list; the provider decides at connect time.
The server records an authorization in progress with a hashed state value, the account key and label, and an expiry. The person is sent to the service's sign-in page.

how_it_works.step: 3. The callback checks state and finishes
how_it_works.detail: The callback reads the state from the URL, rejects a missing or malformed one, and checks it belongs to the person and the service. Then it exchanges the code and stores the grant.

how_it_works.step: 4. The grant is saved per account
how_it_works.detail: Tokens are written encrypted. A new account becomes the default only if no other live default exists. A re-authorization of the same account overwrites that account's row.

how_it_works.step: 5. A token is read only when needed
how_it_works.detail: The grant is read with the account filter if one was given; otherwise the default account is used first. Tokens are decrypted only in this read.
Concurrent callers for the same grant share one in-flight refresh inside the process. The refresh then runs under a database lock. A slow refresh returns a reauthorization result.
The app compares the scopes the person agreed to with the scopes the connector now asks for. Any added scope requires fresh consent.

how_it_works.step: 8. A tool call goes through the gateway
how_it_works.detail: The gateway checks the person and the connector and proxies the MCP call. Built-in service adapters run the call. External sends ask the person first.

how_it_works.step: 9. Calls are logged and health is read
how_it_works.detail: Each call is written to a call log. Health and gate decisions are computed from the recent entries.
Signed events from outside services are checked against a secret before they are routed. Bad signatures get a 401.

Seals and opens custom connector credentials; supports older plain bearer rows.
MCP client: connect, list and call tools, resources and prompts, and probe the server revision.
Runs the product as an MCP server on stdio for other clients.
Loads hooks.json and holds the hook rules, matchers and sandbox setting.
Plugin integrity checks (digest, signature) and package scanning before install.

guide.area: Commercial and administrative components (brief area 100, S100.01 to S100.28)
guide.what_it_is_for: This area is the money and admin side of AGI Workforce. It decides which plan an account holds, what that plan allows, how much each model call costs and is charged, how payments and refunds reach the account, and how workspace admins manage seats, audit logs and directory sync. A person gets a paid plan or credits, sees their usage and invoices, and can ask for support. The area matters because every managed (Cloud) model call passes through it, so a fault here either lets usage run for free or blocks paying customers.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in person uses the plan, usage and checkout parts (their own account). Paid-plan holders get their plan's limits and invoices. Workspace owners and admins use seats, team invitations, usage analytics export, audit export and the admin API. Enterprise customers get contract-based billing. Developers use API keys with scopes (for example usage:read on the usage history route, and admin API keys with scopes for workspace admin calls). Staff see support tickets and operator metrics (apps/web/features/admin/services/operator-metrics.ts is referenced by the brief). Code that is not a person: the Stripe webhook and cron jobs run without a user.

features.name: Plans, prices and what a plan allows
features.use: Defines each plan's tier, its price in each currency and interval, and the rule that says what an account may use right now. Every other feature reads these.
how_people_use_it: Open the pricing or plan page on the web settings or billing screen and compare plans.
Pick a plan and interval (monthly or yearly), then continue to checkout.
Some plans are not sold self-serve: contract-only (enterprise) or seat-upgrade plans are shown differently or not at all.
how_it_should_work: Each plan has one entry in the catalog with its tier, sellability (self_serve, seat_upgrade, contract_only, free_of_charge or withdrawn), catalog version and, when withdrawn, a successor plan (billing-plan-catalog.ts:11-30).
A subscription keeps the catalog version it was sold under, so a later reprice is visible rather than silent.
If a Stripe price lookup fails, the localized price falls back to the catalog USD price and checkout stays closed for that price (localized-pricing-service.ts:44-60).
An account with no live paid subscription is resolved as Free with entitled false and denial reason entitlement_missing (entitlement-resolution.ts:289-302).
A seat member inherits the workspace plan unless the caller asks for own-plan only (entitlement-resolution.ts:250-263).
features.on_each_app: The brief gives one status per item ('platform done'), with no per-app status. The catalog and resolver are server-side and shared. Which app screens show the plan is not established in this read.

features.name: Limits, rate and spend controls
features.use: Stops a person or workspace from using more than the plan or budget allows, by rolling windows, rate, concurrent responses and monthly spend.
how_people_use_it: Send messages normally. When a limit is hit the reply says so and names the window (for example the 5-hour or weekly limit) and the reset point.
Admins set a monthly spend limit for a workspace; when the limit is reached managed usage stops until the owner raises it or the month resets.
Sending a message while the plan's concurrent-response count is full gets a message to stop or wait.
how_it_should_work: Each managed request is checked against plan limits before the model runs. Refusal texts exist for session_limit (rolling 5-hour), weekly_limit, flagship_weekly_limit and declined (monthly) (managed-usage-request-service.ts:440-467).
Daily free caps and monthly metered units come from the tier policy (tier-unit-quota-service.ts:50-75).
Rate limits are shared across instances through the rate limiter, and the limit can depend on the plan tier (rate-limit.ts:961, 1234-1250).
Concurrent responses use a slot per turn. A plan with no concurrency gets a refusal; if the limiter itself is unavailable the reply is HTTP 503 with Retry-After 30 (turn-slot.ts:20-40).
A workspace with a block-mode monthly cap refuses new managed usage with code over_cap (spend-limit-service.ts:175-184).
Limit numbers are configuration from the plan, not constants in the feature.
features.on_each_app: Enforcement is server-side on the managed Cloud path, so every app that calls it gets the same limits. Per-app messages are not verified.

features.name: Metered usage ledger (reserve, settle, release, cost)
features.use: Records each metered model call in a durable ledger. Before a call the estimated cost is held (reserved). After the call the hold is replaced by the real cost. Failed or stranded holds are released.
how_people_use_it: Nothing visible in the normal flow: a message is sent and the cost is taken from the plan window or usage credits.
On a failed reply the hold is released and the person is not charged for it.
Usage credits can be used for extra usage when turned on (usageCreditsEnabled, managed-usage-request-service.ts:715).
how_it_should_work: Reservation takes a parsed idempotency key, the estimated cost, the plan's session and weekly caps, and writes through a database function (managed-usage-request-service.ts:738-827).
Finalization sets the billed amount and the provider cost separately; a failed outcome records zero cost for both (managed-usage-request-service.ts:1140-1170).
Stranded reservations are recovered by a cron job, which releases them and drains the settlement queue; the job is skipped in low-power mode (cron/recover-reservations/route.ts:20-60).
Cost is attributed to user, organization, conversation, API key, schedule run and artifact subject (managed-usage-request-service.ts:614-712).
An artifact (published app) can be capped per app and cannot be billed to usage credits (managed-usage-request-service.ts:763-769).
features.on_each_app: Server-side for all managed calls. The brief gives no per-app difference.

features.name: Buying a plan and paying
features.use: Creates a payment checkout for an eligible account, returns the person to a verified result, and keeps the account's plan in step with the payment provider through webhooks and a daily reconciliation. Tax is calculated for each charge.
how_people_use_it: Choose a plan on the upgrade page and press the upgrade or subscribe button.
Complete payment on the provider's hosted checkout page.
Return to the app; a pending confirmation screen waits until the webhook has landed the change.
Top-ups use the same tax policy (billing/top-up/route.ts:258).
how_it_should_work: Checkout refuses if Stripe already bills a live subscription for the customer, to prevent double billing (checkout/route.ts:420-430).
If a stored Stripe customer id no longer exists the checkout drops it and creates a fresh one (checkout/route.ts:392-410).

Webhook requests are rate-limited, signature-checked (a wrong signature returns 400 and is logged), then de-duplicated by event id before handling (stripe-webhook/route.ts:47-60; lib/verify.ts:29-45).
Subscription events update the plan and status in event order (handlers.ts:133-140).
A daily job reconciles billed plans (vercel.json:174-175; cron/reconcile-billed-plans/route.ts:36).
Tax uses the tax policy module for every charge, including tax IDs and reverse charge (lib/billing/tax-policy.ts:94-110).
features.on_each_app: Web checkout and pending confirmation are in apps/web. Desktop, CLI, VS Code and Chrome flows are not established in this read.

features.name: Mobile store purchases (Apple and Google)
features.use: Lets an iPhone or Android purchase grant a plan or credits after the store receipt is checked on the server.
how_people_use_it: On the mobile Billing screen the store plans and top-ups are listed (only when the deployment turns purchases on).
Tap buy; the store sheet opens; after payment the app sends the receipt to the server to verify.
When purchases are off the screen shows a message that nothing was charged.
how_it_should_work: Off by default: catalog returns enabled false with the reason 'Native purchases are not enabled for this deployment' unless MOBILE_IAP_ENABLED is true (mobile-iap-catalog.ts:53-57, 127-134).
A kill switch for the in_app_purchase capability also turns the catalog off (mobile/iap/catalog/route.ts:50-60).
Verify refuses a product not registered for AGI and an account that has not opened Billing again (mobile/iap/verify/route.ts:58-70).
Store acknowledgement runs after the purchase is recorded; a failed acknowledgement is logged and the result is still returned (mobile/iap/verify/route.ts:70-95).
Consumable and subscription products are split; Google subscriptions need a base plan id (mobile-iap-catalog.ts:100-108).
A user who withdrew store consent or is scheduled for deletion gets the catalog with enabled false (catalog route 80-100).
features.on_each_app: Mobile only. Web and other apps do not sell through the store.

features.name: Invoices, refunds and disputes
features.use: Lists invoices and their documents for an account, and handles refunds and card disputes so the plan and credits follow the money.
how_people_use_it: Open Billing, then Invoices, to list and download invoice documents.
Refunds and disputes are started by staff or the provider, not by the person; the person sees the resulting plan or credit change.
how_it_should_work: Invoices are listed per account (billing/invoices/route.ts:28; billing-invoice-service.ts:46).
A refund reverses the credits it granted; a won dispute reverses the loss (billing-refund-service.ts:580, 764; dispute-events.ts:431).
Refund and dispute events arrive through the same webhook path as checkout.
features.on_each_app: Web billing screens. Other apps not established.

features.name: Promotions and referrals
features.use: Applies promo codes, bonus credits and invite grants at checkout or on upgrade, and gives referral codes whose sign-ups earn rewards.
how_people_use_it: Enter a promo code at checkout or upgrade.
Open Settings, then Referrals, to see your referral code and rewards.
how_it_should_work: Checkout and upgrade apply the promotion to the account (checkout/route.ts:407; upgrade/route.ts:256).
Referral codes are issued and sign-ups are attributed when the new account's first paid event arrives (stripe-webhook/lib/referral-events.ts:128, 211).
The referrals screen reads and shows the code (ReferralsSection.tsx:126).
features.on_each_app: Web settings screen only in the code read. Other apps not established.

features.name: Seats, team admin and admin API
features.use: Tracks paid seats in a workspace and lets admins invite members. Admins can also manage the workspace through an authenticated, scoped API and directory sync (SCIM).
how_people_use_it: A workspace owner opens Team settings, sends an invitation, and sees seats used and available.
An admin creates an API key with specific scopes (admin API keys).
An identity provider syncs users through the SCIM endpoints.
how_it_should_work: Invitations list and create require team admin access; the list also expires pending invites and returns seat state (settings/team/invitations/route.ts:60-80).
Admin API calls by a service principal need an active Team or Enterprise plan, an allowed IP list and a scope check (compliance-caller.ts:60-85).
SCIM calls use a bearer token that acts for one workspace; a workspace under incident lockdown refuses SCIM (scim-auth.ts:30-55).
Seat counts come from the stripe seat sync (stripe-webhook/lib/seats.ts:114) and the seat service (organization-seat-service.ts:33).
features.on_each_app: Web settings and admin APIs. The brief lists platform status only.

features.name: Usage reporting and export
features.use: Shows usage by time, model and feature for a person and for a workspace, and exports it.
how_people_use_it: Open Usage to see the history; choose a time range and granularity.
Admins open usage analytics and press export.
how_it_should_work: Usage history reads the account's ledger for a window (usage/history/route.ts:25-50; account-usage-history-service.ts:95).
API callers need the usage:read scope (usage/history/route.ts:29).
Export is at the usage-analytics export route (settings/organization/usage-analytics/export/route.ts:41).
features.on_each_app: Web. Other apps not established.

features.name: Enterprise contracts
features.use: Stores enterprise agreements (committed seats, invoicing terms, purchase order, offline payment) and uses them to drive billing.
how_people_use_it: Set up by sales or staff, not by the person. The person sees the contract terms on their billing page.
how_it_should_work: Agreements are stored in the agreement store and an invoicing module builds invoices from them (enterprise-contracts/agreement-store.ts:31; enterprise-contracts/invoicing.ts:287).
The same Stripe webhook handler is used for contract subscriptions (handlers.ts:133).
features.on_each_app: Not on the apps; set up through internal tools.

features.name: Support cases
features.use: Lets a signed-in person open a support ticket with account context, see their tickets and read staff replies.
how_people_use_it: Open Help or Support, describe the problem, send. The list shows your tickets; open one to see replies.
how_it_should_work: Create needs a CSRF token, rate limit and a reply email; the ticket gets priority from the contracted support tier (support/tickets/route.ts:44-60; support/tickets/service.ts:131-140).
Staff replies email the customer, with an idempotency key per reply (support/tickets/service.ts:~140-160).
Ticket diagnostics are normalized before saving (support/tickets/route.ts:12).
features.on_each_app: Web API; apps reach it through the same routes. Per-app screens not established.

features.name: Audit trail
features.use: Writes durable records of billing and admin actions, and exports the workspace audit trail when policy allows.
how_people_use_it: Admins open the audit log and press export; a policy can switch export off for the whole workspace.
how_it_should_work: Commercial and admin actions write audit events (lib/security-audit.ts:641).
Export needs the audit.read permission and is refused by a saved organization policy; a refused export is itself recorded as denied (settings/organization/audit/export/route.ts:50-80).
An organization without a policy is treated as allowed.
features.on_each_app: Web admin. Other apps not established.

how_it_works.detail: The catalog defines plans, sellability, versions and prices. Checkout, pricing and enforcement read the same plan records. Tax policy and the plan limits come from the same tier policy.
The person's upgrade request reaches the checkout route. It reuses or creates the payment customer, refuses if a live subscription already exists, and creates the payment-provider checkout session.
The provider calls the webhook. The route rate-limits, checks the signature, de-duplicates by event id, and then dispatches the event. Subscription events update the stored plan in event order.

how_it_works.step: Resolve what the account may do
how_it_works.detail: Each managed request passes the auth gate. It reads the subscription, decides whether it is entitled, and resolves the usage plan. A lapsed paid plan is served as Free.
The shared rate limiter checks the request, then a concurrency slot is taken for the turn. Full slots return an error with a retry or upgrade message.

Spend cap is checked for workspaces; the plan allowance and promotional caps are read; a database function writes the reservation against the session, weekly and flagship caps. Refusals name the window that was hit.
After the model call the request is finalized. Billed cost and provider cost are stored separately. A failed call records zero cost.
A cron job every 15 minutes releases reservations that were never settled, recovers abandoned voice sessions, and drains the settlement queue.
The usage history route reads the ledger by window, granularity and workload. Admin exports go through the audit and usage export routes, which check permissions and policy first.

key_files.role: Reserves, settles and releases the cost of each managed model call; attributes cost.
Single resolver for what an account is entitled to (plan, seat, lapsed paid plan).
Gate every managed model request passes before it runs; enforces surface and terms.
Shared rate limiter and the managed concurrent-turn slot.
Creates the payment checkout and refuses double subscriptions.
Entry point for payment provider events; verifies, de-duplicates and dispatches.
Plan catalog: sellability, catalog version, withdrawn plans and successors.
Reads mobile store configuration and decides whether store purchases are offered.
Verifies an Apple or Google receipt on the server and grants the plan or credits.
Authenticates directory sync calls and enforces the incident lockdown.
Releases stranded cost holds and drains the settlement queue every 15 minutes.
Workspace monthly spend cap; block mode refuses managed usage at the cap.

switches.name: MOBILE_IAP_ENABLED
switches.effect: Turns store purchases on for the deployment. Off or unset means no product is offered.

switches.name: MOBILE_IAP_APPLE_PRODUCT_IDS_JSON and MOBILE_IAP_GOOGLE_PRODUCT_IDS_JSON
switches.effect: Map logical product keys to store product ids. A bad value throws.

switches.name: MOBILE_IAP_GOOGLE_REPLACEMENT_MODES_JSON
switches.effect: Sets how Google subscription upgrades and downgrades replace the old plan.

switches.name: in_app_purchase capability (kill switch)
switches.effect: Turns the mobile catalog off without a deploy.

switches.name: Stripe keys and webhook secret
switches.effect: Required for the webhook and checkout. Missing values log an error and the webhook returns 500.

switches.name: Stripe price ids (STRIPE_PRICE_*)
switches.effect: A missing or badly formed price id makes that price unavailable.

switches.name: Plan limits and concurrent responses
switches.effect: Set per plan; zero or missing concurrency refuses the turn.

switches.name: Workspace spend cap (block or report mode)
switches.effect: Block mode refuses managed usage at the monthly cap.

switches.name: Organization audit export policy
switches.effect: A saved policy can turn audit export off for the workspace.

switches.name: Cron schedules
switches.effect: How often reservations are recovered (every 15 minutes) and billed plans reconciled (daily).

switches.name: Low-power cron skip
switches.effect: Skips the recovery cron when set.

switches.name: Stripe API version pin
switches.effect: Webhook logs a warning when the endpoint API version differs from the pinned one.

guide.shared_code: Shared: the plan, price and product catalogs in packages/contracts/types/src (billing-catalog.ts, billing-plan-catalog.ts) are imported by the web server and the mobile catalog (mobile-iap-catalog.ts imports from @agiworkforce/types). The entitlement resolver, usage ledger, rate limiter, spend cap and audit writer are shared server code in apps/web/lib and are called by all API routes. Mobile-only: the Apple and Google store code (mobile-iap-store-verification.ts, mobile/iap routes). Web-only per code read: the checkout pages, ReferralsSection.tsx, and the team and billing settings screens. Desktop, CLI, VS Code and Chrome extension UI for this area were not read.

things_that_look_wrong.what: Brief says the mobile catalog requires an upgrade-waitlist redemption (beta_redemptions). The catalog route code has no redemption check, and its test asserts that no beta_redemptions query runs. The verify route test still expects a beta_redemptions query, so the two disagree. The brief claim is not confirmed.
Spend cap fails open. When the spend state cannot be read the request is treated as ungoverned and allowed, although the brief says the budget manager stops managed usage at the limit.
Auth gate decides entitlement without the enterprise collection state when that read fails, so a read failure may grant access rather than refuse it.

Mobile verify acknowledges the purchase with the store after recording it. If acknowledgement fails the purchase is still recorded and the response is returned with storeAcknowledged false, so the store may refund later.
Brief says support cases are routed to staff. The code read creates the ticket with priority and emails the support team, but the staff queue routing was not found in the files read.
Stripe webhook logs a configuration error at module load but does not stop; requests then return HTTP 500 'Stripe not configured'.

not_sure: Per-app UI for every item: the brief gives only 'platform' status, so Desktop, Mobile, CLI, VS Code and Chrome screens were not read.
Seat enforcement count at invitation time and the Stripe seat sync were only partly read (seats.ts and organization-seat-service.ts opened at the top only).
Referral reward amounts and the referral-service internals (referral-service.ts lines 194-445 were not read).
Refund and dispute reversal logic internals (billing-refund-service.ts and dispute-events.ts were only partly read).
Invoice document generation and download (billing-invoice-service.ts:46 not read in full).
Tax engine internals beyond tax-policy.ts:94-110 (which provider computes tax was not established).
Whether the local-only and BYOK plan tiers are charged or enforced by this area (the catalog lists them as free_of_charge).
Admin operator metrics (apps/web/features/admin/services/operator-metrics.ts) not opened.
No tests, builds or servers were run, as the task was read-only. The relayed request asks for testing on localhost one surface at a time; that is for a later QA pass and was not done here.
Whether the brief's 'platform done' statuses hold: the code read supports most items, but the status claims were checked only at the cited lines.

guide.what_it_is_for: This area keeps the six apps (Web, Desktop, Mobile, CLI, VS Code extension, Chrome extension) in agreement with each other and with the server. They share one set of request and response shapes, error and event names, plan and capability decisions, sign-in and streaming clients, and design tokens, so a change made once reaches every app. A person does not see this area directly. They feel it as a new device sign-in that works, chats that sync between devices, and a plan that means the same thing on every screen. Without it, each app keeps its own copy of the rules, they drift apart, and one app shows a limit or status the server does not agree with.
guide.who_uses_it: Developers who change shared packages, shared client code, or the CI guard scripts (scripts/check-*.mjs). The six apps use the shared code at run time, so every user of every app is affected indirectly. Workspace admins feel the plan rules through the organization entitlement code (apps/web/lib/services/org-entitlements.ts). The code shows no separate user-facing switch for the area as a whole. Only the team artifact sharing check requires a particular plan (team_admin).

features.name: Shared request and response shapes
features.use: One schema per wire message (projects, files, artifacts, memory, connectors, usage and billing, device sign-in) so the server and every client parse the same shape. Golden fixtures let the CLI test against the same examples.
how_people_use_it: A person does not touch this directly.
A tester sees it when a flow breaks: sign in on a new device, open a project or file, open the connector list, or read usage. A mismatched shape shows up as an error on that screen.
An engineer adds a field to a schema in packages/contracts/cloud-contracts/src and runs the golden-fixture and parity checks.
how_it_should_work: Every client-called route and every client parses its body with the shared schema. The brief says this is partial: 164 routes still lack one (settings 50, admin 30 and smaller families), and the connector routes for bank accounts, exchange and link still fail the route-contract check.
The brief does not describe empty, waiting or failure states for these shapes. A body that does not match its schema should fail, not be guessed at.
Plan limits are not part of these shapes; they come from the plan code (feature 3).
features.on_each_app: The brief gives one status for the whole platform (partial for device sign-in and routes; done for projects, files, artifacts, memory, connectors, usage and golden fixtures). It gives no per-app status. The CLI is Rust and checks its own copies against the golden fixtures (apps/cli/src/cloud/contract_fixtures.rs).

features.name: Shared events, notifications, content blocks, errors and identifiers
features.use: One list of event names, content-block kinds, error codes, identifier rules and notification categories, so every app names and handles the same thing the same way.
how_people_use_it: A person sees the result on screen: a chat message rendered as text, a code block or a tool step, an error message, or a notification in the Mobile notifications feed (apps/mobile/src/features/notifications/accountFeed.ts).
A tester checks a notification's category and target on the Mobile notification preferences screen (apps/mobile/stores/notificationPrefsStore.ts).
An engineer adds a primary key or a domain event; the identifier guard and the domain-event guard then check it.
how_it_should_work: Server audit events map to one domain event name each (apps/web/lib/audit-domain-events.ts:17-30; for example member_removed becomes workspace.member.revoked). Each mapped event must be emitted by a known emitter (scripts/check-domain-event-emitters.mjs).
Content blocks a client does not know must be shown in a degraded way, not dropped silently (scripts/check-content-blocks.mjs). The brief marks this done on all clients.
Error codes and retry rules should be defined once and every client should map them. The code does not match this yet (see things_that_look_wrong).

Primary keys must follow the identifier contract: no key may encode a name, an address, a secret, a file name, a position or another system's id. Ids are minted by the server and carried unchanged by clients.
features.on_each_app: Platform status is done for all five items. Mobile consumes the notification and content-block vocabularies. Platform-specific renderers are not applicable on any app (brief S101.33). The brief does not show error definitions per app.

features.name: Plan, capability, model and policy decisions
features.use: The server decides what a plan allows, which model capabilities a route offers, and which workspace policy keys are enforced. Clients read that decision instead of deciding locally.
how_people_use_it: A workspace admin changes a policy in workspace settings; the policy is then enforced on the server and in the CLI (apps/cli/src/cloud/workspace_policy.rs).
A person on a paid plan sees a sharing or limit option turned on or off on web and desktop; the choice comes from the server.
A visitor to the web marketing page sees the provider list drawn from the catalogue (apps/web/features/marketing/components/RouteFlow.tsx:1-7).
how_it_should_work: Plan entitlements must be resolved only through the single entry point in apps/web/lib/services/entitlement-resolution.ts. The guard fails any other module that reads a subscription row and then decides what the plan allows.

A seat holder in a team must get the plan of the workspace they belong to, not Free. A seat in the organization being asked about must never entitle its holder to own it (apps/web/lib/services/org-entitlements.ts:34-36).
Team artifact sharing needs the team_admin capability (org-entitlements.ts:22, 133-138). When it is off, the user gets the message from getWorkspaceArtifactSharingErrorMessage.
Shared projects and shared custom connectors have plan limits: none, a number, or zero (org-entitlements.ts:124-129, 155-169). Zero means the plan does not include sharing.

Model metadata must come from one compiled registry. The brief says web marketing and the admin route panel now read it, but the Tauri renderer, one web key-prefix check and the mobile provider client still carry their own lists.
features.on_each_app: Platform status is done for capability resolution, entitlements and policy. Model metadata is partial: web marketing and the admin panel read the shared catalogue; the Tauri renderer and the mobile provider stream client keep their own lists (brief). The CLI enforces workspace policy in Rust (workspace_policy.rs:77-183).

features.name: Sign-in, API and streaming clients
features.use: One shared sign-in client (device sign-in: start, poll, refresh, approve), one API client for server calls, and one streaming reader (server-sent events) with reconnect.
how_people_use_it: Sign in on a new device: the device shows a short code, the person opens the approval page and approves it. A tester can run this flow on the web approval page and the device.
Send a chat message and watch the answer stream in on Mobile, Web, the Chrome side panel and VS Code.
Start a cloud run from the Chrome extension or VS Code (the Continue in cloud action).
how_it_should_work: Device sign-in polls the token route until the request is approved, denied or expired. The token route can answer pending, slow-down, denied, expired, invalid, account-unavailable or terms-acceptance-required (device-authorization.ts:55-73). Slow-down tells the device to poll less often.
A refusal that asks for terms or age review must send the person to the review page at the acceptance URL (device-authorization.ts:61-72).

Stream reads must reconnect after a drop and must not show a run as finished when only the connection dropped. The brief marks this done; the Mobile implementation is apps/mobile/services/streaming.ts.
VS Code and Chrome send idempotency keys on chat, schedule and cloud run calls (brief). The Electron main process does not use the shared managed-cloud client.
features.on_each_app: Device sign-in is shared by the approval page and the client runtime (brief: done). Chrome and VS Code have their own cloud clients (apps/extension/src/features/computer-use/cloudAgentClient.ts; apps/extension-vscode/src/features/cloud-tasks/continueInCloud.ts). The Electron main process has no shared managed-cloud client (brief). A guard checks every SSE reader (scripts/check-sse-readers.mjs).

features.name: Conversation state, sync and agent tasks
features.use: One reducer for conversation state (activity, queue, message status), one sync engine (cursors, pushes, pulls, tombstones, conflicts), and one task and run lifecycle vocabulary.
how_people_use_it: Send a follow-up while the assistant is still answering; it waits in a queue and runs next (VS Code uses the shared message queue).
Star, pin or archive a chat on one device and see it on another device.
Cancel a scheduled run from the Chrome extension's schedules list.
how_it_should_work: Follow-up messages wait in a queue with a cap of 20, first in first out; cancelling a queued message removes it (brief; tests named in brief). A full queue should refuse the new message, not drop it silently.

Sync sends each local change with its version and receives server changes after a cursor. Deleted chats leave a tombstone (a marker that says the item was deleted) so the deletion reaches other devices. Mobile now shows starred chats and drops archived ones.
A scheduled run that is partial or timed out must count as finished (the brief says Chrome now treats both as terminal).
features.on_each_app: Web uses the server sync route. Mobile uses the shared conversation sync client (packages/client/sync/src/conversations.ts). Chrome has its own chat state reducer (apps/extension/src/features/side-panel/chat-state.ts) and its own sync code. VS Code uses the shared queue but posts local tool progress straight to its webview. The CLI keeps its own state logic (brief).

features.name: Tools, approvals, skills and the coding-session protocol
features.use: Tool definitions, approval requests and decisions, skill and plugin manifests, and the local coding-session protocol are each defined once and shared by server and clients.
how_people_use_it: Approve or deny an action an assistant wants to take; approval history is shown on the Chrome options page (apps/extension/src/features/options/approval-history-section.ts).
Install a skill or plugin; its manifest is read by the shared skills code and by the CLI.
Use VS Code with a local runtime; the local runtime protocol is generated from the Rust definitions.
how_it_should_work: Every tool that can be offered must be declared once in the tool registry (scripts/check-tool-registry.mjs). The brief says undeclared tools went from 11 to 1.
Skill manifests must parse the same way on every surface; the golden fixture file is the reference.
The coding-session protocol is generated from Rust into TypeScript, and CI fails when the generated file drifts (scripts/generate-protocol-types.mjs; .github/workflows/ci.yml).
features.on_each_app: Approvals: shared by the Chrome extension and the VS Code local runtime client (apps/extension-vscode/src/integrations/localRuntimeClient.ts). Skills: the TypeScript package and the CLI Rust code (apps/cli/src/skills.rs). Protocol: VS Code and the Electron developer session service (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/developerSessionService.ts). The run_command tool stays with the cloud agent's own definitions and approval store (brief).

features.name: Design tokens, UI primitives, text and Markdown
features.use: One place for colours, radii, type and building blocks, and one Markdown renderer per surface, so the apps look and read the same.
how_people_use_it: A person sees chat look the same across apps: the same text sizes, colours and rounded corners.
A tester checks a screen against the design: a Mobile button is a shared primitive, and a Markdown answer looks the same on the Chrome side panel and in VS Code.
An engineer changes a colour: it must come from the design token package and pass the CSS-token guard.
how_it_should_work: Web, Chrome and VS Code read colours from the design token package under a CSS-token guard (scripts/check-css-tokens.mjs).
Native screens must use the native primitive layer, not raw platform controls (scripts/check-mobile-primitives.mjs). The brief says 117 modules moved and 10 remain.
Strings come from the shared localisation catalogue. Web and Mobile use it; VS Code loads its own catalogue through the shared i18n package.
Renderers are not applicable (S101.33); each surface renders the shared content model itself.
features.on_each_app: Web: shared primitives package (packages/ui). Desktop: the hosted web app, so it gets the web primitives. Mobile: native primitives and tokens (see things_that_look_wrong for colours). Chrome: design tokens and its own web controls. VS Code: design tokens, its own webview controls and its catalogue. CLI: none of these (Rust).

features.name: Telemetry, configuration, security helpers and package runtimes
features.use: One vocabulary for analytics, one configuration validator, one set of secret redaction rules, and one declaration of where each shared package may run (browser, server, native or universal).
how_people_use_it: A tester does not see this directly. A misconfigured production deploy is refused at start-up.
An engineer adds an environment key; the config-keys guard requires that it is classified.
A log or support transcript shows a redaction marker where a secret was removed, using the shared redaction rules.
how_it_should_work: The web server validates its configuration at start-up. A production deployment with test-mode payment keys is refused unless the operator sets AGI_ALLOW_INVALID_ENV=1 (apps/web/lib/validate-env.ts:336-342).
Secret redaction must match on every surface; the parity tests compare the shared rules with the web copy (packages/platform/utils/src/__tests__/secretRedaction.parity.test.ts).

Each shared package entry is declared as universal, browser, server, native or asset; the guard checks the import graph against that declaration (scripts/config/package-runtimes.json:1-3; scripts/check-package-runtimes.mjs).
The analytics vocabulary is used by web only; Chrome and VS Code share the error scrubber; mobile telemetry and the CLI use neither (brief).
features.on_each_app: Web validates config and uses the analytics vocabulary. Chrome and VS Code share the error scrubber. Mobile and the CLI validate config ad hoc (brief). Electron validates config ad hoc (brief).

how_it_works.detail: Each wire message is a zod schema in the cloud contracts package. Device sign-in has four route paths and schemas for the start reply, the approval-page lookup, the token reply, the token refusal (a tagged union on the error field), refresh and approve.

how_it_works.step: Identifiers are data, checked by a guard
how_it_works.detail: The identifier rules are a JSON file loaded into one exported constant. The guard reads every primary key from the migration history and applies these rules, so a bad key fails the build.

how_it_works.step: Shared client runtime exports the clients
how_it_works.detail: The client runtime package is the one entry point apps import for device sign-in, auth provider ids, workspace policy, connectors and the event reader.

For a team, the plan is read from the owner's subscription on a privileged connection, because a team administrator who is not the owner cannot see that row. The owner's personal plan is then resolved without seats, so a seat cannot entitle its holder to own the team.

how_it_works.step: Plan limits and the artifact sharing check
how_it_works.detail: The plan becomes shared project and connector limits (a number, or zero for none). Artifact sharing with a team asks whether the team_admin capability is on for the plan.

how_it_works.step: Guard keeps one entitlement entry point
how_it_works.detail: A build-time guard scans the web app. Any module outside the entry point that reads a plan and asks what it allows fails the check, except the listed own-row operations (top-ups, auto-reload, store purchases, account deletion).

how_it_works.step: Chat sync on the server and the client
how_it_works.detail: The server sync route reads the person's own conversations from the database and applies changes. The client conversation record holds the fields sync carries, including a deleted-at tombstone. The mobile store uses the shared sync code.

how_it_works.step: Streaming reads through a guarded fetch
how_it_works.detail: The mobile streaming client sends each request through a guarded fetch, checks the run for a refusal (HTTP 403), and checks for abort after each wait.
The web server validates its environment at start-up. In production, test-mode payment keys are refused unless the explicit override is set.

how_it_works.step: Each shared package declares where it may run
how_it_works.detail: The package runtime file declares each package entry as universal, browser, server, native or asset. A second guard checks each entry's import graph against that declaration.

key_files.role: Shared schemas and route paths for device sign-in (start, poll, refresh, approve) and the refusal list.
Public entry point of the shared client runtime: device sign-in, auth providers, workspace policy, connectors, event reader.
Resolves a team's plan on the server and answers project limits, connector limits and the artifact sharing check.
Guard that fails any plan decision made outside the single entitlement entry point.
Loads the identifier rules from data and exports them for the identifier guard.
Server side of chat sync: reads the person's owned conversations and applies changes.
Shared client sync for conversations: the record shape and tombstone handling.
Mobile streaming client with guarded fetch and refusal handling.
Validates the web server environment at start-up, including the production test-key refusal and the override.
Declares where each shared package entry may run; checked by scripts/check-package-runtimes.mjs.
Holds TimeoutError and withTimeout. The brief expects shared error codes here, but the file does not contain them.
Mobile colour and radius tokens, read from the design token package.

data_kept.what: Plan and subscription rows (user id, Stripe subscription id, plan tier), and organization rows (owner user id, Stripe subscription id), read for entitlement
data_kept.where: Postgres tables public.organizations and public.subscriptions (apps/web/lib/services/org-entitlements.ts:75-111); read only in this area

data_kept.what: Conversation records (id, title, timestamps, message count, pinned, starred, archived, model, project, deleted-at tombstone, server version)
data_kept.where: Client store on each synced surface (shape in packages/client/sync/src/conversations.ts:6-22); server copy read by apps/web/app/api/chat/sync/route.ts:89

data_kept.what: Workspace policy cache
data_kept.where: Browser local storage via localStorageWorkspacePolicyCache, exported at packages/client/client-runtime/src/index.ts:161 (storage key not opened)

data_kept.what: Domain event names mapped from audit event types
data_kept.where: Constant in apps/web/lib/audit-domain-events.ts:17-30; the audit log itself in apps/web/lib/security-audit.ts

data_kept.what: Identifier rules and config key rules
data_kept.where: Read-only JSON data loaded by packages/contracts/types/src/identifier-contract.ts:12

switches.name: Team artifact sharing capability
switches.effect: Turns sharing of a published artifact with the workspace on or off by plan (team_admin).

switches.name: Shared project and connector limits
switches.effect: Number of projects and custom connectors a team may share; zero means none.

switches.name: Seats excluded from the personal plan
switches.effect: A seat in a team never counts toward owning that team.

switches.name: Production test-key refusal and override
switches.effect: Refuses test-mode payment keys in production. The env value AGI_ALLOW_INVALID_ENV=1 lets a billing-degraded incident deploy start anyway.

switches.name: Production detection
switches.effect: Marks a deploy as production from the VERCEL_ENV or NODE_ENV values.

switches.name: Workspace feature policy
switches.effect: Turns workspace features on or off for a member; polled on an interval.

switches.name: Auth providers and passkey sign-in
switches.effect: Chooses which sign-in providers are offered and whether passkey sign-in is on.

switches.name: Mobile feature flags
switches.effect: Imported by the mobile localisation module; the effect was not established.

guide.shared_code: Shared TypeScript packages used by more than one app: @agiworkforce/cloud-contracts (device sign-in, sync, connectors, audit events, managed media); @agiworkforce/types (identifier contract, plan and limit helpers, product analytics, provider list); @agiworkforce/client-runtime (device sign-in, workspace policy, connectors, event reader, queue and agent activity); @agiworkforce/client/sync (conversation sync); @agiworkforce/ui (web primitives and provider marks, used by web and by desktop through the hosted web app); @agiworkforce/design-tokens (colours, radii, type; used by web, Chrome, VS Code and in part by mobile); @agiworkforce/i18n (strings for web and mobile, and the VS Code catalogue); the secret redaction code under packages/platform/utils. Rust code shared between the CLI and the protocol crate: apps/cli/src/cloud and crates/agiworkforce-protocol (generated TypeScript for the coding protocol). Separate per app: the Chrome side panel reducer (apps/extension/src/features/side-panel/chat-state.ts), the VS Code local runtime client, the Chrome cloud agent client, the Electron developer session service, the CLI's own state and workspace policy code (Rust), and the mobile streaming client.
not_sure: Nothing was run. The task was read-only, so the guards, tests and builds named in the brief were not run; each check's pass or fail status comes from the brief, not from a run.
The brief's per-app status lines are platform-level only. Which surface has which item is taken from the brief's Unfinished notes, not verified in each app.
Storage for device sign-in codes and tokens (where refresh tokens are kept on each device) was not opened.
The sync route's conflict, tombstone and cursor logic was not read in full; only the lines cited above were opened.

packages/client/client-runtime/src/deviceAuthorization.ts, packages/client/client-runtime/src/workspacePolicy.ts and packages/platform/utils/src/secretRedaction.ts (beyond its first 30 lines) were not read in full.
The approval page and the device approve route (apps/web/app/api/auth/device/approve) exist, but their code was not read.
Package names for packages/platform/utils and packages/contracts/types were taken from import lines, not from package manifests.
Most brief line numbers were not checked; only files in key_files and how_it_works were opened. The brief's error-utils.ts citations were checked and do not exist.
The effect of the mobile feature flags import (apps/mobile/src/i18n/index.ts:7) was not established.
The brief's statements about the Electron main process, the CLI and the Chrome sync code were not checked in code.
The relayed request to test on localhost one surface at a time does not apply to this read-only job; no surface was tested.

guide.what_it_is_for: This area describes where each part of AGI Workforce runs: in the browser, on our servers, in background workers, on the user's computer, in the command-line app, in the editor and Chrome extensions, and on the phone. A person gets one assistant that behaves the same way on each surface, and can choose to keep some work on their own device. Knowing which runtime does what is how an engineer finds the right code, and how a tester tells a real local run from a cloud run.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user uses the cloud chat path. Deep research is paid only: the route comment says free requests are rejected in processRequest (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/route.ts:561-566). Published-artifact connectors need a plan with the artifact_connectors capability (apps/web/lib/services/artifact-connector-gate.ts:26). Cloud code sandboxes need a server flag and the managed-compute private beta (apps/web/lib/e2b/gate.ts:20-28; apps/web/lib/managed-compute-gate.ts:55). Desktop and CLI users work on folders they grant. Developers run the CLI headless or interactively. Phone users can run a model on the phone (Local mode). Scheduled runs, background jobs and indexing run with no user present. The brief shows platform status only, so it does not say which roles are admins.

features.name: Cloud chat answers, streamed
features.use: The web app, the server-rendered pages and the API route handlers send a question to a managed model and stream the answer back as it is written.
how_people_use_it: Open the web app in a browser and type a message in the chat box.
Watch the answer appear word by word.
Stop a long answer by leaving the page or cancelling; the server sees the dropped connection.
how_it_should_work: The answer streams over server-sent events (a one-way live feed over HTTP). Every 2 seconds of silence the server sends a keepalive line so the connection stays open (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/lib/sse-heartbeat.ts:6, :29).
The model route allows up to 300 seconds per request (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/route.ts:161).
If the client drops, the server logs a stream_disconnected event with the bytes sent so far (sse-heartbeat.ts:24-27).
Conversation creation refuses a project that the user does not own or that is archived or deleted (apps/web/app/api/chat/conversations/route.ts:236-240).
Failure: the route returns an error; the brief does not describe a retry for the stream.
features.on_each_app: The brief gives one platform status (done) and no per-app status. Web is the server that every chat goes through. The desktop app shows the hosted web app, so its chat is this same cloud path (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/dispatcher.ts:3242).

features.name: Durable agent runs and deep research
features.use: A long agent turn or a deep research run is handed to a durable workflow, so it keeps going after the browser request has ended. Stuck runs are cleaned up by a reaper.
how_people_use_it: Start a task that needs many steps, or switch on deep research for a question.
Close the tab and come back later; the run continues on the server.
Cancel a run from the chat (the server checks for a cancellation request).
how_it_should_work: A turn starts a workflow run on the queue named cloud-agent-turn (apps/web/lib/workflows/start-cloud-agent-workflow.ts:63; runCloudAgentTurn at :264).
The workflow loops over steps: wait for a device if one is needed, run one invocation, settle the work plan, close the stream (apps/web/lib/workflows/cloud-agent-workflow.ts:69-100).
If a device is asleep the workflow waits up to 60 minutes, then removes the device tools and continues (cloud-agent-workflow.ts:14-16).
A reaper cron finds orphaned runs and ends them (apps/web/app/api/cron/reap-agent-runs/route.ts:23; apps/web/lib/services/cloud-agent-run-reaper.ts:90). It runs on the schedule in vercel.json.
Deep research: a bounded loop of plan, search and fetch rounds, then a cited answer (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/lib/research-loop.ts, fetch step near :2767). Free users are refused.
Failure: a failed run is marked failed and its stream closed (cloud-agent-workflow.ts:55-62).
features.on_each_app: Platform status is done. The server runs these for the web app and for any surface that starts a cloud agent turn. The brief does not give per-app differences.

features.name: Background jobs, schedules, connector sync and indexing
features.use: Work that is not in a request runs on the server: media and file jobs, scheduled runs, search indexing of uploaded documents, and connector sync (which is missing).
how_people_use_it: Upload a document, and it is indexed in the background (no button).
Set up a scheduled run; the scheduler fires it when due.
Users do not start the cron jobs; they run on the schedule in vercel.json.
how_it_should_work: The drain cron runs queued jobs for up to 250 seconds with at most 12 in flight (apps/web/app/api/cron/drain-background-jobs/route.ts:17-18, :35-36). The job registry lists media generation, file purge, data export and email jobs (apps/web/lib/jobs/job-handlers.ts:347-367).
Scheduled runs: the cron processes due runs in waves of 10 within a 55-second budget (apps/web/app/api/cron/run-schedules/route.ts:14-18, :43-63).
Indexing: each uploaded document starts a durable workflow (apps/web/lib/workflows/start-retrieval-index-workflow.ts:32-50). A run that fails to start stays pending and the cron retries it.
Connector sync: no worker found that syncs mail or drive content. Missing.
Failure: a failed drain returns HTTP 500 (drain route:43-49); a failed start is logged and retried.
features.on_each_app: Platform status: done for jobs, schedules and indexing; missing for connector sync. Server-side only, so no per-app differences in code.

features.name: Cloud code sandbox, cloud browser and cloud computer
features.use: Cloud code runs in an isolated remote sandbox. A cloud browser and a cloud virtual computer that an agent can drive were not found in the code.
how_people_use_it: Open a cloud code session (the code workspace) and run code. The sandbox is used only when it is turned on.
Cloud browser and virtual computer: no user path found.
how_it_should_work: The sandbox runs only when the server flag AGI_E2B_EXECUTION is 1 and a sandbox key is set (apps/web/lib/e2b/gate.ts:6-18 and :20-28). The example file ships the flag as 0 (apps/web/.env.example:384).
Refused on purpose when the sandbox has no price: the provisioning code fails closed (apps/web/lib/e2b/runtime.ts:889-899).

Cloud browser and cloud computer: missing. The extension has a computer-use client that calls a cloud agent (apps/extension/src/features/computer-use/cloudAgentClient.ts:1-15), which is not a cloud browser runtime.
Failure: if the sandbox is off, the cloud code session is not opened (apps/web/lib/services/cloud-code-session-open.ts:44).
features.on_each_app: Platform status: partial for the sandbox (off by default), missing for cloud browser and cloud computer. The code session is a web and desktop feature; the brief gives no per-app status.

features.name: Desktop app shell and its local helper
features.use: The desktop app is an Electron window that shows the hosted web app. Its main process runs native services through a dispatcher. It also starts a local helper (the CLI in app-server mode) and can run local MCP tool servers.
how_people_use_it: Open the desktop app; the window loads the hosted web app.
Grant a folder for coding sessions; the app starts the helper for that folder.
Connect a local tool server (MCP) that runs on the machine.
how_it_should_work: The window loads the hosted sign-in host or the hosted app (apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:345, :745; the API base URL must be first-party HTTPS or localhost, apps/desktop/electron/config.ts:46-50).
The dispatcher is the only way renderer calls reach native services (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/dispatcher.ts:3496 file end; commands listed from :3287).
The helper starts with the app-server argument and a folder consent (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/developerSessionService.ts:1453-1458).
MCP servers run as child processes with stdin and stdout (crates/agiworkforce-mcp/src/client.rs:1097).
Failure: a crashed window is reloaded (apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:905-910).
features.on_each_app: Desktop only. Platform status done for all four rows.

features.name: Local commands and their sandbox
features.use: Commands a coding session runs on the user's computer run in a shell or terminal runtime, inside an operating-system sandbox where one exists.
how_people_use_it: In a coding session, the agent proposes a shell command; the user can approve it (a review step can be forced when the turn has untrusted content).
Interactive or long programs run in the terminal runtime.
how_it_should_work: The shell service checks the command against an allow and deny list and refuses a denied program (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/shellService.ts:575-585 area; dispatcher.ts:395-405 for the policy shape).

On macOS the desktop uses the built-in sandbox tool (Seatbelt) at /usr/bin/sandbox-exec; on Linux it uses bubblewrap if installed (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/shellSandbox.ts:189-202; constant at :23).
The CLI detects Seatbelt or bubblewrap (apps/cli/src/sandbox.rs:196-217). Its run_command tool uses the sandbox workspace (apps/cli/src/features/exec/tools/bash/mod.rs:85-100).
Failure: if no sandbox exists the CLI warns that commands run with unrestricted access (apps/cli/src/sandbox.rs:462). The desktop path for that case is not confirmed.
features.on_each_app: Desktop (shellService and shellSandbox) and CLI (sandbox.rs and run_command). The brief gives no per-app status beyond platform done.

features.name: Command-line app
features.use: The CLI runs an interactive terminal screen (a TUI, with a plain line-based fallback) and a headless mode for one-shot or scripted use.
how_people_use_it: Run the CLI with no prompt to start the interactive screen.
Pass a one-off prompt for a single answer.
Use --json for machine-readable output; the line-based mode is chosen with a flag.
how_it_should_work: Without a prompt, the CLI starts the interactive REPL or TUI (apps/cli/src/lib.rs:186; full-screen mode can be turned off at :362).
Headless approval rendering is in apps/cli/src/lib.rs:3112-3118. The brief gives the headless entry as 3115, which is an approvals renderer, not the entry point; the true entry was not confirmed.
Failure: not confirmed in the code read.
features.on_each_app: CLI only. Platform status done.

features.name: On-device model on the phone
features.use: Local mode runs a model on the phone itself (free, no server call). The desktop does not offer this.
how_people_use_it: On the phone, choose Local mode for a chat; the chat then runs on the phone.
On the desktop, the on-device model is refused.
how_it_should_work: The phone runs a local model through the local-llm package (packages/platform/local-llm/src/tier3.ts:26-40; localGenerate at packages/platform/local-llm/src/selector.ts:105).
A conversation is local when its execution mode is local (apps/mobile/app/_layout.tsx:187-196).
The desktop refuses local inference: the shell says models on this Mac are not one of its runtimes, and returns unsupported-platform (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/dispatcher.ts:3242, :3367).
Failure: if the native module is missing, the loader returns null (tier3.ts:26-31).
features.on_each_app: Mobile only. Desktop refuses on-device inference by design.

features.name: Editor and browser extensions
features.use: The VS Code extension runs in the editor's extension host and shows its UI in a webview side panel. The Chrome extension runs a background service worker and content scripts in pages.
how_people_use_it: In VS Code, open the AGI Workforce sidebar.
In Chrome, the extension runs on pages after the user approves the site.
Settings such as the shell approval setting appear in VS Code's settings list (apps/extension-vscode/package.json:74).
how_it_should_work: VS Code registers the sidebar as a webview view with retained context (apps/extension-vscode/src/core/chatSetup.ts:60-63).
The webview content is built in apps/extension-vscode/src/features/sidebar-webview/webviewContent.ts.
The Chrome extension is Manifest V3, with a service worker (apps/extension/manifest.json:39-41) and content scripts on http and https pages at document idle (manifest.json:43-47).
The background worker checks the site allow list before it acts (apps/extension/src/background.ts:200-215).
Failure: the background code throws BrowserSitePermissionRequired when a site is not approved (background.ts:209-215).
features.on_each_app: VS Code extension and Chrome extension, separate code. Platform status done for all four.

features.name: Mobile app and phone-to-desktop relay

how_it_works.detail: A chat message creates or updates a conversation. The server checks the user owns any project it names before saving.

how_it_works.step: 2. The model route decides the path
how_it_works.detail: The model route checks the plan and the request mode. Deep research starts a cloud agent run; ordinary chat streams directly. A free request is refused for deep research.
The model output is transformed into the streaming shape and wrapped with the keepalive layer, so the connection survives quiet periods.

how_it_works.step: 4. A long turn becomes a durable run
how_it_works.detail: The turn is queued on the cloud-agent-turn queue and the workflow runs it. The workflow waits for a device if one is needed, then runs the invocation step.
The workflow step opens a stream, parses the input, and runs the model and tools. Research runs its loop of search and fetch rounds.
After the run ends, the work plan is settled and cost is recorded by outcome.
A cron drains queued background jobs for up to 250 seconds, running up to 12 at once, using the handler registry.

how_it_works.step: 8. Schedules and stuck runs are swept
how_it_works.detail: The schedule cron runs due schedules in waves. The reaper ends orphaned agent runs.

how_it_works.step: 9. Desktop and CLI run local work
how_it_works.detail: The desktop dispatcher receives a command from the window and runs native services. Shell commands go through a policy check and, where present, a sandbox. The CLI does the same for its run_command tool.

how_it_works.step: 10. Phone runs local inference or sends to the cloud
how_it_works.detail: In Local mode a conversation is answered on the phone by the local model package. Otherwise it goes to the cloud route. The desktop refuses local inference.

guide.shared_code: Shared across apps: the server routes and workflows (apps/web) serve the web app, the desktop app's hosted window, the extensions and mobile through the same API. The UI for the chat artifacts is in packages/ui/unified-chat, shared by desktop, web, the Chrome extension and VS Code. Contracts for connectors, billing and artifact security are in packages/contracts/types. The phone and desktop share the device-steps contract in packages/contracts/local-runtime. The protocol types are generated from crates/agiworkforce-protocol. Separate per app: the desktop main process and dispatcher (apps/desktop/electron), the CLI (apps/cli, Rust), the VS Code extension host (apps/extension-vscode), the Chrome service worker and content scripts (apps/extension), the phone app (apps/mobile, with the local model package packages/platform/local-llm), and the relay (services/signaling-server).

things_that_look_wrong.what: The brief's vercel.json line numbers are stale. The real lines: drain-background-jobs is at vercel.json:150 (brief says :110), index-retrieval-documents at :62 (brief :38), reap-agent-runs at :70 (brief :42), run-schedules at :50 (brief :26).
The brief cites apps/desktop/electron/runtime/dispatcher.ts:799 as the local model runtime. That line is a capability reason text; desktop refuses on-device inference.

The brief cites apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:884 for the desktop renderer and config.ts:39 for the hosted URL. main.ts:884 is a screen-capture picker. config.ts:39 is the localhost check. The window load is at main.ts:345 and main.ts:745.
The brief cites apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:1345 for the privileged host. That line is cloud-request telemetry.
The brief cites developerSessionService.ts:686 for the local daemon. That line is a terminal cleanup. The app-server spawn is at :1453-1458.
The brief cites apps/cli/src/lib.rs:3115 for the headless runtime. That line renders pending approvals. The real headless entry was not confirmed.
The web layout is an async server component, which contradicts the brief's claim that the web app runs as a client-side React application.
e2bExecutionEnabled() is true when the key is set alone, unlike the other gates that need the flag. No caller outside gate.ts was found, so it looks unused.
Connectors are globally coming soon, so the artifact connector route refuses every connector. The file also lists thirteen individually released connector IDs, and the artifact gate never uses them.
The artifact iframe combines allow-scripts with allow-same-origin. Safety depends on the sandbox origin being separate from the app origin; this was not verified.
The brief says the CLI runs commands in an OS sandbox by default. The code warns and runs without one when no sandbox tool is found. Which path is the default was not confirmed.

not_sure: Cloud browser (S102.09) and cloud virtual computer (S102.10): no runtime found in the code. Only the extension's cloud agent client was found (apps/extension/src/features/computer-use/cloudAgentClient.ts), which is not a browser or computer runtime. Treated as missing, as the brief says.
Connector sync (S102.28): no worker for mail or drive content was found. The cron at vercel.json:162 refreshes a connector directory; its handler was not opened.
Whether the sandbox is on in production: the brief says it is off unless the flag is set, and the example file ships 0, but production values were not visible.
What the desktop shell does when detectShellSandbox returns none (shellSandbox.ts:189-203): the shell path after that choice was not traced.
Whether the CLI's default sandbox mode is on: sandbox.rs:536-541 bails when no sandbox is found, but which constructor the default path uses was not confirmed.
Scheduled-run and drain behaviour under failure: the handler bodies were only partly read.
The chat stream's exact fallback when a provider fails mid-answer: the route code is large (1535 lines) and only the streaming and research parts were read.
Per-app status: the brief gives only a platform status for each item, so the per-app parts of each feature are based on which code exists, not on the brief.
No builds, tests or servers were run. The task was read-only, so nothing here was executed or verified in a running app.

guide.what_it_is_for: This area is the set of records the product keeps for a person: accounts, devices, chats, memory, projects, files, generated apps, agent runs, connector grants, billing, audit trail, consent and erasure records. It makes sure each kind of record is stored durably, is marked with a data class (for example customer content or audit trail), and is known to the erasure and retention code, so an account or workspace can be exported or deleted correctly. Without it, a deleted account could leave chats, files or credentials behind, and an audit could not show what happened.
guide.who_uses_it: Every signed-in user has records in this area (chats, memory, files, devices). Workspace admins act on the workspace-level records (organization, roles, policy, retention). Paid plans affect billing and credit records (not yet confirmed in code, see not_sure). Developers and the operations team use the classification guard and the retention matrix. The brief gives one status for the whole area ("platform"), so there is no per-app status.

Device refresh tokens are rotated; a replayed token is recognised and treated as a replay, not accepted again.
Empty state, waiting state and failure messages are not established from the code opened.
Limits by plan: not established.

features.name: Audit, consent, data rights and erasure
features.use: Keeps the append-only security audit trail, consent records with the notice version, data-rights requests (access, correction, erasure), legal holds, and the retention sweeps that delete data at its maximum age.
how_people_use_it: Submit a data-rights request (access, correction or erasure); a reference such as DPDP-xxxx is returned.
Give or withdraw consent for a purpose on a surface.
Administrators create or release a legal hold on a workspace.
how_it_should_work: Audit rows cannot be updated or deleted by the app role; a trigger blocks it (migration 0123), and only the owner can purge for retention.
Consent rows record the notice version and the surface.
A retention sweep runs per workspace and is recorded; a hold stops the sweep for that data.
Erasure is driven by the deletion manifest, which lists what each store erases and its maximum age.

how_it_works.step: Person acts in a surface, call reaches an API route
how_it_works.detail: A request such as starting a conversation enters a Next.js route. The conversations route checks that any project belongs to the user, is not archived and is not deleted, before inserting the conversation.

The memory sync route admits eligible memory items, then writes them in one query that returns applied rows or conflicts against the current server version, so a stale device cannot overwrite newer memory.

Connector OAuth state is stored as a hash and the code verifier as encrypted text. Access and refresh tokens go to encrypted columns. API keys are hashed with argon2; lookup uses a short prefix and the hash is checked on use.

how_it_works.step: Sharing and publishing expire or revoke
how_it_works.detail: A share link gets an expires_at computed from the requested days; a link that is revoked or expired is treated as gone. Published pages have no expiry and end only by unpublish.

A consent row is inserted with purpose, granted flag, notice version and surface. A data-rights request gets a reference derived from a hash of its submission token, so a retried submission maps to the same reference.

how_it_works.step: Audit events are written and protected
how_it_works.detail: Security events are inserted into the audit table. A later migration adds a trigger that blocks update and delete for the app role, and allows only the table owner for retention and erasure purges.

how_it_works.step: Each store is classified in the deletion manifest
how_it_works.detail: A map assigns each table a data class (customer content, derived, operational, audit trail or telemetry). The retention matrix combines this with the account and workspace erasure lists and maximum ages. A table not in the map falls back to operational record.
Each turn writes a context manifest row (versions, token counts, entries). The upsert only updates a row whose user matches, so one user cannot overwrite another user's manifest.
Per-workspace retention sweeps run, are recorded, and respect legal holds created and released by admins.
The account endpoint reads the identity, profile, subscription and entitlement and returns one response with the visible name and billing owner.
